topics.question: Basic SOQL SELECT syntax: SELECT field1, field2 FROM Object WHERE condition ORDER BY field LIMIT n
topics.answer: SOQL is SQL-like but operates only on Salesforce objects. Core clauses: SELECT lists the fields to return. FROM specifies the object. WHERE filters records (supports =, !=, <, >, IN, LIKE, AND, OR). ORDER BY sorts results (ASC or DESC). LIMIT caps the number of returned records. Example: SELECT Id, Name, Amount FROM Opportunity WHERE StageName = 'Closed Won' ORDER BY Amount DESC LIMIT 10.

topics.question: SOQL bind variables: using a colon prefix to bind an Apex variable into a SOQL WHERE clause (e.g., WHERE Name = :varName)
topics.answer: Bind variables inject Apex variables directly into inline SOQL using a colon prefix. Example: String targetName = 'Acme'; List<Account> accs = [SELECT Id FROM Account WHERE Name = :targetName]; The variable is resolved at query parse time. This avoids string concatenation (which risks SOQL injection) and is the preferred approach. Works with primitives, IDs, lists, sets, and maps as collections.

topics.question: SOQL LIKE operator syntax: % as multi-character wildcard, _ as single-character wildcard
topics.answer: The LIKE operator enables pattern matching. % matches any sequence of zero or more characters: WHERE Name LIKE 'Acme%' matches 'Acme', 'Acme Corp', 'Acme Industries'. _ matches exactly one character: WHERE Name LIKE 'Acm_' matches 'Acme' but not 'Acmee'. Combine them: LIKE '%Corp%' finds any name containing 'Corp'. LIKE is case-insensitive in Salesforce SOQL.

topics.question: How to write a SOQL query that traverses a parent relationship: SELECT Name, Account.Name FROM Contact
topics.answer: Parent relationship traversal uses dot notation to walk up the relationship chain. For standard relationships: SELECT Id, Name, Account.Name, Account.Owner.Name FROM Contact. For custom lookup fields, use the __r suffix: SELECT Id, My_Parent__r.Name FROM Child__c. You can traverse up to 5 levels deep. This retrieves parent field values without a separate query.

topics.question: How to write a SOQL query that includes child records (sub-select / relationship query): SELECT Id, (SELECT Id FROM Contacts) FROM Account
topics.answer: A subquery retrieves related child records inline using the child relationship name in a nested SELECT inside parentheses: SELECT Id, Name, (SELECT Id, LastName FROM Contacts) FROM Account. Access the results in Apex: for (Contact c : acc.Contacts) {} Standard child relationship names are plural (Contacts, Opportunities). Custom child relationships use the plural API name with __r.

topics.question: Using a List or Set as a bind variable in a SOQL IN clause: WHERE Id IN :idList — the list is evaluated at query parse time
topics.answer: You can bind an Apex collection into a SOQL IN clause for bulk filtering. Example: Set<Id> accountIds = new Set<Id>{'001...', '001...'}; List<Account> accs = [SELECT Id FROM Account WHERE Id IN :accountIds]; The collection is evaluated when the query is parsed. This is the key bulkification pattern — build a Set<Id> from Trigger.new, then query once with WHERE Id IN :idSet instead of looping.

topics.question: SOQL semi-join and anti-join syntax: WHERE Id IN (SELECT AccountId FROM Opportunity) and WHERE Id NOT IN (...)
topics.answer: Semi-join filters parent records that have at least one matching child: WHERE Id IN (SELECT AccountId FROM Opportunity WHERE StageName = 'Closed Won') — returns Accounts with a Closed Won Opportunity. Anti-join: WHERE Id NOT IN (SELECT AccountId FROM Opportunity) — returns Accounts with no Opportunities at all. These avoid loading child records into Apex memory just to filter parents.

topics.question: SOQL aggregate functions: COUNT(), SUM(), AVG(), MIN(), MAX() — syntax and what they return (AggregateResult objects)
topics.answer: Aggregate functions compute summary values across records. COUNT(Id): number of records. SUM(Amount): total of a numeric field. AVG(Amount): average. MIN/MAX: lowest/highest values. When using aggregates, SOQL returns List<AggregateResult> instead of List<SObject>. Access values with: Integer total = (Integer) result.get('expr0'); Use an alias for clarity: SELECT SUM(Amount) totalAmt FROM Opportunity — then get('totalAmt').

topics.question: GROUP BY clause in SOQL: how to group aggregate results and access AggregateResult fields using get('fieldName')
topics.answer: GROUP BY aggregates results by distinct values of a field. Example: SELECT StageName, COUNT(Id) cnt FROM Opportunity GROUP BY StageName. Returns one AggregateResult per unique StageName. Access values: result.get('StageName'), result.get('cnt'). Filter grouped results with HAVING (like SQL HAVING): GROUP BY StageName HAVING COUNT(Id) > 5. Every field in SELECT must be either in GROUP BY or wrapped in an aggregate function.

topics.question: What causes a QueryException in Apex: assigning a SOQL query that returns 0 rows or more than 1 row to a single sObject variable
topics.answer: When you assign a SOQL query to a single sObject variable (not a List), Salesforce expects exactly one result. Example: Account a = [SELECT Id FROM Account WHERE Name = 'Acme']; If the query returns zero records: QueryException: List has no rows for assignment. If it returns more than one: QueryException: List has more than 1 row. Always use a List when 0 or multiple results are possible, and check list size before accessing index 0.

topics.question: SOQL WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED: inline enforcement of field- and object-level security in a SOQL query; throws an exception if the running user lacks access to a referenced field
topics.answer: Adding WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED to a SOQL query applies the running user's FLS and object-level security inline: [SELECT Id, Name, AnnualRevenue FROM Account WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED]. If the user lacks read access to AnnualRevenue, Salesforce throws an InvalidFieldFaultException immediately. This is a concise, one-keyword approach to FLS enforcement. Limitation: it only applies to fields in SELECT (not WHERE), and throws rather than silently filtering.

topics.question: Dynamic SOQL using Database.query(String): when to use it and SOQL injection risk mitigation using String.escapeSingleQuotes()
topics.answer: Database.query(String soqlString) executes a SOQL query built at runtime as a string. Use it when object names, field names, or filter conditions vary dynamically. Risk: concatenating user input directly creates SOQL injection vulnerabilities — a malicious user can alter the query logic. Mitigation: wrap user-supplied strings with String.escapeSingleQuotes(userInput) before concatenation to escape single quotes, preventing them from being interpreted as SOQL syntax.

topics.question: When to use SOSL versus SOQL: SOSL for full-text search across multiple objects, SOQL for structured queries on known fields
topics.answer: SOQL is best when you know the object and fields to query and need structured, field-specific filtering (e.g., WHERE Status = 'Open'). SOSL performs full-text searches across multiple objects simultaneously using Salesforce's search index — ideal for search bars or finding a name/email value across Contacts, Leads, and Accounts at once. SOSL is faster for text searches; SOQL is more precise for field-level filtering.

topics.question: SOSL syntax: FIND 'searchTerm' IN SearchGroup RETURNING Object(fields) — SearchGroup options: ALL FIELDS, NAME FIELDS, EMAIL FIELDS, PHONE FIELDS
topics.answer: SOSL syntax: FIND {searchTerm} IN SearchGroup RETURNING Object1(field1, field2), Object2(field1). SearchGroup narrows which field types are searched: ALL FIELDS (default — all indexed fields), NAME FIELDS (Name fields only), EMAIL FIELDS (email fields only), PHONE FIELDS (phone fields only). Example: FIND {Acme*} IN NAME FIELDS RETURNING Account(Id, Name), Contact(Id, FirstName, LastName).

topics.question: What SOSL returns: a List<List<SObject>> where each inner list corresponds to one object specified in the RETURNING clause
topics.answer: SOSL returns a List<List<SObject>>. Each inner list contains matching records for one object from the RETURNING clause, in the same order they were listed. Example: List<List<SObject>> results = [FIND {Acme} IN NAME FIELDS RETURNING Account, Contact]; List<Account> accounts = (List<Account>) results[0]; List<Contact> contacts = (List<Contact>) results[1]; Cast each inner list to the appropriate sObject type before working with it.

topics.question: DML statements in Apex: insert, update, delete, undelete, upsert, merge — syntax and what each operation does
topics.answer: insert: creates new records. update: modifies existing records (requires Id). delete: soft-deletes records to the Recycle Bin. undelete: restores records from the Recycle Bin. upsert: inserts if no match found, updates if a match exists (on Id or External ID). merge: combines up to 3 records into one master record and reassigns related child records. All statements accept a single sObject or a List<sObject> for bulk operations.

topics.question: upsert DML behavior: how it decides to insert versus update (by Id or by External ID field), syntax with optional external ID field argument
topics.answer: upsert myRecord MyExternalId__c; — if you provide an External ID field, Salesforce searches for a record with a matching value. If found, it updates; if not found, it inserts. Without specifying an External ID field, upsert uses the record's Id: a populated Id means update; a null Id means insert. This avoids a pre-query to check existence and is essential for integration data loads.

topics.question: Database class DML methods (Database.insert, Database.update, etc.) versus DML statements: allOrNone parameter and partial success behavior
topics.answer: DML statements (insert list;) are all-or-nothing: if one record fails, the entire operation rolls back. Database class methods (Database.insert(list, false)) allow partial success when allOrNone is false — successful records commit even if some fail. The return value is a list of Database.SaveResult objects with per-record success/error info. Use this when you want to process as many records as possible and handle individual failures gracefully.

topics.question: Database.SaveResult and Database.UpsertResult: how to check isSuccess() and getErrors() when using Database methods with allOrNone = false
topics.answer: Database.insert(list, false) returns List<Database.SaveResult>. For each result: result.isSuccess() returns true if saved; result.getErrors() returns List<Database.Error> with failure details. Database.UpsertResult also has isCreated() — true if inserted, false if updated. Pattern: for (Database.SaveResult sr : results) { if (!sr.isSuccess()) { for (Database.Error e : sr.getErrors()) { System.debug(e.getMessage()); } } }

objectives.title: Given a scenario, follow best practices to write Apex classes and triggers.

topics.question: Apex trigger syntax: trigger TriggerName on Object (trigger events) { ... } — valid trigger events (before insert, after insert, before update, after update, before delete, after delete, after undelete)
topics.answer: Syntax: trigger MyTrigger on Account (before insert, after update) {} Valid events: before insert, after insert, before update, after update, before delete, after delete, after undelete. Before triggers fire before the database write — ideal for field validation and derivation without extra DML. After triggers fire after the write — ideal for operations on related records. after undelete fires when records are restored from the Recycle Bin.

topics.question: Trigger record context variables: Trigger.new, Trigger.old, Trigger.newMap, Trigger.oldMap
topics.answer: Trigger.new: List<SObject> of records in their new (post-change) state. Available on insert, update, undelete. Trigger.old: List<SObject> of records in their previous state. Available on update and delete. Trigger.newMap: Map<Id, SObject> version of Trigger.new for O(1) lookup by Id. Trigger.oldMap: Map<Id, SObject> version of Trigger.old. Maps are essential for comparing old vs. new values inside loops without additional SOQL queries.

topics.question: Trigger event context variables: Trigger.isInsert, Trigger.isUpdate, Trigger.isDelete, Trigger.isBefore, Trigger.isAfter, Trigger.isUndelete, Trigger.size, Trigger.isExecuting
topics.answer: Boolean flags that identify which event and phase fired the trigger. Trigger.isInsert/isUpdate/isDelete/isUndelete: which DML operation. Trigger.isBefore/isAfter: which phase. Combine them: if (Trigger.isAfter && Trigger.isUpdate) {} Trigger.size: count of records in the current invocation. Trigger.isExecuting: true when the context is a trigger (vs. anonymous Apex or a controller) — useful in shared utility methods.

topics.question: Trigger.new records in a before trigger are mutable (field values can be changed directly); Trigger.new records in an after trigger are read-only
topics.answer: In a before trigger, records in Trigger.new have not yet been committed. You can modify field values directly — myRecord.Status__c = 'Active' — and those changes persist to the database without an explicit DML update call. In an after trigger, records are already saved; Trigger.new is read-only, and attempting to modify fields throws a runtime error. Any related-record updates in after triggers require explicit DML.

topics.question: Which trigger context variables are available for each DML event: Trigger.old and Trigger.oldMap are null on insert; Trigger.new and Trigger.newMap are null on delete
topics.answer: On insert: only Trigger.new and Trigger.newMap are available (no previous state). On update: all four context variables are available. On delete: only Trigger.old and Trigger.oldMap are available (records being removed have no new state). On undelete: only Trigger.new is available. Accessing a null context variable causes a NullPointerException — always guard with the appropriate isInsert/isDelete checks.

topics.question: Bulkification principle: why Apex code must process records in collections rather than one at a time to avoid hitting governor limits
topics.answer: A single trigger invocation can handle up to 200 records at a time. If your trigger performs one SOQL query per record, 200 records = 200 queries — instantly exceeding the 100-query limit. Bulkification means writing code that works on the entire batch of records at once: collect all relevant IDs, issue one query, process results using a Map. This approach scales to any record volume without hitting limits.

topics.question: Anti-pattern: performing SOQL or DML inside a for loop and why it causes governor limit violations
topics.answer: This is the most common Apex mistake: for (Account a : Trigger.new) { Contact c = [SELECT Id FROM Contact WHERE AccountId = :a.Id LIMIT 1]; /* BAD */ } With 100 records this fires 100 queries, hitting the limit instantly. The correct approach: collect all IDs before the loop, query once with WHERE Id IN :idSet, store results in a Map, then iterate the Map inside the loop. The same applies to DML — accumulate records in a list, then insert/update after the loop.

topics.question: Using Maps to avoid SOQL inside loops: pattern of building a Map<Id, SObject> from a SOQL query before the loop
topics.answer: Pattern: Set<Id> accIds = Trigger.newMap.keySet(); Map<Id, Account> accMap = new Map<Id, Account>([SELECT Id, Name FROM Account WHERE Id IN :accIds]); Then inside your loop: Account acc = accMap.get(someId); This queries all needed records in a single SOQL call and provides O(1) lookup by Id during iteration. This is the single most important Apex bulkification technique to know for the exam.

topics.question: One-trigger-per-object best practice: having a single trigger per object with context-specific method dispatch
topics.answer: Salesforce allows multiple triggers on the same object, but their execution order is not guaranteed. This leads to unpredictable behavior when two triggers interact. Best practice: one trigger per object that routes to a handler class based on context. Example: if (Trigger.isBefore && Trigger.isInsert) { AccountTriggerHandler.onBeforeInsert(Trigger.new); } This makes execution order explicit and the code testable independently.

topics.question: Trigger handler pattern: moving logic out of the trigger body into a dedicated Apex class to improve testability and maintainability
topics.answer: The trigger body should contain only routing logic — nothing else. All business logic lives in a dedicated handler class (e.g., AccountTriggerHandler) with static methods for each context (onBeforeInsert, onAfterUpdate, etc.). Benefits: the handler class can be unit-tested independently of the trigger, logic is easier to read and maintain, and you can selectively disable logic via custom metadata without touching the trigger itself.

objectives.title: Given a scenario, understand governor limits and their implications on Apex transactions.

topics.question: Total number of SOQL queries per synchronous Apex transaction: 100; per asynchronous transaction: 200
topics.answer: Each Apex transaction has a hard cap on SOQL queries: 100 for synchronous (real-time) contexts and 200 for asynchronous contexts (Batch, Future, Queueable, Scheduled). Every inline SOQL query — regardless of how many records it returns — counts as one query. Exceeding it throws a LimitException that cannot be caught. Use Limits.getQueries() / Limits.getLimitQueries() to check consumption at runtime.

topics.question: Total number of DML statements per Apex transaction: 150 (synchronous and asynchronous)
topics.answer: You can issue at most 150 DML statements per transaction regardless of whether it is synchronous or asynchronous. Each call to insert(list), update(list), etc. counts as one statement no matter how many records are in the list. Accumulate all records into lists and perform DML once after loops to stay within this limit. This is the same in both sync and async contexts.

topics.question: Total heap size per Apex transaction: 6 MB synchronous, 12 MB asynchronous
topics.answer: The heap is memory used for Apex variables and collections during a transaction. Sync: 6 MB. Async: 12 MB. Large SOQL results loaded into Lists, deeply nested objects, or string concatenations in loops can quickly exhaust heap. Mitigation: use SOQL for-loops (200-record internal batching), avoid storing full record lists when only a few fields are needed, and clear large collections with = null or new List<>() when done.

topics.question: Maximum CPU time per Apex transaction: 10,000 ms synchronous, 60,000 ms asynchronous
topics.answer: CPU time measures pure Apex code execution on Salesforce servers — not time spent waiting for queries or callouts. Sync: 10  seconds. Complex nested loops, repeated string operations, and recursive algorithms are common culprits. Check with Limits.getCpuTime() / Limits.getLimitCpuTime(). Moving expensive processing to async Apex gives you 6x more CPU budget.

topics.question: Maximum number of records returned by a single SOQL query: 50,000
topics.answer: A single SOQL query can return at most 50,000 records. Returning more throws a QueryException. If you need to process more than 50,000 records, use Batch Apex (start() with a QueryLocator supports up to 50 million records) or SOQL for-loops with chunked processing. For data exports, use the Bulk API. Never try to load 50,000+ records into a List in a single transaction.

topics.question: Maximum number of records processed by a single DML statement: 10,000
topics.answer: A single DML operation can process at most 10,000 records. If your List contains more than 10,000 sObjects, a DmlException is thrown. Use Batch Apex to process records in chunks of up to 2,000 per execute() call for large-scale data operations. In most trigger contexts, the 200-record-per-invocation batch size from Salesforce makes this a non-issue, but large data load jobs must account for it.

topics.question: How asynchronous Apex (Batch, Queueable, Future, Scheduled) has higher governor limits than synchronous Apex and when to choose it
topics.answer: Async Apex runs in a separate transaction from the trigger, giving it higher limits: 200 SOQL queries, 12 MB heap, 60 s CPU. Choose async when: processing is too resource-intensive for a synchronous transaction, you need to make HTTP callouts (required for @future and Queueable), or you need to process large record volumes (Batch Apex). The trade-off is that async runs later — not immediately in the user's session.

topics.question: @future method constraints: must be static void, parameters must be primitive types or collections of primitives (no sObjects), and the maximum number of future calls per transaction (50)
topics.answer: @future(callout=true) methods run asynchronously in a separate transaction. Constraints: must be static, return type must be void, parameters can only be primitives (String, Integer, Boolean, etc.) or collections of primitives — no sObjects (because the record state could change between invocation and execution). Max 50 future calls per synchronous transaction. Pass Set<Id> or List<Id> to reference records instead of the sObjects themselves.

topics.question: Scheduled Apex: implementing Schedulable interface, execute(SchedulableContext sc) signature, and using System.schedule() to schedule execution
topics.answer: Implement Schedulable: public class MySchedule implements Schedulable { public void execute(SchedulableContext sc) { /* logic */ } } Schedule it: System.schedule('Job Name', '0 0 2 * * ?', new MySchedule()); The cron expression is a standard 6-part format (seconds, minutes, hours, day-of-month, month, day-of-week). You can also schedule via Setup > Apex Classes > Schedule Apex. A scheduled job commonly invokes Batch Apex inside execute() to handle large volumes.

topics.question: Queueable Apex: implementing Queueable interface, System.enqueueJob(), chaining jobs, and the limit of 1 child job per execution context in synchronous context
topics.answer: Implement Queueable: public class MyJob implements Queueable { public void execute(QueueableContext ctx) { /* logic */ } } Enqueue: System.enqueueJob(new MyJob()); Queueable is more powerful than @future: it accepts sObject parameters, provides an AsyncApexJob ID for monitoring, and supports chaining (enqueue another job from within execute()). Limit: you can enqueue only 1 child job from within a synchronous context; from async contexts the limit is higher.

topics.question: Batch Apex: implementing Database.Batchable with start(), execute(), finish() methods and the default batch size (200 records) and maximum batch size (2,000)
topics.answer: Implement Database.Batchable<SObject>: start() returns the scope (QueryLocator or Iterable); execute() receives a chunk of records and processes them; finish() runs once after all batches complete. Default batch size: 200 records per execute() call. Max: 2,000. Invoke: Database.executeBatch(new MyBatch(), 200). Each execute() call is a separate transaction with its own full set of governor limits.

topics.question: Database.QueryLocator versus Iterable<SObject> as the return type of the start() method in Batch Apex: QueryLocator allows up to 50 million records, Iterable gives developer-controlled iteration
topics.answer: QueryLocator: return Database.getQueryLocator('SELECT Id FROM Account'); — uses an efficient server-side cursor, supports up to 50 million records, and bypasses the 50,000-record SOQL limit for batch. This is the standard choice. Iterable<SObject>: return myCustomList; — you control the iteration source, but are limited by normal SOQL limits (50,000 records) and heap. Use Iterable only when you need a custom data source that SOQL cannot express.

topics.question: Database.Stateful interface in Batch Apex: preserves instance variable values across execute() batches, allowing accumulation of results
topics.answer: By default, each execute() call gets a fresh instance of the batch class — instance variables reset between batches. Implementing Database.Stateful alongside Database.Batchable preserves instance variable values across all execute() calls. Use this to accumulate totals, error counts, or records to process in finish(). Warning: stateful batches consume more resources — keep instance variables small and avoid storing large collections in state.

objectives.title: Describe the relationship between Apex transactions, the save order of execution, and the potential for recursion and/or cascading.

topics.question: What constitutes a single Apex transaction (one execution context) and how governor limits are shared across all operations within that context
topics.answer: A single Apex transaction is one continuous execution context — from the first line of code invoked (a trigger fires, a REST call starts) until execution completes or rolls back. All governor limit counters (SOQL, DML, CPU time, heap) are shared across everything within that one context. Multiple triggers, helper class calls, and Flow invocations all draw from the same shared pool — there is no per-class or per-trigger limit reset.

topics.question: Salesforce save order of execution: before triggers → system validation → custom validation → after triggers → assignment rules → workflow rules → before/after triggers fired by workflow field updates → escalation rules → process builders/flows → roll-ups
topics.answer: When a DML operation occurs, Salesforce follows a strict order: (1) Load original record. (2) Apply new values. (3) Run before triggers. (4) System validation (required fields, unique, format). (5) Custom validation rules. (6) Save to DB (no commit yet). (7) Run after triggers. (8) Assignment rules. (9) Auto-response rules. (10) Workflow rules (field updates re-run steps 3-7). (11) Escalation rules. (12) Record-triggered flows. (13) Roll-up summaries recalculated. (14) Final commit.

topics.question: How an Apex trigger that performs DML causes another trigger to fire (cascading triggers) and how to reason about transaction boundaries
topics.answer: If an Account after-trigger performs an insert on Contact, that insert fires Contact triggers — all within the same transaction, sharing the same governor limits. The limits consumed by the Account trigger context carry over into the Contact trigger context. Deeply cascading triggers can quickly exhaust SOQL and DML limits. Design triggers to be aware of what operations they initiate and whether those will cascade further.

topics.question: How workflow field updates can re-fire triggers and the risk of infinite recursion; using a static Boolean flag to prevent trigger re-execution
topics.answer: Workflow rules with field updates cause triggers to re-fire after completing (as part of the save order). If that trigger action triggers another workflow field update, triggers fire again — potentially creating an infinite loop. Prevention: use a static Boolean flag in a helper class. Example: if (!MyTriggerHelper.hasRun) { MyTriggerHelper.hasRun = true; /* logic */ } The static flag persists for the duration of the transaction, blocking re-entry.

topics.question: Savepoints and Database.setSavepoint() / Database.rollback(): how partial rollback works within a transaction
topics.answer: A savepoint marks a point in the transaction to which you can roll back. Savepoint sp = Database.setSavepoint(); — captures the current state. Database.rollback(sp); — undoes all DML performed after the savepoint was set, without rolling back the entire transaction. Use this for partial rollback scenarios — try an operation, and if it fails, roll back only that portion while keeping earlier work. Note: governor limit counts (SOQL, DML) are NOT restored after a rollback.

objectives.title: Implement exception handling in Apex, including custom exceptions as needed.

topics.question: try-catch-finally syntax in Apex: block structure, catching specific exception types, and finally block guarantee of execution
topics.answer: Syntax: try { /* risky code */ } catch (DmlException e) { /* handle DML errors */ } catch (Exception e) { /* catch-all */ } finally { /* always runs */ } The try block contains code that may throw. catch blocks handle specific exception types — catch the most specific types first. finally always executes whether or not an exception was thrown — use it for cleanup (closing connections, logging). You can have multiple catch blocks but only one finally.

topics.question: Common built-in Apex exception types: DmlException, QueryException, NullPointerException, LimitException, SObjectException, MathException
topics.answer: DmlException: thrown when a DML operation fails (required field missing, duplicate rule violation). QueryException: SOQL returns 0 or 2+ rows when assigned to a single sObject. NullPointerException: method or field access on a null reference. LimitException: governor limit exceeded — CANNOT be caught, only prevented. SObjectException: invalid field access on an sObject (field not in SELECT clause). MathException: division by zero or other arithmetic errors.

topics.question: Declaring a custom exception class in Apex: class MyException extends Exception {} and how to throw and catch it
topics.answer: Custom exceptions extend the Exception class: public class InsufficientFundsException extends Exception {} You get constructors for free: throw new InsufficientFundsException('Balance too low'); or throw new InsufficientFundsException(); with setMessage(). Catch it specifically: catch (InsufficientFundsException e) {} Custom exceptions make error handling more expressive and let callers distinguish your domain errors from generic system exceptions.

topics.question: Exception getMessage(), getCause(), getTypeName(), getStackTraceString() methods for logging and debugging
topics.answer: All Apex exceptions inherit these methods. getMessage(): human-readable error message. getCause(): inner exception that caused this one (for wrapped exceptions). getTypeName(): returns the exception class name as a String (e.g., 'System.DmlException'). getStackTraceString(): full call stack at the point the exception was thrown — invaluable in debug logs. Use these in catch blocks to log meaningful, actionable error details.

topics.question: DmlException methods: getNumDml(), getDmlMessage(index), getDmlType(index), getDmlId(index) — used to inspect which records failed in a DML operation
topics.answer: When a DML statement fails (not using Database.insert partial success), it throws a DmlException with per-record detail. getNumDml(): how many records failed. getDmlMessage(i): error message for the i-th failed record. getDmlType(i): the StatusCode enum value for the failure type (e.g., REQUIRED_FIELD_MISSING). getDmlId(i): the ID of the failing record. Use these in catch blocks to log precise failure details per record rather than a single generic message.

topics.question: LimitException: thrown when a governor limit is exceeded and cannot be caught — only preventable, not recoverable
topics.answer: LimitException is thrown when any governor limit is breached (SOQL queries, DML statements, CPU time, heap, etc.). Unlike all other Apex exceptions, it CANNOT be caught with a try-catch block — Salesforce terminates the transaction immediately when it is thrown. The only approach is prevention: monitor limits with the Limits class, bulkify code, move heavy work to async Apex, and avoid patterns that grow limit consumption proportionally with record count.

topics.question: AuraHandledException: a special exception class used in @AuraEnabled methods to surface a user-friendly error message to LWC/Aura rather than a generic Apex exception
topics.answer: When an @AuraEnabled method throws a standard exception, LWC receives a generic 'An internal server error has occurred' message — not the actual details. To surface a specific, readable message to the user, throw: throw new AuraHandledException('Custom message here'); The LWC catch block then receives this message in error.body.message. This is the correct pattern for all user-facing error handling in LWC-to-Apex integrations.

objectives.title: Given a scenario, use declarative functionality and Apex together to automate business logic.

topics.question: @InvocableMethod annotation: how to expose an Apex method to Flow, and required method signature (public static, List parameter, optional List return)
topics.answer: @InvocableMethod makes an Apex method callable from Flow, Process Builder, and Agentforce. Required signature: public static List<OutputType> methodName(List<InputType> inputs) — must be public static, accept a single List parameter (Salesforce passes a list even for one record), and return a List or void. Add metadata: @InvocableMethod(label='My Action' description='Does something'). Input/output types must use @InvocableVariable on their properties.

topics.question: @InvocableVariable annotation: marking instance variables of the input/output class so they appear as inputs/outputs in Flow Builder
topics.answer: @InvocableVariable marks properties of your input/output wrapper class so they appear as named inputs/outputs in Flow Builder's action configuration. Example: public class InputWrapper { @InvocableVariable(label='Account Name' required=true) public String accountName; } Properties without @InvocableVariable are invisible to Flow. Mark variables required=true to force Flow builders to provide a value — omitting it causes a runtime error.

topics.question: Scenario: choosing between a before-save Flow and an Apex trigger for a field derivation — before-save Flow is preferred when no DML on other objects is needed
topics.answer: If you need to derive or update a field on the triggering record based on its own values (no related record queries or DML on other objects), a before-save Record-Triggered Flow is the best choice. It runs fast (no extra DML), requires no code or tests, and admins can maintain it. Use an Apex trigger when the logic requires: querying related records, performing DML on other objects, calling async Apex, or implementing complex algorithms that would be impractical in Flow.

topics.question: How to call a Flow from Apex using Flow.Interview: creating an instance, setting input variables, starting the interview, and getting output variables
topics.answer: Pattern: Map<String, Object> inputs = new Map<String, Object>{'inputVar' => 'value'}; Flow.Interview myFlow = Flow.Interview.createInterview('My_Flow_API_Name', inputs); myFlow.start(); Object output = myFlow.getVariableValue('outputVar'); The flow runs synchronously in the same transaction. The flow API name uses underscores not spaces. Use this when you need to trigger a complex declarative flow based on conditions determined programmatically in Apex.

objectives.title: Given a scenario, prevent user interface and data access security vulnerabilities.

topics.question: with sharing versus without sharing in Apex classes: enforces or ignores the running user's sharing rules; inherited sharing keyword
topics.answer: with sharing: Apex enforces the running user's record-level sharing rules — they only see records they have access to. without sharing: Apex ignores sharing rules and operates on all records regardless of user (runs in system mode). inherited sharing: the class inherits the sharing context of its caller — if called from a with sharing context, it runs with sharing. Always declare sharing explicitly. Classes with no keyword default to without sharing — dangerous if unintentional.

topics.question: Object-level CRUD enforcement in Apex: checking Schema.SObjectType.isCreateable(), isReadable(), isUpdateable(), isDeletable() before performing DML or returning data
topics.answer: with sharing enforces row-level access but NOT CRUD (object-level). You must check object permissions explicitly before DML: if (!Schema.SObjectType.Account.isCreateable()) { throw new AuraHandledException('No create access'); } isReadable() — before querying. isCreateable() — before insert. isUpdateable() — before update. isDeletable() — before delete. Alternatively, Security.stripInaccessible() and WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED are modern, cleaner approaches.

topics.question: Schema.SObjectType.fields.isAccessible() / isCreateable() / isUpdateable() for programmatic field-level security checks before DML or returning data
topics.answer: Field-level security (FLS) restricts access to individual fields per profile/permission set. Check FLS in Apex: Schema.DescribeFieldResult dfr = Schema.SObjectType.Account.fields.Name.getDescribe(); if (!dfr.isAccessible()) { /* hide field */ } isAccessible() — before reading/returning. isCreateable() — before insert. isUpdateable() — before update. This is verbose but precise. Security.stripInaccessible() is a cleaner bulk alternative that removes inaccessible fields from a list of records at once.

topics.question: stripInaccessible() method: removes fields from sObject records that the running user cannot read or create, preventing field exposure in server responses
topics.answer: SObjectAccessDecision decision = Security.stripInaccessible(AccessType.READABLE, recordList); List<Account> cleaned = (List<Account>) decision.getRecords(); This removes any fields from the records that the running user cannot access under FLS for the given AccessType (READABLE, CREATABLE, UPDATABLE, UPSERTABLE). It is the cleanest way to bulk-enforce FLS on SOQL results before returning data to an LWC or Visualforce page.

topics.question: WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED in SOQL: inline enforcement of field- and object-level security
topics.answer: Adding WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED to a SOQL query applies FLS and CRUD checks inline: [SELECT Id, Name, AnnualRevenue FROM Account WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED]. If the running user lacks read access to AnnualRevenue, Salesforce throws an exception immediately — the query fails rather than silently returning the field. This is a one-keyword approach to FLS enforcement. Limitation: only applies to fields in SELECT, not WHERE conditions.

topics.question: SOQL injection: how user-supplied strings in dynamic SOQL can alter query logic, and how String.escapeSingleQuotes() prevents it
topics.answer: If a user enters: ' OR Name != '' AND '1' = '1 and you concatenate it directly into a dynamic SOQL string, they can bypass your WHERE clause and access all records. String.escapeSingleQuotes() escapes single quotes in the user input so they are treated as literal characters, not SOQL syntax. Example: String safe = String.escapeSingleQuotes(userInput); Always sanitize any user-supplied or external input used in dynamic SOQL.

topics.question: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) in Visualforce: how {! formula} output is HTML-encoded by default and when HTMLENCODE() is needed for explicit encoding
topics.answer: In Visualforce, the {! expression } merge syntax automatically HTML-encodes output, converting < to < and > to > to prevent script injection. However, if you build strings manually or use JSENCODE() for JavaScript contexts, you must explicitly call HTMLENCODE(myField). Never use <apex:outputText escape='false'> with user-supplied data — it bypasses encoding entirely and opens XSS vulnerabilities.

topics.question: CSRF protection in Salesforce: Visualforce automatically includes an anti-CSRF token on form submissions; developers must not disable it
topics.answer: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) tricks authenticated users into unknowingly submitting malicious requests. Visualforce automatically generates and validates a hidden anti-CSRF token on every form submission, tied to the user's session. Developers must not disable this protection. For custom REST endpoints, validate requests using Connected App OAuth flows rather than relying on session cookies, which are susceptible to CSRF.

topics.question: How LWC enforces Lightning Locker and what it prevents: direct DOM access across namespaces, access to unsupported global objects
topics.answer: Lightning Locker wraps each LWC in a secure sandbox: (1) Components cannot access the DOM of components in different namespaces. (2) Global browser objects like document and window are proxied — some methods are blocked. (3) eval() and other dangerous JavaScript patterns are disallowed. (4) Components can only access their own shadow DOM via this.template.querySelector(). This prevents malicious components from stealing data from your org's components.

objectives.title: Given a scenario, display and use custom user interface components, including Lightning components, Flow, and Visualforce.

topics.question: Standard Controller in Visualforce: automatic binding to an sObject record, standard actions (save, cancel, edit, delete), and how to access the record in the controller
topics.answer: The Standard Controller (standardController='Account') automatically loads the record whose Id is in the URL and binds it to the page. Standard actions — save, cancel, edit, delete, view — are available for free via action='{!save}'. In a controller extension, access the record: Account acc = (Account) stdController.getRecord(). Fields referenced on the page are automatically populated; unreferenced fields must be explicitly queried.

topics.question: Custom Controller versus Controller Extension in Visualforce: when to replace Standard Controller (custom controller) versus augment it (extension)
topics.answer: Controller Extension: augments the Standard Controller. The page keeps standardController='Account' and adds extensions='MyExtension'. The extension constructor receives the Standard Controller as a parameter — keeping standard save, cancel, etc. Use this to add methods or properties while preserving standard behavior. Custom Controller: replaces the Standard Controller entirely with controller='MyController'. Use when standard behavior doesn't fit or there is no single record context.

topics.question: Standard List Controller in Visualforce: iterating over a list of records with <apex:pageBlockTable> or <apex:repeat>, pagination methods (next, previous, first, last)
topics.answer: Use recordSetVar='records' with standardController='Account' to get a Standard List Controller that auto-paginates Account records. Iterate: <apex:pageBlockTable value='{!records}' var='acc'>. Pagination actions: {!previous}, {!next}, {!first}, {!last} — call these as action attributes on buttons. hasNext and hasPrevious are Boolean properties to conditionally show pagination buttons. Default page size is 20, configurable with pageSize.

topics.question: Visualforce page access: how to expose a VF page as a custom tab, button, or link; the rendering context (Standard Controller vs. custom controller)
topics.answer: VF pages can be surfaced as: (1) Custom Tabs — add the VF page as a tab in App Manager; no record context, needs a custom controller. (2) Custom Buttons/Links — on an object layout; the Standard Controller auto-provides the record Id. (3) Override standard actions (New, Edit, View) on an object. The rendering context determines controller type: record buttons use Standard Controller; standalone tools need custom controllers.

topics.question: Visualforce view state: what it is (serialized controller state sent to the client between requests), its size limit (170 KB), and how to reduce it using transient keyword
topics.answer: Visualforce uses partial page refresh (AJAX). Between requests, the entire controller state (all instance variables) is serialized to a hidden form field — the view state. Size limit: 170 KB. Exceeding it causes an error. Reduce view state by: marking variables transient (excluded from serialization), using pagination to avoid loading all records at once, and querying fresh on each request instead of storing data in instance variables.

topics.question: apex:actionSupport: fires a controller action on DOM events
topics.answer: <apex:actionSupport> is nested inside another component and fires a controller action when a specified DOM event occurs. Example: <apex:inputText value='{!myField}'><apex:actionSupport event='onchange' action='{!handleChange}' reRender='resultPanel'/></apex:inputText> — whenever the user changes the text field, handleChange() is called and resultPanel is re-rendered. Common events: onchange, onclick, onkeyup. This eliminates the need for explicit submit buttons for simple interactions.

topics.question: apex:actionPoller: fires a controller action on a time interval
topics.answer: <apex:actionPoller action='{!refreshData}' interval='30' reRender='dataPanel'/> — calls refreshData() every 30 seconds and re-renders dataPanel. Minimum interval is 5 seconds. Use for dashboards or monitoring pages that need periodic data refresh. Warning: the poller continues firing even if the user is idle, generating unnecessary server load. Always provide a way for the user to stop it.

topics.question: apex:actionFunction: calls a controller method from JavaScript
topics.answer: <apex:actionFunction name='callApex' action='{!serverMethod}' reRender='panel'/> generates a JavaScript function named callApex() that you can call from any JavaScript on the page. Pass parameters using <apex:param> nested inside. Calling callApex() from a button's onclick invokes the server-side serverMethod() and re-renders panel. This bridges custom JavaScript UI interactions with Apex server logic in Visualforce pages.

topics.question: How to add a Lightning Web Component to a Lightning App Page, Record Page, or Home Page using the Lightning App Builder
topics.answer: In the .js-meta.xml file, configure the targets: <targets><target>lightning__AppPage</target><target>lightning__RecordPage</target><target>lightning__HomePage</target></targets>. Deploy the component to your org. In Setup, go to Lightning App Builder, open an App/Record/Home page, and drag the component from the left panel onto the canvas. Save and Activate. Components without the correct target declared will not appear in App Builder.

topics.question: target configurations for LWC: which targets allow a component to appear in App Builder (lightning__AppPage, lightning__RecordPage, lightning__HomePage) and which require specific configuration
topics.answer: The .js-meta.xml targets determine where a component can be placed. lightning__AppPage: standalone app pages. lightning__RecordPage: record detail pages (grants @api recordId automatically). lightning__HomePage: home page. lightning__FlowScreen: usable inside a Flow screen. lightning__UtilityBar and lightning__GlobalAction are also valid targets. Each target can have its own <targetConfig> block for design-time properties exposed to App Builder.

topics.question: How to embed a Flow in a Visualforce page using <flow:interview> component and pass input variables
topics.answer: <flow:interview name='My_Flow_API_Name' finishLocation='{!finishPage}'><apex:param name='inputVariableName' value='{!apexProperty}'/></flow:interview> The name attribute references the Flow's API name (underscores, not spaces). Pass input variables using nested <apex:param> elements — the name must match the Flow's input variable name exactly. After the flow finishes, finishLocation redirects the user. The Flow runs in the VF page's user context.

objectives.title: Describe the use cases and best practices for Lightning Web Components, including the framework, benefits, and events.

topics.question: LWC file structure: the mandatory .html, .js, and .js-meta.xml files, and the purpose of the .css and .svg files
topics.answer: Mandatory: componentName.html (template markup), componentName.js (controller/logic), componentName.js-meta.xml (metadata: targets, API version, visibility). Optional: componentName.css (scoped styles — automatically applied only to this component's shadow DOM, no class conflicts), componentName.svg (custom icon shown in App Builder). All files must share the exact same name as their containing folder.

topics.question: LWC template syntax: rendering with {expression}, conditional rendering with lwc:if / lwc:elseif / lwc:else, and list rendering with for:each and for:item
topics.answer:
Data binding:

{greeting}

renders the greeting property. Conditionals (API 59+): (replaces older if:true/if:false). Lists: — the key attribute is required on the immediate child for efficient DOM diffing.

topics.question: LWC component lifecycle hooks: connectedCallback, disconnectedCallback, renderedCallback, errorCallback — when each fires
topics.answer: connectedCallback(): fires when the component is inserted into the DOM — use for initial data fetching, event subscriptions, and listener setup. disconnectedCallback(): fires when removed from the DOM — use for cleanup (unsubscribe, remove listeners to avoid memory leaks). renderedCallback(): fires after every render cycle — use sparingly; avoid state changes here to prevent infinite render loops. errorCallback(error, stack): fires when a child component throws an error — use to display fallback UI.

topics.question: @api decorator: exposes a property or method as public so parent components or App Builder can set it
topics.answer: @api is imported from 'lwc'. Applying it to a property makes it public-facing: <c-child-component my-prop='hello'></c-child-component> sets the @api myProp on the child. Applying it to a method lets a parent call childComponent.myMethod() after getting a reference via querySelector. @api properties are reactive — updating them from the parent triggers re-rendering. Never mutate an @api property from inside the child component.

topics.question: LWC parent-to-child communication via @api properties
topics.answer: Parents pass data down to children using HTML attributes that map to @api properties. In the child: @api title; In the parent template: <c-child-component title={parentTitle}></c-child-component>. When parentTitle changes in the parent, the child's title property updates and re-renders automatically. This is one-way data flow — parent to child. Children should fire events to request changes from the parent rather than mutating @api properties directly.

topics.question: @wire decorator: declaratively call an Apex method or wire adapter to fetch data, the reactive property/function pattern, and how to handle the data and error properties
topics.answer: @wire connects a component property or function to a data source reactively. Property pattern: @wire(getAccountList) accounts; — accounts has .data and .error. Function pattern: @wire(getRecord, {recordId: '$recordId', fields: FIELDS}) wiredRecord({data, error}) { this.record = data; } The $ prefix on '$recordId' makes it reactive — when recordId changes, the wire re-fetches automatically. Wire is ideal for data loaded when the component mounts.

topics.question: Calling an Apex method imperatively versus with @wire: when to use each — imperative for conditional/user-triggered calls, @wire for automatic reactive calls
topics.answer: @wire: best for data you always need on load and that should auto-refresh when reactive properties change. It is declarative and automatic. Imperative: import getAccounts from '@salesforce/apex/MyController.getAccounts'; then getAccounts({param}).then(result => {}).catch(err => {}); Use imperatively when: the call happens on a button click, depends on runtime conditions, or involves DML (methods with DML cannot be wired with cacheable=true).

topics.question: JavaScript getter properties in LWC: using get keyword to derive computed values without storing redundant state, and how they behave reactively
topics.answer: A getter is defined with the get keyword: get fullName() { return this.firstName + ' ' + this.lastName; } In the template: {fullName}. Getters are recalculated every time the template renders — they are not cached. Because they reference other reactive properties (firstName, lastName), any change to those triggers re-rendering and the getter returns the updated value. Avoid storing derived values in separate tracked variables — use getters instead.

topics.question: Custom events in LWC: dispatching with this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('eventname', { detail: payload })) and listening with oneventname in parent template
topics.answer: In the child component: this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('selected', { detail: { id: this.recordId } })); In the parent template: <c-child-component onselected={handleSelected}></c-child-component> In parent JS: handleSelected(event) { const id = event.detail.id; } Event names must be lowercase. The on prefix is added in the template listener attribute. The detail object can hold any serializable payload.

topics.question: LWC child-to-parent communication via custom events
topics.answer: Children communicate upward by dispatching custom events that the parent listens to. The parent registers a listener via the on[eventname] attribute in its template. This maintains one-way data flow: parent pushes data down via @api properties; child pushes notifications up via events. The parent then decides what to do — update its own state, call Apex, or pass updated data back down to the child.

topics.question: Event bubbling and propagation in LWC: bubbles and composed options on CustomEvent and their effect on whether the event crosses shadow DOM boundaries
topics.answer: By default, a CustomEvent does not bubble and stays within the dispatching component. bubbles: true — the event bubbles up through the DOM tree (ancestors can listen). composed: true — the event crosses shadow DOM boundaries (visible outside the component's shadow root). Combined: new CustomEvent('myevent', { bubbles: true, composed: true }) allows the event to propagate across the whole page. Use sparingly — prefer explicit parent listeners for clarity.

topics.question: LWC sibling or cross-hierarchy communication via Lightning Message Service (LMS) or shared parent
topics.answer: Siblings without a shared direct parent cannot communicate easily via events. Two approaches: (1) Shared parent — both siblings are children of the same parent; one fires an event, the parent catches it and updates the other child's @api property. (2) Lightning Message Service (LMS) — a pub/sub channel that works across any components on the page regardless of DOM hierarchy. LMS is the recommended pattern for truly decoupled cross-component communication.

topics.question: Lightning Message Service (LMS): MessageChannel, publish(), subscribe(), unsubscribe() — cross-component communication across DOM hierarchies
topics.answer: LMS uses a named MessageChannel (create a .messageChannel-meta.xml file). Publisher: import { publish, MessageContext } from 'lightning/messageService'; import MY_CHANNEL from '@salesforce/messageChannel/My_Channel__c'; @wire(MessageContext) msgContext; publish(this.msgContext, MY_CHANNEL, { payload }); Subscriber: this.subscription = subscribe(this.msgContext, MY_CHANNEL, (msg) => { this.handleMessage(msg); }); Always unsubscribe in disconnectedCallback. Works across VF pages, Aura, and LWC.

topics.question: Accessing DOM elements in LWC using this.template.querySelector() and this.template.querySelectorAll(): the shadow boundary means you can only query within the component's own shadow DOM
topics.answer: Use this.template.querySelector('c-child') or this.template.querySelector('[data-id="myEl"]') to find elements inside your component's own shadow DOM. querySelectorAll() returns all matches as a NodeList. You can only reach your own shadow DOM — never a child component's internal elements. Never use document.querySelector() in LWC — it bypasses the shadow boundary and violates Locker Service. Access child methods via @api-decorated methods instead.

topics.question: LWC slots: default slot for projecting content from parent into child component, and named slots (<slot name='header'>) for multiple projection points
topics.answer:
Slots allow a parent to inject markup into a child component's template. Default slot: in child template: ; in parent:

Injected content

. Named slot: in child: ; in parent:

Header here

. Slots enable flexible, composable UI patterns where the outer container controls layout and the inner child provides structure.

topics.question: lightning-record-form, lightning-record-edit-form, and lightning-record-view-form: differences and when to use each
topics.answer: lightning-record-form: simplest option — auto-generates a full view or edit form based on page layout or field list. Least customizable. lightning-record-view-form: displays fields read-only with full layout control using lightning-output-field. lightning-record-edit-form: editable form with lightning-input-field components; you control submission logic and validation. Use record-form for quick prototypes; use view/edit-form when you need custom field layout, conditional rendering, or custom submit handling.

topics.question: Using getRecord and getFieldValue wire adapters from lightning/uiRecordApi in LWC
topics.answer: import { getRecord, getFieldValue } from 'lightning/uiRecordApi'; import NAME_FIELD from '@salesforce/schema/Contact.Name'; @wire(getRecord, { recordId: '$recordId', fields: [NAME_FIELD] }) contact; get name() { return getFieldValue(this.contact.data, NAME_FIELD); } getRecord reactively fetches record data via the UI API (respects FLS). getFieldValue safely extracts the field value. Using schema imports (not string literals) provides compile-time field reference validation.

topics.question: createRecord, updateRecord, deleteRecord from lightning/uiRecordApi: imperative DML from LWC without calling Apex
topics.answer: import { createRecord, updateRecord, deleteRecord } from 'lightning/uiRecordApi'; createRecord({ apiName: 'Contact', fields: { LastName: 'Smith' } }).then(record => {}); updateRecord({ fields: { Id: this.recordId, LastName: 'Jones' } }); deleteRecord(this.recordId); These methods use the UI API, respect FLS and sharing, and automatically refresh wired data on mutations. Use them for simple CRUD operations on standard objects with no complex business logic — no Apex needed.

topics.question: CurrentPageReference wire adapter: subscribing to the current page's reference object to read URL parameters and page state in LWC
topics.answer: import { CurrentPageReference } from 'lightning/navigation'; @wire(CurrentPageReference) pageRef; The pageRef object includes: type (page type), attributes (recordId, objectApiName, etc.), and state (URL query parameters). Use getters to extract values: get recordId() { return this.pageRef?.attributes?.recordId; } This is the correct way to read URL parameters in LWC. It is reactive — changes to the URL automatically update the wired value.

topics.question: NavigationMixin in LWC: importing NavigationMixin from lightning/navigation, applying it to a class, and calling this[NavigationMixin.Navigate]() to navigate to pages, records, or named pages
topics.answer: import { NavigationMixin } from 'lightning/navigation'; export default class MyComp extends NavigationMixin(LightningElement) { navigateToRecord() { this[NavigationMixin.Navigate]({ type: 'standard__recordPage', attributes: { recordId: this.recordId, actionName: 'view' } }); } } Common page types: standard__recordPage, standard__objectPage, standard__namedPage, standard__webPage. Always prefer NavigationMixin over hard-coded URL strings.

topics.question: @track decorator: legacy reactive decorator (now largely redundant since all properties are reactive by default for primitive reassignment)
topics.answer: In early LWC (API 39 and below), @track was required to make properties reactive. Since Spring '20 (API 39+), all class properties are reactive by default for primitive reassignments and shallow object/array changes. @track is still relevant for deep reactivity on nested object mutations — e.g., mutating this.obj.nestedProp without reassigning the whole object. In modern LWC, reassign the entire object or array to trigger reactivity instead of relying on @track.

objectives.title: Given a scenario, implement Apex to work with various types of page components, including Lightning components, Flow, and Agentforce.

topics.question: @AuraEnabled annotation: required to expose an Apex method to LWC or Aura components; cacheable=true enables client-side caching and is required for @wire
topics.answer: @AuraEnabled makes an Apex method callable from LWC and Aura components. Without it, the method is invisible to the UI layer. cacheable=true stores the result client-side and allows the method to be used with @wire. Cached results are served without a server round-trip for identical parameters. Key requirement: cacheable=true methods cannot perform DML. Methods with DML must use @AuraEnabled without cacheable and be called imperatively.

topics.question: Restrictions of @AuraEnabled(cacheable=true): method cannot perform DML; attempting DML throws an exception
topics.answer: When you mark a method @AuraEnabled(cacheable=true), it is strictly read-only. Any DML operation (insert, update, delete, upsert) inside the method throws: 'System.AuraHandledException: Read access is not allowed'. Solution: separate data-fetch methods (cacheable=true, used with @wire) from data-mutation methods (@AuraEnabled without cacheable, called imperatively on button click). This is a very common exam scenario.

topics.question: How to handle Apex exceptions in LWC: catching errors in .catch() on imperative calls and from the error property in @wire responses
topics.answer: Imperative: getAccounts().then(data => { this.accounts = data; }).catch(error => { this.error = error.body.message; }); @wire function pattern: @wire(getRecord, {recordId: '$recordId', fields: FIELDS}) wiredRecord({data, error}) { if (error) { this.errorMsg = error.body.message; } } error.body.message holds the user-facing message. Always handle both data and error paths — components that only handle the happy path show blank UI on server failures.

topics.question: Visualforce Apex controller: how a custom controller method is invoked from the page using action attributes and how data bindings work with controller properties
topics.answer: In VF, action attributes call controller methods: <apex:commandButton action='{!saveRecord}' value='Save'/>. The method must be public and return a PageReference or null (null re-renders the current page). Data bindings link page components to controller properties: <apex:inputText value='{!myProperty}'/> — the binding is two-way, so user input updates the Apex property on postback. Properties must have public getter/setter methods (or use {get; set;} auto-properties).

topics.question: ApexPages.addMessage() and ApexPages.Message: how to surface error/info messages on a Visualforce page from an Apex controller method
topics.answer: To display messages on a VF page: ApexPages.addMessage(new ApexPages.Message(ApexPages.Severity.ERROR, 'Something went wrong')); The VF page must include <apex:pageMessages/> or <apex:messages/> to render these. Severity options: INFO, CONFIRM, WARNING, ERROR — each renders with different styling. Call addMessage() in your controller action to show validation errors or success notifications without a redirect.

topics.question: PageReference class in Visualforce Apex controllers: constructing a PageReference and using redirect for post-action navigation
topics.answer: A controller action method returns a PageReference to redirect after the action, or null to re-render the current page. PageReference to a VF page: return new PageReference('/apex/MyPage'); PageReference to a record: return new PageReference('/' + recordId); For external URLs: PageReference ref = new PageReference('https://example.com'); ref.setRedirect(true); return ref; setRedirect(true) forces a full browser redirect (HTTP 302) instead of a server-side forward.

topics.question: How to expose Apex to Agentforce agent actions via @InvocableMethod and how agent invocations count against governor limits
topics.answer: Apex methods annotated with @InvocableMethod automatically become available as Agentforce agent actions — no additional configuration is required beyond making them accessible. When Agentforce invokes an @InvocableMethod, it runs in a standard Apex execution context subject to all normal governor limits (SOQL, DML, CPU, heap). Agent invocations are not exempt from limits — design invocable methods to be efficient and bulkified like any other Apex code.

objectives.title: Write and execute tests for triggers, controllers, classes, and flows using various sources of test data.

topics.question: @isTest annotation: marks a class or method as a test, excluded from production code coverage calculation and not deployed
topics.answer: @isTest on a class marks it as a test class — its lines are excluded from code coverage calculations and it is not deployed to production as executable code. @isTest on an individual method makes it a runnable test method. Test classes cannot be instantiated from non-test code. Best practice: one test class per production class or trigger, named with a 'Test' suffix (e.g., AccountTriggerHandlerTest).

topics.question: Minimum test coverage requirement for deploying Apex to production: 75% code coverage across all Apex classes and triggers
topics.answer: Salesforce requires at least 75% code coverage across all Apex classes and triggers in the org (not per individual class) to deploy to production. Each individual trigger must have at least 1% coverage. Meeting 75% is the minimum — aim for 90%+ to ensure quality. Coverage is measured on executable lines only. Tests run automatically during deployment — if coverage drops below 75%, the deployment fails.

topics.question: How code coverage is calculated: the percentage of Apex lines executed during test runs versus total executable lines; comments and blank lines do not count
topics.answer: Coverage = (lines executed by tests / total executable lines) x 100. Executable lines include: method calls, assignments, conditionals, loop iterations, and DML. Non-executable lines (comments, blank lines, { and } braces) do not count. A line is covered if any test method causes that line to execute. Assertions are not required for coverage but are required for test quality — coverage without assertions is worthless.

topics.question: System.assertEquals(), System.assertNotEquals(), System.assert(): proper assertion usage in Apex tests and the optional message parameter
topics.answer: System.assertEquals(expected, actual, 'optional message'): passes if expected == actual; throws AssertException with the message if not. System.assertNotEquals(notExpected, actual, 'message'): passes if values differ. System.assert(condition, 'message'): passes if condition is true. Always assert meaningful outcomes — not just that no exception was thrown. The optional message parameter tells you what was expected when a test fails, saving debugging time.

topics.question: Why Apex tests cannot access real org data by default (SeeAllData=false) and the risk of using @isTest(SeeAllData=true)
topics.answer: By default, test methods run in an isolated data context — only data created within the test is visible. This ensures tests are deterministic and don't depend on whatever data happens to be in the org. @isTest(SeeAllData=true) allows tests to read real org data, but this is dangerous: tests break when data changes, they may modify real records, and they violate test isolation. Avoid SeeAllData=true except for the rare cases where certain standard objects don't support DML in tests.

topics.question: @TestSetup annotation: shared setup method that runs once before all test methods in a class; data is rolled back and re-created for each test method
topics.answer: @TestSetup marks a static void method that runs once before any test method executes. It creates shared test data available to all test methods. After each test method completes, the data is rolled back, and before the next test method starts, the @TestSetup data is restored to its original state. This avoids duplicating setup code across test methods while maintaining test isolation between individual tests.

topics.question: Test data factory pattern: a separate @isTest utility class with static methods for creating test records consistently across multiple test classes
topics.answer: Instead of duplicating test record creation in every test class, create a dedicated @isTest class (e.g., TestDataFactory) with static helper methods: public static Account createAccount(String name) { Account a = new Account(Name=name); insert a; return a; } Any test class calls these methods. Benefits: consistent test data, a single place to update when object fields change, and reduced duplication across the test suite.

topics.question: Test.startTest() and Test.stopTest(): resets governor limits for the test code in between and forces asynchronous operations to complete synchronously
topics.answer: Test.startTest() resets all governor limit counters — SOQL, DML, CPU — giving the code under test a clean slate separate from setup. Test.stopTest() marks the end of the test scope and forces any async operations (future methods, queueable jobs, batch jobs enqueued between startTest and stopTest) to complete synchronously before execution continues. Always wrap the code being tested — not setup or assertion code — between these two calls.

topics.question: Testing asynchronous Apex (@future, Queueable, Batch): wrapping enqueue/start calls between Test.startTest() and Test.stopTest() to force execution
topics.answer: Async Apex does not execute during test runs unless forced. Pattern: Test.startTest(); Database.executeBatch(new MyBatch()); Test.stopTest(); // batch runs synchronously here System.assertEquals(expectedCount, actualCount); At Test.stopTest(), Salesforce runs all async jobs enqueued during the test — @future methods, queueable jobs, batch start/execute/finish — synchronously, enabling you to assert on results immediately after stopTest.

topics.question: System.runAs(user): runs the enclosed block of test code as the specified user to test sharing rules, permission sets, and user-context-specific logic
topics.answer: System.runAs(testUser) { /* code runs as testUser */ } Use this to verify that with sharing classes correctly restrict records, that permission sets grant the right access, or that user-context-dependent logic works correctly. Create a test user in setup, assign the relevant profile and permission sets, then use runAs to simulate their session. runAs does NOT change governor limits or bypass system permissions for DML on most setup objects.

topics.question: Testing a Visualforce page controller: using ApexPages.StandardController and ApexPages.currentPage() setup in the test method
topics.answer: Setup in the test: PageReference pageRef = Page.MyVFPage; Test.setCurrentPage(pageRef); pageRef.getParameters().put('id', testRecord.Id); ApexPages.StandardController sc = new ApexPages.StandardController(testRecord); MyControllerExtension ext = new MyControllerExtension(sc); ext.myMethod(); System.assertEquals(expectedValue, ext.myProperty); Test.setCurrentPage() is required so the controller can read URL parameters via ApexPages.currentPage().getParameters().

topics.question: Test.setMock(): how to mock HTTP callouts in tests using HttpCalloutMock interface and StaticResourceCalloutMock
topics.answer: Apex tests cannot make real HTTP callouts — Salesforce blocks them for test determinism. Implement HttpCalloutMock: global class MockResponse implements HttpCalloutMock { public HTTPResponse respond(HTTPRequest req) { HTTPResponse res = new HTTPResponse(); res.setBody('{"key":"value"}'); res.setStatusCode(200); return res; } } In the test: Test.setMock(HttpCalloutMock.class, new MockResponse()); StaticResourceCalloutMock is a built-in alternative that uses a static resource file as the response body.

topics.question: Test.isRunningTest(): returns true when Apex is executing in a test context; used to conditionally bypass logic that cannot run in tests (e.g., callouts without a mock)
topics.answer: Test.isRunningTest() returns true when the executing code runs inside a test context. Use it sparingly to skip code paths impossible to test: if (!Test.isRunningTest()) { makeCallout(); } This means that code path has zero coverage. A better pattern is always to use Test.setMock() to mock callouts rather than bypassing the logic. Reserve Test.isRunningTest() only for truly untestable platform behaviors.

topics.question: Flow testing using the FlowTestCoverage API or running flow tests in the Salesforce CLI: what constitutes coverage for a Flow
topics.answer: Flows require coverage for deployment like Apex. Coverage can be achieved by: (1) Running flow interviews from Apex tests — triggering record DML that fires a record-triggered flow, or using Flow.Interview to invoke an autolaunched flow directly. (2) Using Flow Test coverage in Flow Builder — define test scenarios with input values and expected outcomes and run them. SF CLI: sf apex run test also executes flow tests. A flow is covered when its test scenarios execute and verify at least one logical path.

objectives.title: Given a scenario, know how and when to use the Salesforce Developer tools such as Salesforce DX, Salesforce CLI, and Developer Console.

topics.question: Developer Console capabilities: log inspector, query editor, Apex execution, checkpoint inspector
topics.answer: The Developer Console is a browser-based IDE. Key features: Log Inspector — view and filter debug logs with stack trace and execution tree views. Query Editor — run SOQL and SOSL queries interactively and see results in a grid. Execute Anonymous — run ad-hoc Apex code without saving it as a class. Checkpoint Inspector — view heap dumps (variable snapshots) at checkpoint lines. Test Runner — execute and view results for Apex test classes.

topics.question: Developer Console limitations: no version control, not recommended for team projects
topics.answer: The Developer Console is useful for quick debugging and ad-hoc queries but has significant limitations: no version control integration, no collaboration features, can struggle with large files or long logs, and has no syntax highlighting parity with modern editors. For any team project, use VS Code with the Salesforce Extension Pack, which integrates with Git and provides a full, modern IDE experience.

topics.question: VS Code with Salesforce Extensions: the recommended development environment for modern Salesforce development
topics.answer: VS Code with the Salesforce Extension Pack is Salesforce's recommended IDE. It provides: IntelliSense for Apex, SOQL, and LWC. Integrated Salesforce CLI commands. Source control via Git. Scratch org management. Local deployment and retrieval of metadata. Apex test runner with inline coverage highlighting. It replaces the Developer Console for serious development and enables Salesforce DX-based workflows with version control.

topics.question: Salesforce DX project structure: sfdx-project.json, force-app directory, and source format versus metadata API format
topics.answer: A Salesforce DX project has: sfdx-project.json — config defining the project name, API version, and package directories. force-app/main/default/ — the default package directory with organized subdirectories per metadata type (classes/, triggers/, lwc/, flows/, etc.). Source format splits metadata into smaller, readable files (one .field-meta.xml per field) unlike the metadata API format which bundles everything into large XML files. Source format is far better for Git diffs and code review.

topics.question: Scratch orgs: short-lived developer orgs created from a project definition file, used for isolated feature development and CI/CD pipelines
topics.answer: Scratch orgs are temporary Salesforce orgs (max 30 days) created from a scratch org definition JSON file that specifies features, settings, and org preferences. They start completely clean — no production data — perfect for isolated feature development (one scratch org per developer per feature). They integrate natively with CI/CD: create a scratch org, deploy code, run tests, then discard it. This ensures repeatable, environment-independent builds.

topics.question: Salesforce CLI (sf / sfdx) commands: sf org login, sf project deploy start, sf apex run test, sf data query — primary command-line interface for org operations
topics.answer: The Salesforce CLI is the command-line tool for all org operations. Key commands: sf org login web — authenticate to an org via browser. sf project deploy start --source-dir force-app — deploy source to the connected org. sf apex run test --class-names MyTest — run specific test classes and see results. sf data query --query 'SELECT Id FROM Account' — execute SOQL. sf org create scratch -f config/scratch-def.json — create a scratch org. These commands are the backbone of CI/CD pipelines.

objectives.title: Describe how to approach debugging system issues and monitoring flows, performance, asynchronous, and batch jobs.

topics.question: System.debug() and log levels: how to write debug statements at different levels and how to read the log to find a specific statement
topics.answer: System.debug('message') logs at DEBUG level by default. Specify level: System.debug(LoggingLevel.WARN, 'message'). In a debug log, search for 'USER_DEBUG' to find your statements. Log line format: timestamp|event|level|line|message. Use meaningful prefixes (e.g., System.debug('>>> AccountId: ' + accId)) to quickly locate entries in long logs. The Developer Console's Log Inspector can filter by event type to reduce noise.

topics.question: Debug logs in Salesforce: how to set up a trace flag for a user, the log levels (NONE, ERROR, WARN, INFO, DEBUG, FINE, FINER, FINEST), and where to view logs
topics.answer: To capture debug logs: Setup > Debug Logs > New. Set the traced entity (user, Apex class, trigger, etc.) and expiry time. Log levels from least to most verbose: NONE, ERROR, WARN, INFO, DEBUG, FINE, FINER, FINEST. Higher levels capture more detail but generate larger logs (up to 20 MB per log). Logs are stored for 24 hours. View them in Setup > Debug Logs, Developer Console (Logs tab), or VS Code.

topics.question: Checkpoints in the Developer Console: how to set a checkpoint on a line of Apex code to capture a heap dump for variable inspection
topics.answer: In Developer Console, open an Apex class and click the gutter next to a line number to set a checkpoint (max 5 at a time). Execute the code that triggers that line. After execution, go to Checkpoint Inspector to view the heap dump — a full snapshot of all variable values at that point. This is invaluable for debugging complex state issues where System.debug alone isn't sufficient. Checkpoints have no effect on production code behavior.

topics.question: Flow debugging with the Debug button in Flow Builder: step-through execution, inspecting variable values at each element
topics.answer: Flow Builder has a built-in debugger: click Debug, set input variable values, and choose whether to roll back data changes after the debug run. The debugger steps through each flow element one at a time, showing the path taken and the value of every variable at each step. This is the primary tool for diagnosing Flow errors and logic issues — you can see exactly which decision branch was taken and what value caused it.

topics.question: Paused Flow Interviews (Setup > Paused Flow Interviews): where to view and resume or delete screen flows that a user has paused
topics.answer: Screen Flows can include a Pause element that saves the flow state and allows users to resume later. Paused interviews are stored and visible in Setup > Paused Flow Interviews.
