Admins can view all paused interviews, see which user paused them and when, and either resume or delete them. This is also where you look when a flow appears stuck — the interview may have paused waiting for user action rather than failing.

topics.question: Apex Jobs UI (Setup > Apex Jobs): monitoring status of Batch Apex, Queueable, Scheduled, and Future jobs — fields: Status, JobType, MethodName, TotalJobItems, NumberOfErrors
topics.answer: Setup > Apex Jobs shows a log of all asynchronous Apex jobs. Key fields: Status (Queued, Processing, Completed, Failed, Aborted). JobType (BatchApex, Queueable, Future, ScheduledApex). MethodName: the class/method that was invoked. TotalJobItems: number of batches processed. NumberOfErrors: batches that failed. Use this to monitor batch job progress, spot failures, and diagnose performance issues with async jobs.

topics.question: Scheduled Jobs UI (Setup > Scheduled Jobs): viewing and aborting scheduled Apex jobs, and using CronTrigger / CronJobDetail objects in SOQL to query them
topics.answer: Setup > Scheduled Jobs lists all currently scheduled Apex jobs with their next fire time, created by, and status. You can abort a scheduled job from this UI. Programmatically, query scheduled jobs using SOQL: SELECT Id, CronExpression, NextFireTime FROM CronTrigger. Join with CronJobDetail for the job name: SELECT Id, CronJobDetail.Name FROM CronTrigger. Use System.abortJob(cronTriggerId) to cancel a job from Apex.

objectives.title: Describe the environments, requirements, and process for deploying code and associated configurations.

topics.question: Deployment environments in Salesforce: Production, Full Sandbox, Partial Copy Sandbox, Developer Sandbox, Developer Pro Sandbox — and their differences
topics.answer: Production: the live org with real data. Full Sandbox: exact copy of production including all data — most expensive, refreshes monthly. Partial Copy Sandbox: copy of metadata plus a configurable subset of data — refreshes every 5 days. Developer Sandbox: metadata only (no data), 200 MB storage — refreshes daily, cheapest, most orgs have many. Developer Pro Sandbox: metadata only, 1 GB storage — refreshes daily, good for larger development teams. All sandboxes use sandbox.salesforce.com login.

topics.question: Sandbox refresh: copying production (or another sandbox) data/metadata into a sandbox, and the fact that a refresh resets the sandbox to the source org's current state
topics.answer: A sandbox refresh overwrites the sandbox completely with a fresh copy of the source org (usually production). All customizations made in the sandbox since the last refresh are lost. The refresh resets the sandbox to match the source org's metadata — and data in the case of Full or Partial Copy sandboxes. Refresh frequency varies by sandbox type: Developer/Dev Pro can refresh daily, Partial Copy every 5 days, Full monthly.

topics.question: Change Sets: Outbound Change Sets in the source org, Inbound Change Sets in the target org, and the requirement to upload and then deploy
topics.answer: Change Sets are a point-and-click deployment mechanism between connected orgs. Create an Outbound Change Set in the source org (e.g., a sandbox), add metadata components to it, and upload it to the target org. In the target org, the Inbound Change Set appears and must be validated then deployed. Change Sets are one-directional, do not support version control, and can only move between orgs that are connected via a Deployment Connection in Setup.

topics.question: Package.xml (manifest file): how to specify metadata components for retrieval or deployment, component name and member syntax
topics.answer: package.xml is the manifest file used with the Metadata API and Salesforce CLI to specify which metadata components to retrieve or deploy. Structure: <types><members>MyClass</members><name>ApexClass</name></types>. Use <members>*</members> to retrieve all components of a type. The name element uses the metadata type name (ApexClass, CustomObject, Flow, etc.). This file drives sf project retrieve start and sf project deploy start commands.

topics.question: Metadata API deployment using sf project deploy start: what gets included, how to specify components, and the --test-level flag options
topics.answer: sf project deploy start --source-dir force-app deploys all source in the directory. Use --metadata ApexClass:MyClass to deploy specific components. The --test-level flag controls which tests run during deployment: NoTestRun (sandbox only), RunSpecifiedTests, RunLocalTests (all tests not from managed packages — default for production), RunAllTestsInOrg. The deployment fails if tests fail or coverage drops below 75% in production.

topics.question: Test level options for production deployments: RunLocalTests, RunAllTestsInOrg, RunSpecifiedTests — and which is the default for production
topics.answer: RunLocalTests: runs all tests in the org that are not part of installed managed packages — this is the DEFAULT for production deployments. RunAllTestsInOrg: runs every test including those from managed packages — slower but most thorough. RunSpecifiedTests: runs only tests you explicitly list — useful when you know exactly which tests cover your code. NoTestRun: only allowed in sandboxes. Production always requires tests and 75% coverage regardless of the test level chosen.

topics.question: Destructive changes: how to delete metadata from a target org using destructiveChanges.xml or destructiveChangesPre.xml alongside a deployment
topics.answer: To delete metadata from a target org, include a destructiveChanges.xml file alongside your package.xml in a deployment. destructiveChanges.xml deletes components AFTER the deployment completes. destructiveChangesPre.xml deletes components BEFORE the deployment (use when the components to be deleted conflict with new code being deployed). The XML format is the same as package.xml — list the component type and API name. The deployment package.xml can be empty if you are only deleting.

topics.question: Unlocked packages versus Change Sets: version-controlled, testable, and promotable packaging model versus the traditional point-and-click approach
topics.answer: Change Sets are manual, point-and-click, non-versioned, and have no built-in test execution before upload. Unlocked Packages are part of the Salesforce DX model: they are version-controlled via Git, tested as part of CI/CD pipelines, have a versioned install history, and can be installed across any org. Unlocked packages support dependency management and give you fine-grained control over what metadata is packaged. They are the modern, recommended approach for complex deployments.

topics.question: Managed versus unmanaged packages: unmanaged packages allow full code visibility and are not upgradeable; managed packages lock code, support versioning, and are distributed via AppExchange
topics.answer: Unmanaged packages: all Apex code and metadata are visible and editable after installation. There is no upgrade path — you reinstall from scratch for updates. Ideal for open-source templates and one-time installs. Managed packages: Apex code is obfuscated (not visible), have a namespace prefix, support version upgrades, and can be listed on AppExchange. Managed packages lock you into a public API contract — once global, always global. ISVs use managed packages for commercial products.

objectives.title: Given a scenario, identify the boundaries of declarative customization and the use cases for programmatic customization.

topics.question: A business requires real-time complex calculations on record save that involve iterating over multiple child records and updating a set of fields conditionally. Which tool should be used?
topics.answer: An Apex trigger (or Apex class invoked by a trigger) is required. Flow Builder cannot iterate over large sets of child records with conditional field updates in a single performant transaction. Apex handles bulkification natively, respects governor limits, and executes synchronously on record save.

topics.question: Which categories of logic can be fully implemented with declarative tools (Flow Builder, formula fields, validation rules) without writing any code?
topics.answer: Declarative tools cover: field calculations (formula fields), data validation (validation rules), single/multi-record updates (record-triggered Flows), cross-object field updates (Flow Get/Update Records), approval routing, scheduled automation, screen-guided processes (Screen Flows), and simple callouts via Flow HTTP actions. Basically, anything that does not require looping over thousands of records, complex data structures, or custom UI rendering.

topics.question: What types of requirements typically exceed Flow Builder's declarative capabilities and require Apex?
topics.answer: Requirements that exceed Flow: processing hundreds of thousands of records in batch jobs, complex recursive algorithms, custom REST/SOAP integrations with multi-step authentication, generating binary files (PDF, CSV), calling unsupported HTTP methods, implementing custom Visualforce controllers, and handling complex exception management with rollback logic.

topics.question: When is an Apex batch class required rather than a scheduled Flow to process large volumes of records?
topics.answer: Apex Batch is needed when the record volume exceeds Flow's per-transaction limits (50,000 record collection cap in Flow) or when you need chunked processing with configurable batch sizes, sophisticated error handling per chunk, or complex multi-object logic that would hit Flow governor limits. Scheduled Flows work well for smaller, simpler sets but are not designed for millions of records.

topics.question: A business requirement calls for generating a formatted PDF document from Salesforce record data. Does Salesforce provide a native declarative solution for this, or is code/AppExchange required?
topics.answer: Salesforce has no native declarative PDF generation tool. The options are: (1) a Visualforce page rendered as PDF using Apex, or (2) an AppExchange managed package (e.g., Conga Composer, Nintex DocGen). For a no-code approach, an AppExchange solution is the recommended path.

topics.question: A company needs to send an HTTP callout to an external REST API when a record is saved. Can this be done declaratively, and if so, how?
topics.answer: Yes, this can be done declaratively using a Flow with an HTTP Callout action (available in Winter '23+). You configure a Named Credential for authentication and use the 'HTTP Callout' core action in an after-save record-triggered Flow. For complex scenarios (authentication flows, multi-step API chains), Apex remains the more robust option.

topics.question: When is a Visualforce page or Lightning Web Component required rather than a standard Lightning page layout for a user interface requirement?
topics.answer: Custom UI code is needed when: the UI requires custom rendering logic not achievable with standard components, you need interactive data tables with inline editing, the page must embed third-party JavaScript libraries, you need a wizard-style multi-step UI beyond what Screen Flow supports, or the user experience requires real-time data manipulation without page refreshes.

topics.question: What is the declarative boundary for complex branching logic that must evaluate dozens of conditions and update many unrelated records in a single transaction?
topics.answer: Flow Builder's Decision element can handle dozens of conditions, and Update Records can update unrelated objects. However, if those unrelated updates span more than a handful of object types, or if the branching is deeply nested with hundreds of paths, maintainability suffers and Apex becomes the better long-term choice. The practical boundary is complexity of maintenance, not a hard platform limit.

topics.question: Which operations cannot be performed by any declarative automation tool and always require Apex code?
topics.answer: Operations always requiring Apex: parsing/generating binary data, implementing custom REST API endpoints (Apex REST), bulk processing with Batchable/Queueable patterns, complex SOSL searches with programmatic result handling, implementing custom iterable patterns, and triggering before-insert logic that must manipulate the record before it receives an ID.

topics.question: When is a custom Apex trigger required rather than a record-triggered Flow to handle record logic?
topics.answer: An Apex trigger is required when: you need before-insert logic that sets fields before the record gets an ID (Flow before-save can do some of this but is more limited), you need to process extremely large batches with custom governor limit management, you require complex recursive guard patterns across multiple objects, or you need to call future/queueable methods with specific chaining logic.

topics.question: Select two requirements that would exceed Flow Builder's declarative capabilities and require Apex.
topics.answer: Two good examples: (1) Processing a nightly batch of 500,000 records with conditional updates — exceeds Flow's per-transaction limit, requires Apex Batch. (2) Generating a formatted PDF from record data — no native declarative solution, requires Visualforce/Apex or AppExchange. Other valid examples include complex multi-step HTTP OAuth flows and custom Visualforce UI logic.

topics.question: What are the key functional differences between Lightning Experience and Salesforce Classic that a platform app builder must understand?
topics.answer: Lightning Experience offers: Lightning App Builder for drag-and-drop pages, Dynamic Forms, component-based architecture, improved report/dashboard UI, Kanban views, Path component, Activity Timeline, and mobile-responsive design. Classic lacks these modern features and uses S-controls/JavaScript buttons (now deprecated). Lightning components (LWC/Aura) only work in Lightning Experience or Experience Cloud, not Classic.

topics.question: What is My Domain in Salesforce and why is it required before Lightning components can be embedded in App Builder pages or used for single sign-on?
topics.answer: My Domain is an org-specific subdomain (e.g., mycompany.my.salesforce.com). It is required because Lightning components use the domain for secure cross-frame communication (clickjack protection). Without My Domain, the platform cannot reliably scope cookies and authenticate component requests. It is also a prerequisite for SAML-based SSO and OAuth connected apps.

objectives.title: Identify common scenarios for extending an org using the AppExchange.

topics.question: What types of solutions are available on the AppExchange (apps, components, flows, data services)?
topics.answer: AppExchange hosts: full apps (CRM add-ons, CPQ, ERP connectors), Lightning components (individual LWC or Aura components for App Builder), Flow templates and solutions, Bolt Solutions (Experience Cloud templates), and data services (data enrichment, cleansing). Both free and paid offerings exist.

topics.question: What is the difference between a managed package and an unmanaged package on the AppExchange?
topics.answer: Managed package: code is protected (Apex is compiled, not readable), the ISV can push upgrades, and the namespace prefix prevents conflicts. Unmanaged package: all metadata is fully editable after install, no upgrade path, used for sharing open templates. AppExchange publicly listed solutions are always managed packages.

topics.question: A company needs advanced document generation capabilities that Salesforce does not provide natively. What is the recommended approach?
topics.answer: Install a managed AppExchange package such as Conga Composer, Nintex DocGen, or Docusign for document generation. These solutions integrate natively with Salesforce data, support PDF/Word output, and can be triggered from buttons or automation. This avoids custom Apex development and leverages pre-built, security-reviewed solutions.

topics.question: What security process must every AppExchange managed package pass before it can be listed publicly?
topics.answer: Every AppExchange managed package must pass a Salesforce Security Review. This includes automated scanning plus manual review of code and metadata for security vulnerabilities, compliance with Salesforce security standards, and protection of customer data. Only after passing this review can a package be publicly listed.

topics.question: Can an AppExchange solution be installed in a sandbox before deploying to production?
topics.answer: Yes. Best practice is to install and test any AppExchange package in a sandbox first. During installation you select the target environment (sandbox or production). This allows UAT, configuration testing, and conflict assessment before rolling out to production users.

topics.question: What are common business scenarios where AppExchange packages provide value over native Salesforce features (e.g., CPQ, ERP integration, advanced analytics)?
topics.answer: Common scenarios: CPQ (Configure-Price-Quote) for complex pricing logic, ERP integration connectors (SAP, NetSuite), advanced analytics (Tableau CRM pre-built apps), document generation, e-signature, telephony/CTI integrations, project management, territory management extensions, and advanced marketing automation beyond Marketing Cloud basics.

topics.question: When should a company choose to build a custom solution rather than installing an AppExchange package?
topics.answer: Build custom when: no suitable package exists, the requirement is highly proprietary and a competitive differentiator, data privacy restrictions prevent third-party access, the package's cost/complexity outweighs building it internally, or the business process is too unique to map to an off-the-shelf product. AppExchange is preferred when a well-reviewed solution already exists.

objectives.title: Apply features and capabilities available to restrict and extend object, record, and field access.

topics.question: What is the difference between a profile and a permission set in terms of access control?
topics.answer: A profile is mandatory — every user has exactly one. It sets baseline object permissions, field access, login hours, IP restrictions, and app visibility. A permission set is additive and optional — it grants additional permissions on top of the profile without removing anything. Permission sets are the recommended way to grant elevated access without changing profiles.

topics.question: What is object-level security and how is it configured?
topics.answer: Object-level security controls whether a user can Read, Create, Edit, Delete, View All, or Modify All records on an object. It is configured on profiles and permission sets. If a user lacks Read on an object, they cannot see that object's tab, records, or related lists anywhere in the org.

topics.question: What is record-level security and how does it layer on top of object-level security?
topics.answer: Record-level security determines which specific records a user can see and edit, given they already have object access. It is configured through: OWD (org-wide defaults), role hierarchy, sharing rules, manual sharing, and teams. A user must first pass object-level security, then record-level security restricts which records are visible.

topics.question: What does the 'View All' object permission do, and how does it differ from the role hierarchy granting access to records?
topics.answer: 'View All' on an object grants read access to every record regardless of OWD, sharing rules, or ownership. The role hierarchy grants access only to records owned by subordinates in the hierarchy. 'View All' is a flat permission ignoring the hierarchy entirely, and it overrides all sharing restrictions.

topics.question: What does the 'Modify All' object permission do?
topics.answer: 'Modify All' grants full read, edit, delete, transfer, and approve access to every record on that object, regardless of OWD or sharing. It also implicitly includes 'View All'. It is the most powerful record-level permission and is typically reserved for system admins or data stewards.

topics.question: What is a permission set group and when would you use one?
topics.answer: A permission set group bundles multiple permission sets into a single assignable unit. Instead of assigning five separate permission sets to a user, you create one group containing all five and assign the group. Useful when a persona (e.g., 'Field Sales Rep') consistently needs a defined set of permissions across multiple domains.

topics.question: How does a muting permission set work within a permission set group?
topics.answer: A muting permission set removes specific permissions from a permission set group for a subset of users. For example, if a group grants 'Delete Accounts' but certain users in that group should not have delete access, you create a muting permission set that revokes 'Delete Accounts' and apply it to those users. It only suppresses — it cannot grant new permissions.

topics.question: What is field-level security (FLS) and how does it differ from object-level security?
topics.answer: FLS controls access to specific fields on an object — whether a user can see (Read) or edit (Edit) individual fields. Object-level security controls whether the user can access the object at all. FLS is more granular: a user may have Read on Accounts but have the 'Annual Revenue' field hidden via FLS.

topics.question: What is the difference between 'Read' and 'Edit' object permissions when assigned on a profile?
topics.answer: 'Read' allows viewing records but not modifying them. 'Edit' allows modifying records the user has access to, but does not automatically grant access to all records — record-level security still applies. Edit includes Read by default. To create records, the 'Create' permission must also be granted.

topics.question: A user needs temporary elevated access to an object for a specific project. Which approach is preferred: editing their profile or assigning a permission set?
topics.answer: Assign a permission set. Editing a profile affects all users on that profile — a broad, high-risk change. A permission set is assigned specifically to the individual user, can be removed when the project ends, and follows the least-privilege principle. Profiles should be changed only when the entire group needs the new access.

topics.question: If a user's profile denies read access to a field but a permission set grants read access to that field, what is the effective access?
topics.answer: The user gets Read access to the field. Salesforce uses a 'most permissive wins' model for combining profiles and permission sets. Permission sets can only add permissions, not remove them. So if any assigned permission set grants field access, the user has that access regardless of what the profile says.

topics.question: Select two statements that are true about the relationship between profiles and permission sets in Salesforce access control.
topics.answer: True statements: (1) Every user must have exactly one profile, but can have zero or more permission sets. (2) Permission sets can only grant additional access — they cannot revoke permissions granted by the profile (except via muting permission sets in a permission set group). These two facts are frequently tested on the exam.

topics.question: What are login hours on a Salesforce profile and how do they restrict when a user can log in?
topics.answer: Login Hours on a profile define a time window (by day of week) during which users on that profile can log in. If a user is already logged in when their login hours expire, they are logged out at the next page load. This is commonly used for external user profiles or shift-based internal users.

topics.question: What are the three tab visibility settings available on a profile or permission set (Default On, Default Off, Tab Hidden) and how does each affect what the user sees?
topics.answer: Default On: the tab appears in the navigation bar unless the user removes it. Default Off: the tab is available but hidden by default; users can add it themselves. Tab Hidden: the tab is completely invisible to the user and cannot be added. Object access is separate from tab visibility — hiding a tab does not remove record access.

topics.question: What are login IP ranges on a Salesforce profile and how do they restrict from where a user can log in?
topics.answer: Login IP Ranges on a profile restrict logins to specified IP address ranges. If a user attempts to log in from an IP outside the defined range, they are blocked (or challenged with email verification, depending on org settings). This adds a location-based security layer, useful for internal users who should only access Salesforce from corporate networks.

topics.question: A user with 'Read' object permission on Accounts should see only accounts they own, but their manager must also see them. What combination of OWD and sharing mechanism satisfies this without changing profiles?
topics.answer: Set Account OWD to 'Private'. Enable 'Grant Access Using Hierarchies' on the Account object (enabled by default). The manager will automatically see subordinates' account records through the role hierarchy. The user's profile Read permission remains unchanged — OWD and the role hierarchy handle the visibility.

topics.question: What is the 'View All Data' system permission and how does it differ from 'View All' on an individual object?
topics.answer: 'View All Data' is a system-level permission that grants read access to all records across every object in the org — it is essentially 'View All' applied org-wide. 'View All' on an individual object is scoped only to that one object. 'View All Data' is typically reserved for system administrators.

topics.question: What is a restriction rule and how does it differ from a sharing rule — does it open or restrict record visibility?
topics.answer: A restriction rule restricts record visibility — it narrows down which records a user can see below what OWD and sharing rules would normally allow. Sharing rules only open up access (from Private OWD). Restriction rules are the declarative way to reduce access for specific users or groups without changing the overall OWD.

topics.question: Select two things that can be controlled by a permission set that cannot be controlled by a profile.
topics.answer: Permission sets can: (1) be assigned to individual users without affecting other users on the same profile, and (2) be packaged and distributed in managed packages (enabling ISVs to ship permissions with their app). Profiles cannot be assigned to multiple configurations per user, and they cannot be packaged the same way. Both tools control object/field permissions, but permission sets offer user-level granularity.

objectives.title: Given a set of business requirements, determine the appropriate sharing solution.

topics.question: What are the possible Organization-Wide Default (OWD) settings for a custom object?
topics.answer: For custom objects, OWD options are: Private (only owner and users above in hierarchy see records), Public Read Only (everyone can read, only owner/hierarchy can edit), Public Read/Write (everyone can read and edit), and Public Read/Write/Transfer (for cases/leads, allows changing ownership). Controlled by Parent is available when the object has a master-detail to another object.

topics.question: What is the role hierarchy in Salesforce and how does it grant record access upward?
topics.answer: The role hierarchy is a tree structure representing the reporting chain. When 'Grant Access Using Hierarchies' is enabled, users in roles above the record owner automatically gain at least the same access level as the owner. Access flows upward only — a manager sees subordinates' records, not vice versa.

topics.question: What is the difference between an owner-based sharing rule and a criteria-based sharing rule?
topics.answer: Owner-based sharing rule: shares records owned by users in a specific role/group with another group. Criteria-based sharing rule: shares records whose field values match specified criteria (e.g., Region = 'West') with a group, regardless of who owns the record. Criteria-based is more flexible for data-attribute-driven sharing.

topics.question: When can sharing rules NOT be used to open up access (i.e., when OWD is already Public Read/Write)?
topics.answer: Sharing rules can only grant access that is more permissive than the OWD. If OWD is already Public Read/Write, sharing rules have nothing to add because everyone already has maximum access. Sharing rules are only relevant when OWD is set to Private or Public Read Only.

topics.question: What is manual sharing and when is it available to users?
topics.answer: Manual sharing allows a record owner (or admin) to share a specific record with a specific user or group on a one-off basis using the 'Sharing' button. It is available only when the object's OWD is Private or Public Read Only — not when OWD is Public Read/Write. Manual shares are removed when record ownership changes.

topics.question: A company has sensitive opportunity records that should only be visible to the owner and their management chain. Which OWD setting and sharing components support this?
topics.answer: Set Opportunity OWD to Private. Enable 'Grant Access Using Hierarchies' (default on Opportunities). Managers in roles above the owner will automatically see those records. No sharing rules are needed unless cross-team visibility is required. This is the most restrictive, secure baseline for sensitive pipeline data.

topics.question: What is a public group and when should you use a public group instead of a role for a sharing rule?
topics.answer: A public group is a manually curated collection of users, roles, or other groups used as a sharing target. Use a public group instead of a role when: the sharing audience does not map neatly to a single role (e.g., members from multiple roles), or when the set of users changes independently of the role hierarchy. Public groups are more flexible for ad-hoc groupings.

topics.question: What is the maximum number of sharing rules allowed per object?
topics.answer: Salesforce allows up to 300 sharing rules per object (combined owner-based and criteria-based). This limit is rarely hit in practice, but it is important to be aware of when designing a complex sharing model with many criteria-based rules.

topics.question: A requirement states that users in the 'Support' role should have read access to all cases owned by users in the 'Sales' role. What sharing feature satisfies this?
topics.answer: Create an owner-based sharing rule on the Case object: share records owned by users in the 'Sales' role with users in the 'Support' role, granting Read Only access. This is a straightforward role-to-role owner-based sharing rule, the most common use case for sharing rules.

topics.question: What is the order of evaluation Salesforce uses to determine whether a user can access a specific record?
topics.answer: Salesforce evaluates access in this order: (1) Is the object accessible via the user's profile/permission set? (2) Is the record owned by the user, or are they above the owner in the role hierarchy? (3) Does a sharing rule grant access? (4) Is there a manual share? (5) Does the user have 'View All' or 'View All Data'? The most permissive applicable rule wins.

topics.question: What are the limitations of manual sharing (e.g., it is removed when record ownership changes, not available when OWD is Public Read/Write)?
topics.answer: Manual sharing limitations: (1) Removed automatically when the record owner changes. (2) Not available when OWD is Public Read/Write — no need to share manually when everyone already has access. (3) Cannot be automated — it requires a human to click 'Sharing' or use Apex. (4) It does not persist across ownership transfers.

topics.question: A company needs to grant read access to all Opportunity records owned by users in a specific territory role to a cross-functional team. Select two sharing tools that can accomplish this declaratively.
topics.answer: Two declarative options: (1) Owner-based sharing rule — share records owned by users in the territory role with the cross-functional public group/role. (2) Criteria-based sharing rule — if territory is stored as a field on the Opportunity, share based on that field value. Both are valid; the right choice depends on whether ownership or field value is the better trigger.

topics.question: How does assigning a record to a queue affect who can access that record?
topics.answer: When a record is assigned to a queue, all members of that queue gain access to the record (at the OWD access level or above). Any queue member can then accept (take ownership of) the record. This is commonly used for case or lead routing where a pool of users should be able to pick from a shared workload.

topics.question: What is a Salesforce queue and which standard objects support it?
topics.answer: A queue is a holding area for records awaiting assignment. Standard objects supporting queues: Cases, Leads, Orders, Knowledge Articles, and custom objects. Contacts, Accounts, and Opportunities do not support queues natively. Queue members can be individual users, roles, or public groups.

topics.question: What are account teams, and what types of access (Read/Write) can account team members be granted on the account and its related records?
topics.answer: Account teams are a group of users who collaborate on an account. Each team member can be granted Read or Edit access to the Account itself, and separately Read or Edit access to related Contacts, Opportunities, and Cases. The account owner defines the team. This provides fine-grained related-object sharing without public groups or sharing rules.

topics.question: What is the 'Grant Access Using Hierarchies' setting on a custom object, and what happens to record access through the role hierarchy when it is disabled?
topics.answer: This setting controls whether users above the record owner in the role hierarchy automatically inherit record access. When disabled on a custom object, the role hierarchy does NOT grant upward access — managers do not automatically see their subordinates' records on that object. Sharing rules and manual sharing would need to compensate. Standard objects cannot disable this setting.

topics.question: What are opportunity teams and what access levels can team members be granted on an opportunity?
topics.answer: Opportunity teams let multiple users collaborate on a single opportunity. Each member can be granted Read Only or Read/Write access to the opportunity record. Unlike account teams, opportunity team access is scoped only to that specific opportunity — it does not automatically extend to related objects.

topics.question: How does implicit sharing work for Contacts, Opportunities, and Cases that are related to an Account — what access does a user gain to child records when they have access to the parent Account?
topics.answer: Implicit sharing means that if a user has Read access to an Account, Salesforce automatically grants Read access to that Account's related Contacts, Opportunities, and Cases — even if the OWD on those child objects is Private. This is a built-in platform behavior designed to ensure users can navigate related records contextually.

topics.question: A company needs 10 regional reps to each own a queue of cases. When a rep picks a case, it should leave the queue and be owned by the rep. Which sharing feature supports this assignment model?
topics.answer: Queues support this model. Cases are assigned to the queue (shared with all queue members). When a rep 'accepts' the case, they change the owner to themselves, removing it from the queue. Each region can have its own queue. This is the standard Salesforce case assignment model.

topics.question: A company uses a Opportunities object with OWD set to Private. A sales manager needs real-time access to all opportunity records owned by their direct reports but not by peers in other regions. Which sharing mechanism provides this without writing any code?
topics.answer: The role hierarchy with 'Grant Access Using Hierarchies' enabled provides this automatically. The sales manager's role must be positioned above their direct reports' roles in the hierarchy. They will see all subordinate-owned opportunities. Peer records in other regions remain private because there is no hierarchical relationship between the peers.

objectives.title: Identify the features and capabilities available when creating reports, report types, and dashboards.

topics.question: What are the four report formats available in Salesforce (Tabular, Summary, Matrix, Joined)?
topics.answer: Tabular: simple row list, no grouping, good for exports. Summary: groups rows by a field (e.g., by Stage), allows subtotals and charts. Matrix: groups by both rows and columns, great for pivot-style analysis. Joined: up to five report blocks of different report types side-by-side in one report, used for comparing disparate data sets.

topics.question: What is the difference between a standard report type and a custom report type?
topics.answer: Standard report types are pre-built by Salesforce for common object relationships (e.g., Accounts with Contacts). Custom report types are admin-created and allow you to define which objects (up to 4 related objects) are included and whether child records must or may exist, and you can add any fields from those objects.

topics.question: When would you create a custom report type instead of using a standard report type?
topics.answer: Create a custom report type when: the standard type doesn't include the fields or related objects you need, you want to report on a custom object relationship, you need to specify include/exclude behavior for child records (e.g., Accounts without Contacts), or you need to expose formula fields or related object fields not in any standard type.

topics.question: What is a joined report and when is it appropriate to use one?
topics.answer: A joined report displays up to 5 report blocks side-by-side, each based on a different report type but sharing a common standard object. Use it when you need to compare data from different object contexts in one view — for example, comparing Opportunities and Cases for the same Account. Each block can have its own filters and groupings.

topics.question: What is a dashboard in Salesforce and what types of components can it contain?
topics.answer: A dashboard is a visual display of report data. Component types include: charts (bar, line, donut, funnel, scatter), gauges, metrics (single number KPIs), tables, and Visualforce pages. Each component is powered by a source report. Dashboards are stored in folders and can be filtered by viewers.

topics.question: What is the maximum number of records a standard Salesforce report displays?
topics.answer: A standard Salesforce report displays a maximum of 2,000 rows in the report viewer. However, if you export the report, you can retrieve up to 200,000 rows (via export to CSV). The 2,000-row limit applies only to the on-screen display, not to report subscriptions or exports.

topics.question: What is a dynamic dashboard and how does it differ from a standard dashboard?
topics.answer: A dynamic dashboard shows data based on the logged-in user's own record access, rather than the 'Run As' user defined on the dashboard. Each user sees their own data in real time. Standard dashboards show data as a single fixed user. Dynamic dashboards are useful for sales rep scorecards where each person should see only their own pipeline.

topics.question: What is the maximum number of components on a single dashboard?
topics.answer: A single Salesforce dashboard can contain up to 20 components. This is a key exam fact. If you need more than 20 visualizations, you must create multiple dashboards or combine data more efficiently in fewer components.

topics.question: What is the 'Run as' setting on a dashboard, and what options are available?
topics.answer: The 'Run as' setting determines whose security context is used to pull dashboard data. Options: (1) Run as specified user — data always reflects that user's access (good for a manager's view), (2) Run as logged-in user (dynamic dashboard) — each viewer sees their own data, (3) Run as scheduled user — used for scheduled dashboard refreshes. The 'Run as' user must have access to all source reports.

topics.question: Can a custom report type include fields from objects that are up to four levels away in a lookup relationship chain?
topics.answer: Yes. A custom report type can span up to 4 related objects (e.g., Object A > Object B > Object C > Object D). Fields from all four objects can be included in the report. This is the maximum depth for a custom report type relationship chain.

topics.question: What is a bucket field in a report and when would you use one?
topics.answer: A bucket field lets you categorize report records into groups (buckets) on the fly without creating a formula field. For example, bucket 'Annual Revenue' into Small (<1M), Medium (1M-10M), Large (>10M). Use it for ad-hoc segmentation in a report without modifying the data model. Buckets support Numeric, Text, and Picklist field types.

topics.question: What is a dashboard filter and how does it allow a viewer to adjust the dashboard display without editing it?
topics.answer: Dashboard filters are pre-configured filter options that viewers can select from a dropdown on the dashboard. The admin defines up to 3 filters per dashboard, specifying which fields and values are available. Viewers toggle filters to slice the dashboard data (e.g., by Region or Quarter) without needing edit access to the dashboard.

topics.question: What is a cross filter in a report, and what type of question does it answer (e.g., Accounts without Opportunities)?
topics.answer: A cross filter lets you filter the primary report object based on the presence or absence of related records. For example: 'Show all Accounts where NO Opportunities exist.' This answers 'with/without' questions about related objects. Cross filters can also be refined with sub-filters on the related object's fields.

topics.question: How is report and dashboard folder visibility controlled, and which settings determine which users can view or edit a given folder?
topics.answer: Folder access is controlled by sharing the folder with users, roles, public groups, or the entire org. Access levels are Viewer (can run reports/view dashboards), Editor (can also create/edit within the folder), and Manager (can also share and rename the folder). Reports/dashboards are always stored in a folder — 'My Personal Reports' is visible only to the owner.

topics.question: What is a report subscription in Salesforce and how does it differ from scheduling a dashboard refresh?
topics.answer: A report subscription sends the report results by email on a defined schedule (daily, weekly, monthly) to specified users. Dashboard refresh scheduling re-runs the dashboard's source reports and caches the data at a set time. Report subscriptions deliver a snapshot of the data to inboxes; dashboard scheduling ensures the on-screen dashboard is up-to-date when users log in.

topics.question: What is conditional highlighting (formatting) in a Salesforce report and on which report formats is it available?
topics.answer: Conditional highlighting colors cell backgrounds based on numeric thresholds (e.g., green for >90%, yellow for 70-90%, red for <70%). It is only available on Summary and Matrix report formats — not Tabular or Joined. It applies to numeric summary fields like totals, averages, or counts.

topics.question: What is a row limit on a Tabular report and when is it required before the report can be used as a dashboard source?
topics.answer: A Tabular report must have a row limit applied (max 2,000) before it can be used as a dashboard source. Without a row limit, Tabular reports cannot power dashboard components. The row limit defines how many rows the dashboard component will draw from. Summary and Matrix reports do not require this step.

topics.question: In a custom report type that spans two objects, what is the difference between selecting 'Each A record must have at least one related B record' versus 'A records may or may not have related B records'?
topics.answer: 'Each A must have at least one B' acts like an inner join — only A records with at least one related B appear in the report. 'A may or may not have B' acts like an outer join — all A records appear, and B fields are blank for those without related B records. The second option is needed for 'Accounts without Opportunities' style reporting.

topics.question: What is a summary formula column in a Summary or Matrix report and how does it differ from a standard report field?
topics.answer: A summary formula column is a custom calculated column built using report-level aggregate functions (SUM, AVG, MAX, MIN, COUNT) on other report fields. It exists only in the report — not in the Salesforce schema. A standard report field maps directly to an object field. Summary formulas allow KPIs like 'Win Rate = Closed Won / Total Opportunities' that cannot exist as a schema-level field.

topics.question: What are the available chart types for a dashboard component and what data shapes (Summary, Matrix) support them?
topics.answer: Chart types include: bar, horizontal bar, line, donut, funnel, scatter, and combo. Summary reports support bar, line, donut, funnel, and scatter charts. Matrix reports also support those types. Gauge and Metric components don't use charts but show a single aggregated value. Tabular reports with a row limit can use table components.

topics.question: What is the maximum number of columns on a single Salesforce dashboard?
topics.answer: A Salesforce dashboard supports up to 3 columns. This is a fixed layout constraint. Dashboard components can be sized to span 1, 2, or all 3 columns, allowing flexible arrangements while staying within the 3-column maximum.

topics.question: What is the maximum number of components on a single Salesforce dashboard?
topics.answer: A single Salesforce dashboard supports a maximum of 20 components. This limit applies regardless of column layout. If more visualizations are needed, additional dashboards must be created, or data must be consolidated into fewer components using more efficient report designs.

objectives.title: Given a set of requirements, determine the appropriate global, object-specific actions and layouts to optimize the Salesforce mobile user experience.

topics.question: What is the difference between a global action and an object-specific quick action?
topics.answer: A global action is available from anywhere in Salesforce (the global header action bar, Chatter, mobile navigation) and is not associated with a specific object. An object-specific quick action belongs to a specific object and appears on that object's record page. Global actions are best for org-wide tasks (Log a Call, New Task); object-specific actions are best for context-driven tasks (Create related Contact from Account).

topics.question: What types of quick actions exist (Create, Update, Log a Call, Custom Visualforce, Flow)?
topics.answer: Quick action types: Create (creates a new record, optionally pre-populating related fields), Update (updates fields on the current record), Log a Call (creates a Task with Call type), Custom Visualforce (opens a VF page), Flow (launches a Screen Flow), Send Email (sends an email), and Custom Canvas (for connected apps). Each type serves a different UX goal.

topics.question: When would you use an 'Update a Record' quick action instead of a 'Create a Record' quick action?
topics.answer: Use 'Update a Record' when the user needs to edit specific fields on the current record quickly — for example, a status update action showing only 3 fields instead of the full page layout. This reduces cognitive load and is ideal for mobile where screen space is limited. 'Create a Record' is for adding new records, not modifying existing ones.

topics.question: How are quick actions surfaced in the Salesforce mobile app?
topics.answer: In the Salesforce mobile app, quick actions appear in the action bar at the bottom of a record (the row of icons). The order and selection of actions in the action bar is controlled by the page layout's 'Salesforce Mobile and Lightning Experience Actions' section. The first few actions in the layout become the visible quick-access icons; the rest appear in an overflow menu.

topics.question: What is the mobile navigation menu and how can it be customized?
topics.answer: The mobile navigation menu is the left-side menu in the Salesforce mobile app that users access via the hamburger icon. Admins customize it in Setup under 'Salesforce Navigation' by selecting which items (objects, apps, smart search items, Visualforce pages, Lightning pages) appear and in what order. The first item becomes the mobile app's home screen.

topics.question: What is a compact layout and when is it displayed in the mobile app?
topics.answer: A compact layout defines which fields appear in the highlights panel at the top of a record (the card header with the record's most important fields). In the mobile app, compact layouts also appear in record cards in list views and related lists. An admin selects 4-10 fields for the compact layout. The top 4 fields get the most prominent display.

topics.question: A sales rep needs to quickly log a call note after a client meeting from their phone. Which action type should be configured?
topics.answer: Configure a 'Log a Call' quick action on the relevant object (e.g., Contact or Opportunity). This action creates a Task record pre-set to Call type, with a notes/description field. It is optimized for fast data entry and is prominently displayed in the mobile app action bar. No navigation away from the record is needed.

topics.question: A requirement states that users need to create a new Case from anywhere in the app, not just from the Cases object. Which action type satisfies this?
topics.answer: Create a global action of type 'Create a Record' targeting the Case object. Add it to the global publisher layout. This makes the 'New Case' action available from the global header and the mobile action bar everywhere in the app — not just on the Cases tab. Global actions are the go-to for org-wide, context-independent record creation.

topics.question: What is the maximum number of fields recommended in an action layout for optimal mobile usability?
topics.answer: Salesforce recommends no more than 8 fields on an action layout for mobile usability. Fewer fields mean less scrolling and faster data entry on small screens. Action layouts are separate from full page layouts and should be intentionally minimal, capturing only the essential fields needed to complete the action.

topics.question: How does the action layout differ from the full page layout, and how does it affect the mobile user experience?
topics.answer: The action layout is a stripped-down layout specific to a quick action — it contains only the fields needed for that action (e.g., 3-5 fields to create a lead). The full page layout contains all sections, related lists, and components. On mobile, action layouts load faster, require less scrolling, and are optimized for one-handed entry. Full page layouts are used when viewing/editing a full record.

objectives.title: Describe the customizations and use cases for Chatter.

topics.question: How do you post to a record feed vs. a personal user feed vs. a Chatter group feed?
topics.answer: Record feed: post from the Chatter component on a record page — posts are visible to all users with access to that record. Personal user feed: post from your own profile page — visible to your followers. Chatter group feed: post inside a group — visible to group members. Each context scopes who can see the post and who gets notified.

topics.question: What is Chatter and what core collaboration features does it provide?
topics.answer: Chatter is Salesforce's built-in enterprise social collaboration platform. Core features: record and user feeds, @mentions, file sharing, groups (public/private/broadcast/unlisted), polls, publisher actions, feed tracking (automated field-change posts), mobile notifications, and integration with Salesforce records. It enables contextual collaboration without leaving the CRM.

topics.question: What are Chatter groups and what types of groups can be created (public, private, broadcast-only, unlisted)?
topics.answer: Public group: anyone in the org can see and join. Private group: membership requires approval; non-members cannot see content. Broadcast-only group: only group owners/managers can post; members can only read (good for announcements). Unlisted group: hidden from search; members must be invited; used for sensitive discussions. Customer groups also allow external users.

topics.question: What is the Chatter @mention feature and which types of Salesforce entities can be mentioned?
topics.answer: @mentions in Chatter notify the mentioned entity and create a hyperlink in the post. You can @mention: users, Chatter groups, and (in some contexts) records. When a user is @mentioned, they receive a notification email and an in-app bell notification. @mentioning a group notifies all group members.

topics.question: How can an administrator enable or disable Chatter for specific users or for the entire org?
topics.answer: Org-level: Chatter is enabled/disabled in Setup under 'Chatter Settings'. User-level: admins can disable Chatter for specific users by unchecking the 'Chatter' permission on their profile. Note that disabling Chatter org-wide also disables Feed Tracking and Chatter notifications for all users. Partial rollouts can be managed via profiles.

topics.question: When would Chatter notifications be a more appropriate collaboration tool than standard Salesforce email alerts?
topics.answer: Chatter notifications are better when: the communication is contextual to a Salesforce record (keeps conversation in context), team members should be able to reply and thread the discussion, you want to avoid inbox overload with non-actionable alerts, or when @mentioning a group is more efficient than maintaining an email distribution list.

topics.question: What is a Chatter publisher action and how is it different from a standard quick action?
topics.answer: A Chatter publisher action appears in the Chatter feed publisher (the '+' menu above the feed) and is designed for social/collaboration tasks like posting to a group or sharing a file. A standard quick action (in the action bar) is designed for CRM tasks like creating records or logging calls. Publisher actions are feed-centric; quick actions are record-centric.

topics.question: What is the maximum number of fields that can be enabled for Chatter feed tracking per object?
topics.answer: Up to 20 fields per object can be enabled for Chatter Feed Tracking. When a tracked field changes on a record, a post is automatically added to that record's Chatter feed showing the old and new value. This makes it easy to see a record's history of changes without opening audit trails.

topics.question: What is Chatter feed tracking, and how does an administrator configure which field changes are surfaced in a record's Chatter feed?
topics.answer: Feed tracking automatically posts a message to a record's Chatter feed whenever selected fields change. To configure: go to Setup > Feed Tracking, select the object, enable tracking, and check the specific fields to track (up to 20). Standard and custom fields are eligible. Changes show as 'Field changed from X to Y' posts, visible to all users with record access.

objectives.title: Given a scenario, determine the appropriate data model.

topics.question: A business needs to associate multiple products with multiple campaigns, where each association tracks its own campaign-specific attributes. What data model satisfies this requirement?
topics.answer: Create a junction object (e.g., 'Campaign Product') with two master-detail relationships — one to Campaign and one to Product. Each junction record represents one Campaign-Product association and can hold its own fields (e.g., discount rate, start date). This is the standard many-to-many pattern in Salesforce.

topics.question: What is a junction object and when is it used to model a many-to-many relationship?
topics.answer: A junction object is a custom object with two master-detail relationship fields pointing to two different parent objects. It represents the intersection in a many-to-many relationship. Each record on the junction represents one instance of the relationship between the two parents, plus any attributes specific to that pairing.

topics.question: When should you create a custom object rather than extending a standard object?
topics.answer: Create a custom object when: the data does not semantically fit any standard object, the standard object's built-in behaviors (like Opportunity stages) don't apply, you need a separate tab/UI independent of standard objects, or the relationship structure requires a new entity. Extend a standard object (with custom fields) when the core data concept matches (e.g., adding fields to Contact).

topics.question: What is the maximum number of master-detail relationships a custom object can have?
topics.answer: A custom object can have a maximum of 2 master-detail relationships. This is a hard platform limit. This restriction exists because each master-detail relationship determines record ownership and OWD inheritance, and conflicting rules from two or more masters would create ambiguity.

topics.question: A company wants to track individual line items for each order, where each line item cannot exist without an order. Which relationship type is most appropriate?
topics.answer: Use a master-detail relationship with Order as the master and Line Item as the child. Master-detail enforces that child records cannot exist without a parent (required relationship, no blank allowed), provides cascade delete (deleting the order deletes its line items), and enables roll-up summary fields on the parent.

topics.question: What is the maximum number of custom objects allowed per Salesforce org (standard edition considerations)?
topics.answer: The limit varies by edition: Developer Edition allows up to 400 custom objects, Enterprise Edition up to 2,000, Unlimited Edition up to 2,000. Professional Edition is much lower (50-100 depending on add-ons). The exam typically focuses on the general concept that limits exist by edition, not on memorizing every number.

topics.question: When is it appropriate to denormalize data into a formula field rather than maintaining a separate related object?
topics.answer: Denormalize into a formula field when: the value is always derivable from other fields on the same record or a parent record, the data is read-only and does not need to be stored independently, you want to avoid creating additional objects and relationships, and the calculation is simple enough for a formula. Avoid denormalization when the data needs independent lifecycle management.

topics.question: What are record types and what three things do they control on an object: picklist values available to users, the page layout displayed, and the business process applied?
topics.answer: Record types control: (1) which picklist values are available to users (subset of the master picklist), (2) which page layout is displayed to users with that record type, and (3) which business process is applied (Sales Process for Opportunities, Support Process for Cases, Lead Process for Leads). A user's profile determines which record types they can create.

topics.question: How are record types assigned to users, and which mechanism determines which record type(s) a specific user can create?
topics.answer: Record types are assigned through profiles and permission sets. In the profile (or permission set), you specify which record types on each object the user has access to, and which is the default. When a user creates a new record and has access to multiple record types, they are prompted to choose one. The profile/permission set assignment is the gatekeeper.

topics.question: A company has two sales teams — Enterprise and SMB — that need different Stage picklist values and different page layouts on Opportunity records. What is the correct Salesforce feature to implement this?
topics.answer: Use Record Types on Opportunity object. Create two record types (Enterprise and SMB), each linked to a different Sales Process (controlling Stage values) and a different page layout. Assign each record type to the respective team's profiles. This is the canonical Salesforce solution for team-specific picklist values and layouts on the same object.

topics.question: What is the Master record type and what is its behavior when a user's profile has no explicit record type assignment?
topics.answer: The Master record type is the system default that exists on every object automatically. It includes all picklist values and uses the object's default page layout. If a user's profile has no explicit record type assignment for an object, they receive the Master record type by default, seeing all picklist values and the master page layout.

topics.question: What is a sales process in Salesforce and how does it control which Opportunity Stage values are available for a specific record type?
topics.answer: A Sales Process is a subset of Opportunity Stage picklist values curated for a specific business scenario. You create a Sales Process by selecting which Stage values from the master list to include. You then associate that Sales Process with a record type. Users with that record type can only see and select the Stage values in the linked Sales Process.

topics.question: What is a custom metadata type and how does it differ from a custom object in terms of deployment, access in Apex, and use in validation rules?
topics.answer: Custom metadata type records are metadata — they are deployable via change sets and packages (unlike custom object data records). They can be referenced in formula fields, validation rules, and Flows natively. In Apex, they are queried with SOQL but are not subject to DML governor limits for reads. Custom object records are data — not deployable, not usable in validation formulas directly.

topics.question: What is the difference between a Hierarchy custom setting and a List custom setting, and when would you use each?
topics.answer: Hierarchy custom setting: stores values at the org, profile, or user level — the most specific level wins. Ideal for feature flags or thresholds that may differ by user group. List custom setting: stores a simple name-value set (like a lookup table) accessible to any user. Use Hierarchy for user/profile-level overrides; use List for org-wide reference data that doesn't vary by user.

topics.question: What is a support process and how does it define the Case Status picklist values for a specific Case record type?
topics.answer: A Support Process is analogous to a Sales Process but for Cases. It defines which Case Status picklist values (from the master list) are available for a given Case record type. For example, a Technical Support process might include 'Pending Engineering' while a Billing process would not. Assign the Support Process to the Case record type.

topics.question: A business needs to store configurable threshold values (e.g., discount limits per product line) that can be referenced in validation rules, formulas, and Flows, and must be deployable via change sets. Which feature is most appropriate?
topics.answer: Custom Metadata Types. They are deployable via change sets and packages, can be referenced directly in formulas and validation rules (unlike custom settings in formulas), and are accessible in Flows. Custom settings are not directly referenceable in validation rule formulas. Custom objects require data migration, not metadata deployment.

topics.question: Can custom metadata type records be deployed via change sets and packages, unlike custom object records which must be loaded separately?
topics.answer: Yes. Custom metadata type records are treated as metadata, not data. They travel with change sets and managed/unmanaged packages automatically. Custom object data records are data and must be migrated separately using Data Loader or similar tools. This is the key operational advantage of custom metadata types for configuration data.

topics.question: Select two capabilities that custom metadata types have that regular custom objects do not, making them preferred for app configuration data.
topics.answer: Two key capabilities: (1) Records are deployable as metadata via change sets and packages — no separate data migration needed. (2) Records can be referenced directly in formula fields and validation rules using the $CustomMetadata merge field — custom object records cannot be referenced in validation rule formulas. Both make custom metadata types superior for app configuration.

objectives.title: Given a scenario, explain the capabilities of the various relationship types and the implications of each on record access, user interface, and reporting.

topics.question: Can a master-detail relationship field be left blank on a child record?
topics.answer: No. A master-detail relationship field is always required on the child record. The child record cannot exist without a parent. This enforces referential integrity. If you need an optional parent relationship, use a lookup relationship instead.

topics.question: What happens to child records when a master record in a master-detail relationship is deleted?
topics.answer: Child records are cascade deleted when the master is deleted. This is automatic and cannot be prevented by configuration. If you need child records to survive parent deletion, use a lookup relationship instead. The cascade delete also fires any before/after delete triggers on the child records.

topics.question: What happens to child records when a parent record in a lookup relationship is deleted?
topics.answer: In a lookup relationship, child records are NOT automatically deleted when the parent is deleted. Depending on the 'What to do if the lookup record is deleted' setting, the lookup field is either cleared (set to blank) or the deletion is blocked. No cascade delete occurs. Child records survive independently.

topics.question: Can a lookup relationship field be left blank on a child record?
topics.answer: Yes, by default. Lookup relationship fields are optional — the child record can exist with no parent specified. However, you can make a lookup field required on the page layout or at the field definition level to enforce that a parent must be selected. This still does not create cascade delete behavior.

topics.question: How does record sharing work for child records in a master-detail relationship vs. a lookup relationship?
topics.answer: Master-detail: child records inherit the sharing and OWD of the master record — they don't have independent sharing. Lookup: child records have their own OWD and sharing model independently of the parent. This means in a master-detail, securing the parent automatically secures children; in a lookup, each object's sharing is configured separately.

topics.question: How does a master-detail relationship affect the ownership of child records?
topics.answer: In a master-detail relationship, the child record does not have its own Owner field — ownership is inherited from the master record. The master's owner is the effective owner of all child records. In a lookup relationship, child records have their own Owner field and ownership is independent of the parent.

topics.question: On which relationship type can roll-up summary fields be created — master-detail or lookup?
topics.answer: Roll-up summary fields can only be created on the master record in a master-detail relationship. They aggregate child record values (COUNT, SUM, MIN, MAX) up to the parent. Lookup relationships do not support roll-up summary fields natively. (Lookups can use cross-object formula fields, but not roll-up summaries.)

topics.question: Can a master-detail child record be reparented (reassigned to a different parent)?
topics.answer: Yes, but only if the master object allows reparenting. By default, master-detail child records can be reparented — the 'Allow reparenting' option on the relationship field must be enabled. If disabled (the default before Summer '12), child records cannot change their master. Reparenting changes the child's effective owner and sharing to match the new master.

topics.question: What is a hierarchical relationship field and which standard object uses it?
topics.answer: A hierarchical relationship is a special lookup relationship where a record can look up to another record of the same object, creating a tree structure. It is only available on the User standard object (the 'Manager' field is a hierarchical relationship). It cannot be created on custom objects.

topics.question: What is a self-relationship (lookup to the same object) and what is a common use case for it?
topics.answer: A self-relationship is a lookup field on an object that points to another record of the same object. Common use case: an Account 'Parent Account' field (a lookup to Account itself) to model a corporate hierarchy. Another example: an 'Escalated From' field on Case pointing to another Case. These create hierarchical or associative structures within a single object.

topics.question: A business needs both cascade delete behavior and roll-up summaries on a child object. Which relationship type must be used?
topics.answer: Master-detail relationship. Both cascade delete and roll-up summary fields are exclusive to master-detail relationships. If either of these features is required, the relationship must be master-detail. Lookup relationships support neither capability.

topics.question: What is the maximum number of lookup relationships a single custom object can have?
topics.answer: A custom object can have up to 25 lookup relationships (in addition to the 2 master-detail relationships). This limit rarely becomes an issue in practice, but it is good to know for the exam. Each lookup adds a field on the child object pointing to a parent record.

topics.question: What are the reporting implications of a master-detail vs. a lookup relationship when creating standard reports?
topics.answer: Master-detail: roll-up summaries on the parent can be reported on; standard report types include both parent and child data naturally. Lookup: no roll-up summary fields, so parent-level aggregation must use cross-object formulas or custom report types. Both relationship types appear in standard report types, but roll-up fields only exist for master-detail.

topics.question: A developer is deciding between a master-detail and a lookup relationship for a new child object. Select two capabilities that are ONLY available with a master-detail relationship.
topics.answer: Two master-detail-only capabilities: (1) Roll-up summary fields on the parent (COUNT, SUM, MIN, MAX of child values). (2) Cascade delete — deleting the parent automatically deletes all child records. Both are critical for data integrity and aggregation scenarios. Lookup relationships offer neither.

topics.question: In a junction object that has two master-detail relationship fields pointing to two different parent objects, how is record ownership determined and which parent's OWD governs access to the junction record?
topics.answer: The junction record's access is governed by the more permissive of the two parent OWDs. For example, if Parent A is Private and Parent B is Public Read Only, a user who has access to either parent can access the junction record. Ownership of the junction record belongs to the user who created it (or the record owner), but sharing follows the most permissive parent.

topics.question: What is a lookup filter on a relationship field and how does it restrict which records a user can select in the lookup?
topics.answer: A lookup filter restricts the records shown in the lookup search dialog based on field criteria. For example, a Contact lookup on Opportunity filtered to show only Contacts related to the same Account. Filters can be based on fields on the source record, the target object's fields, or running user attributes. This prevents incorrect parent selections.

topics.question: What is the difference between a required lookup filter and an optional lookup filter, and how does each behave when the user selects a value that does not match the filter?
topics.answer: Required filter: only matching records appear in search; the user cannot select a non-matching record — the system blocks the save with an error. Optional filter: only matching records appear by default, but the user can override the filter and search for all records. A required filter is an enforcement mechanism; optional is a convenience filter.

topics.question: How are related lists displayed differently in the UI for master-detail vs. lookup relationships?
topics.answer: Both master-detail and lookup relationships create a related list on the parent record's page layout. However, master-detail related lists include a 'New [Child Object]' button by default (because the child requires a parent). Lookup related lists also include the 'New' button, but the child can potentially exist without the parent. Functionally the display is similar, but cascade behavior differs.

objectives.title: Given a scenario, determine the considerations when selecting or changing a field data type.

topics.question: What is the maximum character length of a standard Text field in Salesforce?
topics.answer: A standard Text field supports up to 255 characters. If more text is needed, use Text Area (up to 255 chars with line breaks), Text Area (Long) up to 131,072 chars, or Text Area (Rich) up to 131,072 chars with HTML formatting. Choose the field type based on the data length and formatting needs.

topics.question: What is an auto-number field and when would you use one?
topics.answer: An auto-number field automatically generates a unique, sequential ID for each record (e.g., CASE-0001, CASE-0002). Use it for: record numbering systems (ticket numbers, invoice IDs, case numbers), unique identifiers that must be human-readable and sequential, and external references. Auto-number fields are read-only, cannot be edited, and are always unique.

topics.question: What is the difference between a Number field, a Currency field, and a Percent field in Salesforce?
topics.answer: Number: stores a pure numeric value with no currency or percentage symbol. Currency: stores a monetary value, respects the org's currency locale, and displays the currency symbol. Supports multi-currency. Percent: stores a numeric value and displays it with a % sign, but the stored value is the raw number (e.g., 50 displays as 50%). All three support decimal places.

topics.question: What is the formula field character (compile size) limit?
topics.answer: A formula field has a maximum compile size of 5,000 characters (not the text you type, but the compiled formula after expansion of referenced formulas). The raw formula you write is limited to 3,900 characters. This is why deeply nested formulas or formulas that reference many other formula fields can fail to save — they exceed the compile size.

topics.question: What data types can be marked as External ID on a Salesforce object?
topics.answer: External ID can be enabled on: Text, Number, Email, and Auto Number field types. The External ID checkbox makes the field indexed for faster querying and enables upsert operations in Data Loader and the API. Each object can have up to 25 External ID fields. Only fields on custom objects can be set as External ID (some standard fields are already External IDs by design).

topics.question: What are the implications of changing a Text field to a Picklist field (data loss, existing values)?
topics.answer: Changing Text to Picklist does not delete existing data, but existing text values that don't match any picklist value will become invalid picklist entries. Salesforce displays them as stale values. If 'Restrict picklist to the values in the value set' is enabled, reports and validation rules may reject these stale values. Always review existing data before converting.

topics.question: What happens to existing data when you change a Number field to a Text field?
topics.answer: Existing numeric data is preserved but converted to text representation. The field type change does not erase data. However, the field can no longer be used in numeric calculations, roll-up summaries, or range filters after the change. Reports and formulas that referenced the field as a number will need to be updated.

topics.question: What is the difference between a Text Area and a Text Area (Rich) field in Salesforce?
topics.answer: Text Area: allows multi-line plain text up to 255 characters, no formatting. Text Area (Rich): allows HTML-formatted text (bold, italic, bullet lists, hyperlinks, images) up to 131,072 characters. Rich text is rendered in the UI as formatted HTML. Text Area (Rich) fields cannot be used in formula fields, report filters, or standard SOQL WHERE clauses.

topics.question: What are the limitations of a Text Area (Rich) field when used in formula fields and report filters?
topics.answer: Text Area (Rich) fields cannot be referenced in formula fields at all. They cannot be used as report filter criteria. They are also not searchable via standard SOQL WHERE clause equality filters. These limitations exist because the field stores HTML content, which is not conducive to exact-match comparisons or formula calculations.

topics.question: What is the maximum number of custom fields allowed per standard or custom object?
topics.answer: The maximum is 500 custom fields per object for Enterprise and Unlimited editions. This includes all custom field types — text, number, formula, etc. Developer Edition has lower limits. This limit encourages thoughtful data modeling rather than creating fields indiscriminately.

topics.question: A field currently stores unformatted text but users now need to enter formatted content with bullets and links. Which field type should it be changed to?
topics.answer: Change it to Text Area (Rich). This field type supports HTML formatting including bullet lists, hyperlinks, bold/italic, and image embedding. Remember the trade-offs: Rich text fields cannot be used in formulas or report filters. If the field is already used in formulas or reports as a filter, that usage must be redesigned.

topics.question: When would you choose a Checkbox field over a Required Picklist with Yes/No values?
topics.answer: Use a Checkbox when the answer is strictly binary (true/false, yes/no) and you want a compact, clear UI element. Checkbox fields default to 'false' (unchecked), are never null, and work cleanly in boolean formula logic. A Yes/No picklist has three states (Yes, No, blank), which adds complexity. Checkboxes are preferred for simple boolean flags.

topics.question: What is the difference between a Date field and a Date/Time field, and when does the distinction matter in formulas?
topics.answer: Date stores only a calendar date (no time component). Date/Time stores both date and time, stored in UTC and displayed in the user's time zone.
