The distinction matters in formulas when calculating differences: DATE - DATE returns a number (days); DATETIMEVALUE operations must account for time zones. Use Date for birthdays or deadlines; use Date/Time for events, timestamps, or SLA calculations.

topics.question: What field type should be used to store a unique integration ID from an external system that will be used for upsert operations?
topics.answer: Use a Text field with the 'External ID' checkbox enabled and 'Unique' checkbox enabled. This allows the field to be used as an upsert key in Data Loader and the API. External ID + Unique ensures no duplicate integration IDs exist, and the field is indexed for fast lookup during upsert matching.

topics.question: An admin is considering changing a custom field from Text to Picklist. Select two consequences that will occur as a result of this field type change.
topics.answer: Two consequences: (1) Existing text values in the field will not automatically match any picklist value — they become stale/invalid picklist entries that display but may cause issues in validation and reporting. (2) If 'Restrict picklist to value set' is enabled, those stale values will fail validation on save. Data cleanup is needed post-conversion.

topics.question: What is the INCLUDES() formula function and when is it required instead of ISPICKVAL() when referencing a multi-select picklist field?
topics.answer: INCLUDES() is required for multi-select picklist fields. It checks whether a specific value is among the selected values in a multi-select picklist. ISPICKVAL() only works with single-value picklist fields. Since multi-select picklists store a semicolon-delimited string of values, INCLUDES() parses that string correctly. Example: INCLUDES(Multi_Select_Field__c, 'Option A').

topics.question: What is the maximum number of fields per object that can be enabled for field history tracking?
topics.answer: A maximum of 20 fields per object can be enabled for field history tracking. History data is retained for 18 months (or longer with a data archive add-on). Field history tracking records who changed a field, when, and from what value to what value — viewable in the History related list on the record.

topics.question: What is a multi-select picklist field and what are its key limitations in reports (cannot group by, cannot use standard filters) and formula fields?
topics.answer: A multi-select picklist allows users to select multiple values from a list. Key limitations: in reports, you cannot group by a multi-select picklist field, and standard filter operators (equals, contains) do not work as expected. In formulas, you must use INCLUDES() to check for a value. ISPICKVAL() does not work. These constraints make multi-select picklists harder to report on and automate.

topics.question: What is a global picklist value set and how does it differ from the values defined locally on an individual picklist field?
topics.answer: A global picklist value set is a centrally managed list of values that multiple picklist fields across different objects can share. Changes to the global set propagate to all fields using it. A locally defined picklist has its own values managed independently. Use global picklists for consistency (e.g., a standard 'Region' list used across Accounts, Opportunities, and Cases).

topics.question: What is a geolocation field type, what does it store, and what is a common declarative use case for it?
topics.answer: A geolocation field stores latitude and longitude coordinates. Declarative use cases: calculating distance between records using the DISTANCE() and GEOLOCATION() formula functions, proximity-based list view filters, and mapping integrations. For example, finding all Accounts within 50 miles of a given location using a report filter or formula.

topics.question: When values are added to or removed from a global picklist value set, which picklist fields that reference that set are automatically updated?
topics.answer: All picklist fields that reference the global value set are automatically updated when values are added or removed from the set. This is the key operational benefit of global value sets — one change propagates everywhere. However, removing a value from a global set may leave existing records with stale values, so data impact assessment is important.

topics.question: What is a field dependency (dependent picklist) and what are the roles of the controlling field versus the dependent field?
topics.answer: A field dependency links two fields so the values available in the dependent field are filtered based on the value selected in the controlling field. Controlling field: drives which values appear in the dependent field (must be a picklist or checkbox). Dependent field: shows only the values mapped to the controlling field's selected value. Example: selecting 'Country' filters which 'State' values appear.

topics.question: Which field types can serve as a controlling field in a field dependency?
topics.answer: Controlling fields must be either a standard or custom picklist field (single-select) or a checkbox field. Multi-select picklists cannot be controlling fields. The controlling field drives the filtering logic for the dependent field. Radio button-style picklists and checkboxes are the only supported controlling field types.

topics.question: Which field types can serve as a dependent field in a field dependency?
topics.answer: Dependent fields must be picklist fields (single-select) or multi-select picklist fields. Text fields, numbers, and other field types cannot be dependent fields. The values shown in the dependent field are filtered by what is mapped in the dependency matrix to the controlling field's selected value.

topics.question: When a record type is applied to an object, what controls which picklist values are available to users assigned that record type?
topics.answer: The record type's picklist value configuration controls this. In each record type, an admin selects a subset of the master picklist values for each picklist field. Users assigned that record type only see those selected values. This is separate from field dependencies — record types filter by user persona, dependencies filter by another field's value.

topics.question: A company needs the 'Product Family' picklist to filter which values appear in the 'Product Sub-type' picklist on the same record. Which feature implements this?
topics.answer: Field Dependencies (dependent picklists). Make 'Product Family' the controlling field and 'Product Sub-type' the dependent field. In the dependency matrix, map which Sub-type values should be available for each Product Family value. When the user selects a Product Family, only the relevant Sub-type values appear.

topics.question: What is field history tracking and what types of field changes does it capture on a Salesforce record?
topics.answer: Field history tracking automatically logs changes to enabled fields. For each change it captures: the date/time of the change, the user who made it, the old value, and the new value. It is viewable in the '[Object] History' related list. It supports up to 20 fields per object and retains data for 18 months. It tracks changes from UI, API, automation, and imports.

topics.question: What does marking a field 'Required' at the field definition level mean, and in which save contexts (API, Flow, page layout) does it enforce a value?
topics.answer: Marking a field Required at the field level (in field setup) makes it mandatory in every save context — UI, API, and automation (Flow, Apex, Data Loader). No record can be saved without a value, regardless of how the save is initiated. This is the strongest enforcement level and is appropriate when the field is always business-critical.

topics.question: What does marking a field 'Required' on a page layout mean, and how does this differ from the field definition level requirement?
topics.answer: Marking a field Required on a page layout only enforces the value when a user saves through that specific page layout in the UI. API calls, Flows, and other automated saves that bypass the page layout are NOT affected. This is a UI-only enforcement. Use this when the field is contextually required for a specific user workflow but not universally mandatory.

topics.question: When should you enforce a field as required using a validation rule rather than at the field definition level or on a page layout?
topics.answer: Use a validation rule for conditional requirements — for example, 'Close Date is required only when Stage = Closed Won.' Field-level requirement is unconditional (always required). Page layout requirement is layout-context-only. Validation rules are the only mechanism that can enforce conditional field requirements across all save contexts (UI and API).

topics.question: If a field is marked Required on a page layout but not at the field definition level, what happens when the record is saved via an API call or a Flow that does not include that field?
topics.answer: The record saves successfully without a value in that field. Page layout requirements only apply to UI-based saves through that specific layout. API and Flow saves bypass page layouts entirely. If enforcement across all save contexts is needed, either mark the field Required at the field definition level or write a validation rule.

topics.question: What is the maximum character length of a Text Area (Long) field in Salesforce?
topics.answer: A Text Area (Long) field supports up to 131,072 characters (128 KB). This makes it suitable for storing large blocks of plain text such as notes, descriptions, or log data. Unlike Rich Text, it does not support HTML formatting but can be used in more formula and automation contexts.

objectives.title: Explain the capabilities and considerations of the Schema Builder.

topics.question: What can be accomplished in Schema Builder that is also possible through standard Setup object management?
topics.answer: Schema Builder allows you to: create new custom objects, create new custom fields on existing objects, define relationships between objects, and view field properties. All of these actions are also available through individual object management pages in Setup. Schema Builder just provides a visual canvas instead of navigating menus.

topics.question: What actions CANNOT be performed in Schema Builder (e.g., deleting fields, managing field dependencies, creating custom settings)?
topics.answer: Schema Builder cannot: delete fields or objects, manage field dependencies (dependent picklists), create or manage custom settings or metadata types, configure validation rules, configure page layouts, or manage picklist values. For these tasks, you must navigate to the individual object's setup page.

topics.question: Can you create new custom objects and fields directly from the Schema Builder canvas?
topics.answer: Yes. You can drag a new object onto the Schema Builder canvas to create it, and you can add fields to existing objects by clicking the object and using the 'Add fields' option. Relationship fields (lookup and master-detail) can also be created by drawing a line between objects on the canvas. This is one of Schema Builder's most useful features for rapid prototyping.

topics.question: What is the primary use case for using Schema Builder over individual object management pages in Setup?
topics.answer: The primary use case is visualizing and understanding a complex data model. Schema Builder displays all objects and their relationships on one canvas, making it easy to see the full entity-relationship diagram. This is especially valuable when reviewing an unfamiliar org or planning changes to a multi-object data model without navigating dozens of separate Setup pages.

topics.question: How does Schema Builder help a developer or admin understand a complex data model with many relationships?
topics.answer: Schema Builder renders objects as entity boxes connected by relationship lines (master-detail and lookup). You can filter which objects to display, zoom in/out, and drag objects around the canvas. This visual representation immediately shows how objects relate — which is a master, which has lookup relationships, and the cardinality of each relationship — far faster than reading object setup pages individually.

objectives.title: Given a scenario, determine the options and considerations when importing and exporting data, including the capabilities of external data sources.

topics.question: What is the Data Import Wizard and what types of standard objects does it support natively?
topics.answer: The Data Import Wizard is a browser-based import tool in Setup. It natively supports: Accounts, Contacts, Leads, Solutions, Campaign Members, and custom objects. It does not support all standard objects (e.g., Opportunities, Cases are not supported). It is simple to use, has a guided interface, and handles duplicate matching via matching rules.

topics.question: What is the maximum record count supported by the Data Import Wizard in a single import?
topics.answer: The Data Import Wizard supports up to 50,000 records per import file. For larger volumes, Data Loader or Bulk API must be used. The 50,000 record limit makes the Import Wizard suitable for moderate data imports but inadequate for large-scale migrations.

topics.question: How does Data Loader differ from the Data Import Wizard in terms of record volume, object support, and automation?
topics.answer: Data Loader: supports up to 5 million records per operation, works with all standard and custom objects, supports all DML operations (insert, update, upsert, delete, hard delete, export), can be run via command line for automation, and requires a desktop installation. Data Import Wizard: browser-based, max 50,000 records, limited object support, no automation capability.

topics.question: What is the difference between a hard delete and a soft delete when using Data Loader?
topics.answer: Soft delete (standard delete): moves records to the Recycle Bin, where they can be restored within 15 days. Hard delete: permanently removes records, bypassing the Recycle Bin. Hard delete requires the 'Hard Delete' permission on the user's profile. Hard deleted records cannot be recovered and free up data storage immediately.

topics.question: What is an external object in Salesforce and how does it differ from a custom object?
topics.answer: An external object is a Salesforce object that maps to data stored in an external system (outside Salesforce) via Salesforce Connect and OData or custom adapters. Data is accessed in real time — not stored in Salesforce. A custom object stores data natively in Salesforce's database. External objects are used when you want to view external data in Salesforce without importing and storing it.

topics.question: What is Salesforce Connect and what does it enable in terms of accessing external data?
topics.answer: Salesforce Connect is a middleware feature that allows Salesforce to display data from external systems in real time without storing it in Salesforce. It uses OData protocol or custom adapters. Data appears as external objects in Salesforce with related lists, list views, and record detail pages — but the data lives in the external system. Ideal for read-heavy, real-time integration needs.

topics.question: What is an External ID field and how is it used during an upsert operation in Data Loader?
topics.answer: An External ID field is a custom field with the External ID checkbox enabled, making it an indexed unique identifier from an external system. During an upsert operation in Data Loader, you specify the External ID field as the match key. If a record with that External ID value exists, it is updated; if not, a new record is inserted. This prevents duplicates during repeated imports.

topics.question: A company needs to import 200,000 account records from an external system. Which tool should be used?
topics.answer: Data Loader. The Data Import Wizard is limited to 50,000 records and does not support Accounts in all scenarios cleanly at scale. Data Loader handles up to 5 million records, supports Account imports fully, and can be run in batch mode via command line. For 200,000 records, Data Loader is the appropriate tool.

topics.question: What is a matching rule and how does it work with duplicate rules to prevent data duplication?
topics.answer: A matching rule defines the logic for identifying potential duplicate records (e.g., match on Email + Last Name + Company). A duplicate rule uses matching rules to determine what happens when a match is found — either alert the user, block the save, or allow with a warning. Together, they form Salesforce's native duplicate management framework.

topics.question: What duplicate management features exist in Salesforce for handling duplicate records during import?
topics.answer: Salesforce provides: (1) Matching Rules — define what fields constitute a match, (2) Duplicate Rules — define the action when a match is found (block, alert, allow), (3) Duplicate Jobs — a batch process that scans existing data for duplicates and surfaces them for review. Data Import Wizard also has built-in duplicate handling using matching rules.

topics.question: What is the Data Export Service in Salesforce Setup and what are the two available export frequency options?
topics.answer: The Data Export Service allows full org data exports as ZIP files of CSV data. It is available in Setup under Data > Data Export. Two frequency options: Weekly (export every 7 days) and Monthly (export once per month, typically on a scheduled date). Enterprise and Unlimited editions support weekly exports; lower editions are limited to monthly. Exports include all standard and custom object data.

objectives.title: Given a scenario, demonstrate the use of formula fields to meet stated business requirements.

topics.question: What is the IF() function in a formula field and how is it structured?
topics.answer: IF(logical_test, value_if_true, value_if_false). It evaluates a condition and returns one of two values. Example: IF(Amount > 100000, 'High Value', 'Standard'). The return type must be consistent across both branches (both text, both number, etc.). IF() can be nested for multiple conditions, though CASE() is cleaner for many discrete values.

topics.question: What is the difference between the TODAY() and NOW() formula functions?
topics.answer: TODAY() returns the current date (no time component) as a Date value. NOW() returns the current date and time as a DateTime value in UTC. Use TODAY() for date arithmetic (days until close, days since created). Use NOW() when time precision matters (SLA violations calculated in hours/minutes). Mixing Date and DateTime in formulas causes errors.

topics.question: What is the CASE() function in a formula field and how does it differ from nested IF() statements?
topics.answer: CASE(expression, value1, result1, value2, result2, ..., else_result) compares an expression against a list of discrete values and returns the matching result. It is cleaner and more readable than deeply nested IF() for multiple exact-match scenarios (like translating picklist values to text labels). IF() is better for range-based or boolean conditions.

topics.question: What is the difference between ISNULL() and ISBLANK() in formula fields?
topics.answer: ISNULL() checks if a field is null — but for text fields, it returns false even for empty strings (because empty string != null in Salesforce). ISBLANK() checks for both null AND empty string, making it the correct function for text fields. For non-text fields (number, date, checkbox), both behave the same. Best practice: use ISBLANK() for text fields always.

topics.question: What is the BLANKVALUE() function and when should it be used instead of ISNULL()?
topics.answer: BLANKVALUE(field, replacement_value) returns the replacement value if the field is blank or null, otherwise returns the field value. Use it instead of ISNULL() for text fields because BLANKVALUE() treats both null and empty string as blank. Example: BLANKVALUE(Phone, 'N/A') returns 'N/A' if Phone is blank, otherwise returns the phone number.

topics.question: What does the NULLVALUE() function do and when would you use it over BLANKVALUE()?
topics.answer: NULLVALUE(field, replacement_value) returns the replacement value only if the field is null, not if it is an empty string. Use NULLVALUE() for non-text fields (numbers, dates, checkboxes) where null is the only 'no value' state. For text fields, BLANKVALUE() is the safer choice since it handles both null and empty string.

topics.question: What is the ISPICKVAL() function and when is it required in a formula instead of a direct equality comparison?
topics.answer: ISPICKVAL(picklist_field, 'value') is required when comparing a single-value picklist field to a specific value in a formula. You cannot use picklist_field = 'value' directly in formulas. ISPICKVAL() correctly handles the picklist data type. Example: ISPICKVAL(Stage, 'Closed Won'). For multi-select picklists, use INCLUDES() instead.

topics.question: What is the maximum compile size (character limit) for a formula field?
topics.answer: The maximum compile size for a formula field is 5,000 characters. This is the size after all referenced formula fields are expanded inline. The raw formula text you write is limited to 3,900 characters. Large formulas that reference many other formulas may hit the 5,000 compile limit even if the source text is under 3,900 characters.

topics.question: What is the TEXT() function used for in a formula field?
topics.answer: TEXT() converts a non-text value (picklist, date, date/time, number, currency) into a text string so it can be concatenated with other text or used in text-returning formulas. Example: 'Stage: ' & TEXT(Stage) converts the picklist value to text. Without TEXT(), you cannot concatenate a picklist or number directly with a text literal.

topics.question: What is the maximum number of unique cross-object relationships that can be referenced in a single formula field?
topics.answer: A formula field can reference up to 10 unique relationships (cross-object hops). This means you can traverse up to 10 different parent-child links in a single formula. Additionally, formulas can only traverse up to 5 levels deep in a single relationship chain. These limits prevent formula fields from becoming excessively resource-intensive.

topics.question: A formula must display a picklist field's value as part of a text string. Which function is required to convert the picklist value to text?
topics.answer: The TEXT() function is required. Picklist fields are not text data types in formulas — they are a special picklist type. To concatenate a picklist value into a text string or return it from a text-returning formula, you must wrap it with TEXT(). Example: 'Current Status: ' & TEXT(Status__c).

topics.question: What is the IMAGE() formula function and when would you use it on a record?
topics.answer: IMAGE(image_url, alt_text, height, width) embeds an image (from a URL) in a formula field result on a record. Use it to display icons, color-coded status indicators, or thumbnail images based on field values. Example: use IMAGE() to show a red/yellow/green traffic light icon based on a risk score. The formula field return type must be Text for IMAGE() to work.

topics.question: What is the HYPERLINK() formula function used for and what parameters does it require?
topics.answer: HYPERLINK(url, friendly_name, target) creates a clickable hyperlink in a formula field. Parameters: url (the destination URL, can use field merge syntax), friendly_name (display text), target (optional: '_blank' opens in new tab, '_self' in same window). Use it to create links to external systems, record pages, or filtered views directly from a record.

topics.question: Can a formula field reference a field on a related (parent) object, and what is the syntax for doing so?
topics.answer: Yes. For lookup relationships, the syntax is: Object__r.Field__c (using __r to traverse the relationship). For standard relationships, use the relationship name (e.g., Account.Industry for a Contact's parent Account). This is called a cross-object formula. You can traverse up to 5 levels deep and reference up to 10 unique relationships per formula.

topics.question: What formula function returns the number of days between two Date fields?
topics.answer: Simple subtraction: Date2 - Date1 returns the number of days as a number. There is no special function — Salesforce Date arithmetic directly supports subtraction of two Date values. Example: CloseDate - TODAY() returns the number of days until close. For Date/Time subtraction, the result is in fractional days (divide by 1 for days, multiply by 24 for hours).

topics.question: What return data types can a formula field produce?
topics.answer: Formula fields can return: Text, Number, Currency, Percent, Date, Date/Time, Checkbox (Boolean), and URL. The selected return type determines which functions and operators are valid in the formula and how the result is displayed and used in reports, filters, and automation.

topics.question: A business requires a formula that returns different text values based on a numeric range. Which function is best suited for this (CASE vs. IF vs. nested IF)?
topics.answer: Nested IF() is best for numeric range conditions because CASE() only works with exact-match equality checks. For ranges like 'if score > 80, then Excellent; if > 60, then Good; else Needs Work,' nested IF() handles the range comparisons correctly. CASE() cannot evaluate greater-than or less-than conditions.

topics.question: What is the LEN() formula function and when would you use it in a validation or formula context?
topics.answer: LEN(text) returns the number of characters in a text string. Use it in validation rules to enforce minimum/maximum text length (e.g., REQUIRE that a description is at least 50 characters: LEN(Description__c) < 50). In formula fields, use it to display text length or conditionally evaluate fields based on character count.

topics.question: What is the CONTAINS() function in a formula and what data type does it return?
topics.answer: CONTAINS(text, search_string) returns a Boolean (TRUE or FALSE). It checks whether the text field contains the search string anywhere within it (case-insensitive in most contexts). Use it in validation rules and IF() conditions to check for substring presence. Example: CONTAINS(Email__c, '@company.com') to validate internal email addresses.

topics.question: What is the BEGINS() formula function and how does it differ from CONTAINS()?
topics.answer: BEGINS(text, search_string) returns TRUE if the text starts with the search_string. CONTAINS() checks anywhere in the string. Use BEGINS() when you need to validate a prefix (e.g., phone numbers starting with '+1') or categorize records based on the start of a code. Both return Boolean and are usable in IF() and validation rules.

topics.question: An admin is building a formula field that must handle both empty text fields and null values safely. Select two functions that address blank/null handling in formula fields.
topics.answer: Two functions: (1) ISBLANK() — returns TRUE if the text field is null OR empty string, safe for text fields. (2) BLANKVALUE(field, default) — returns a default value when the field is null or empty string. Together these cover all blank/null states for text fields. ISNULL() should be avoided for text fields as it misses empty strings.

objectives.title: Given a scenario, determine the capabilities and use cases for approval processes.

topics.question: What are entry criteria in an approval process and what happens if a record does not meet them when submitted?
topics.answer: Entry criteria define the conditions a record must meet to enter the approval process (e.g., Discount > 20%). If a record is submitted but does not meet the entry criteria, the process is automatically approved (or skipped) based on the 'If the submitter's profile does not have authority' setting, or it moves to the next step. By default, records not meeting criteria are auto-approved.

topics.question: What types of approvers can be defined in an approval process step (user, related user, manager field, queue)?
topics.answer: Approver types in a step: (1) Specific user(s) — named individuals, (2) Related user — a user referenced by a field on the record (e.g., the record's Account Manager), (3) Manager field — the submitting user's manager from the user hierarchy, (4) Queue — any member of a specified queue can approve. Multiple approver types can be combined in a single step.

topics.question: What is an initial submission action in an approval process and when does it execute?
topics.answer: The initial submission action executes immediately when a user submits the record for approval — before any approver reviews it. Common uses: lock the record to prevent editing, update a Status field to 'Pending Approval', send a notification to the submitter confirming receipt. It runs regardless of whether the record is eventually approved or rejected.

topics.question: What is a final approval action in an approval process and when does it execute?
topics.answer: The final approval action executes when the record has been approved by all required approvers and the process is complete. Common uses: update a Status field to 'Approved', unlock the record, send a congratulations notification, trigger downstream automation. It runs only after the last approval step is approved.

topics.question: What is a final rejection action in an approval process and when does it execute?
topics.answer: The final rejection action executes when any approver rejects the record and the rejection is final (no further steps). Common uses: unlock the record, update Status to 'Rejected', send a notification to the submitter explaining rejection. If the process has multiple steps with different rejection behaviors, the final rejection action runs after the rejection cascade completes.

topics.question: What is a recall action in an approval process?
topics.answer: A recall action executes when the submitter (or an admin) recalls (withdraws) a pending approval request. Common uses: unlock the record, update Status back to its pre-submission value (e.g., 'Draft'), notify the approver that the request has been withdrawn. Recall removes the pending approval from the approver's queue.

topics.question: What does record locking mean in an approval process and which types of users can still edit a locked record?
topics.answer: Record locking prevents regular users from editing a record while it is pending approval. Only: (1) administrators, (2) the current approver in the step, and (3) users with 'Modify All' on the object can edit a locked record. Locking is typically configured as an initial submission action. It ensures the record is not changed while under review.

topics.question: What is a delegated approver in an approval process?
topics.answer: A delegated approver is an alternate user designated to approve on behalf of a primary approver when that approver is unavailable (e.g., on vacation). Each user can set a delegated approver in their user settings. When configured in the approval process to 'Allow delegation', the delegated approver receives approval tasks in addition to the primary approver.

topics.question: What is the maximum number of steps allowed in a single approval process?
topics.answer: A single approval process can have up to 30 steps. Each step can have different approvers, criteria, and actions. In practice, most approval processes have far fewer steps (typically 1-5). The 30-step limit is sufficient for even complex multi-tier approval hierarchies.

topics.question: What is the difference between 'Approve or reject based on the first response' and 'Require unanimous approval from all selected approvers' in a multi-approver step?
topics.answer: 'First response' means whichever assigned approver acts first determines the outcome — if one approves, it is approved; if one rejects, it is rejected. 'Unanimous' means ALL assigned approvers must approve for the step to advance; a single rejection rejects the entire step. Use first-response for speed; use unanimous for consensus-required decisions.

topics.question: What types of automated actions can be configured as approval, rejection, recall, or initial submission actions?
topics.answer: Supported action types in approval processes: Field Update (change a field value), Email Alert (send a templated email), Task (create a follow-up task), and Outbound Message (send a SOAP message to an external endpoint). Flows can also be triggered from approval process actions via the 'Launch a Flow' action type.

topics.question: A manager must approve any discount greater than 20% before an opportunity can advance to 'Negotiation/Review'. Which Salesforce feature best models this requirement?
topics.answer: An Approval Process on the Opportunity object. Configure: entry criteria = Discount__c > 20%, approver = the submitting user's manager (manager field), initial submission action = lock the record, final approval action = update Stage to 'Negotiation/Review'. This precisely matches the business requirement with native Salesforce declarative tools.

topics.question: Can an approval process be triggered programmatically from a Flow?
topics.answer: Yes. A Flow can submit a record for approval using the 'Submit for Approval' core action in Flow Builder. This allows automated submission based on trigger conditions without user action. For example, a record-triggered Flow could automatically submit an Opportunity for approval when Discount is set above a threshold.

topics.question: What is an approval page layout and what fields does it display to the approver?
topics.answer: The approval page layout defines which fields the approver sees on the approval detail page when reviewing a request. It is separate from the record's page layout. Admins configure it to show only the fields relevant to the approval decision (e.g., Discount %, Opportunity Name, Amount). A well-designed approval page layout gives approvers focused context without information overload.

topics.question: A business requires that when an approval request is rejected, the record is unlocked and a field is updated to 'Rejected'. Select two approval process action types that must be configured to achieve this outcome.
topics.answer: Two actions needed: (1) Field Update action — set the Status (or Approval_Status__c) field to 'Rejected'. (2) Field Update action — set the record lock: use an 'Unlock the record for editing' field update, OR configure the rejection action to unlock. Both actions are configured in the 'Final Rejection Actions' section of the approval process. These two together satisfy both requirements.

objectives.title: Given a scenario, determine the tool or action needed to meet business requirements.

topics.question: What are the four action types that Workflow Rules support (field updates, email alerts, tasks, outbound messages)?
topics.answer: Workflow Rules support exactly four action types: (1) Field Update — change a field value on the record or its master, (2) Email Alert — send a templated email to specified recipients, (3) Task — create a follow-up task and assign it, (4) Outbound Message — send a SOAP XML notification to an external endpoint. No other action types are supported. Workflow Rules are considered legacy — Flow is the recommended replacement.

topics.question: Can Workflow Rules create new records?
topics.answer: No. Workflow Rules cannot create new records. They can only update the triggering record or its master (via field update), send emails, create tasks, or send outbound messages. To create new related records declaratively, use a record-triggered Flow with a Create Records element.

topics.question: What is the current Salesforce recommendation for new automation — Workflow Rules, Process Builder, or Flow Builder?
topics.answer: Salesforce recommends Flow Builder for all new automation. Workflow Rules and Process Builder are retired (or being retired) — Salesforce announced the end-of-life for both. Existing Workflow Rules continue to function, but new automation should be built in Flow Builder, which supersedes both with greater capability and maintainability.

topics.question: What is a record-triggered Flow and what record events can trigger it?
topics.answer: A record-triggered Flow executes automatically when a record is created, updated, or deleted. Trigger options: (1) A record is created, (2) A record is updated, (3) A record is created or updated, (4) A record is deleted. You can further refine with entry conditions so the Flow only runs when specific field criteria are met — preventing unnecessary executions.

topics.question: What is the difference between a before-save and an after-save record-triggered Flow?
topics.answer: Before-save Flow: runs before the record is committed to the database. Can update fields on the triggering record without a DML operation (fast). Cannot create/update/delete other records. After-save Flow: runs after the record is committed. Can create, update, or delete other records. Uses DML operations. Before-save is more efficient for field updates on the triggering record.

topics.question: When is a before-save record-triggered Flow preferred over an after-save Flow?
topics.answer: Before-save is preferred when you only need to set/update fields on the triggering record itself — it does not consume a DML operation, making it faster and more governor-limit-friendly. Use before-save for: setting values, calculating derived fields, formatting text on save. Use after-save when you need to interact with other records (create child records, update related objects).

topics.question: What is a scheduled-triggered (Scheduled Path) Flow and when would you use one?
topics.answer: A Scheduled Path (on a record-triggered Flow) runs at a specified time relative to a date/time field on the record (e.g., '30 days after CloseDate'). Use it for: sending follow-up reminders, escalating cases after SLA breach, automatically advancing records after a time delay. The record must still meet entry criteria at the time the scheduled path fires.

topics.question: What is a Screen Flow and how is it surfaced to users in a Lightning app?
topics.answer: A Screen Flow is an interactive, guided wizard-style Flow that displays UI screens to collect input from users. It is surfaced via: a Lightning component on a record page (Flow component in App Builder), a Quick Action, a Utility Bar component, a custom Tab, or embedded in an Experience Cloud page. Users interact with the screens and the Flow processes their input.

topics.question: What is an auto-launched Flow and when would it be used instead of a Screen Flow?
topics.answer: An auto-launched Flow runs without any user interaction — no screens. It is triggered by: record events (record-triggered Flow), Apex code, a process, another Flow (subflow), a REST API call, or a schedule. Use auto-launched Flows for background automation that does not need user input. Screen Flows are only for user-interactive guided processes.

topics.question: What is a Platform Event-triggered Flow and what is its primary use case?
topics.answer: A Platform Event-triggered Flow fires when a specific Platform Event message is published. Primary use case: real-time integrations where an external system or Apex publishes a Platform Event and the Flow handles the resulting business logic (e.g., create a record, send a notification). It decouples the publishing system from the business logic handler.

topics.question: A business needs to automatically create a follow-up Task 30 days after an Opportunity closes. Which automation tool and feature should be used?
topics.answer: Use a record-triggered Flow on Opportunity with a Scheduled Path set to '30 days after CloseDate'. When the CloseDate is reached (with the record in a Closed stage), the scheduled path fires a Create Records element to create a Task. This is the declarative, modern replacement for time-based workflow actions.

topics.question: What does an outbound message (Workflow) do vs. an HTTP callout action in a Flow?
topics.answer: Outbound Message: sends a one-way SOAP/XML notification to an external endpoint — no response is processed back into Salesforce. HTTP Callout action (Flow): sends an HTTP request to a REST or SOAP endpoint and can process the response back into the Flow to update Salesforce records. HTTP Callout is bidirectional; Outbound Message is one-way notification only.

topics.question: A business requirement is to update a related Account field whenever a related Opportunity Stage changes. Legacy Workflow Rules are already in use. Which tool handles this?
topics.answer: A record-triggered Flow on Opportunity (triggered on update, entry condition: Stage changed) with an Update Records element targeting the related Account. Flow Builder handles cross-object field updates natively and is the recommended modern tool. Legacy Workflow Rules can also do this via a Field Update on the master (Account), but Flow is the preferred path.

topics.question: A company needs to send a one-way SOAP notification to an external system when a record status changes and does not need a response. Which automation feature handles this?
topics.answer: An Outbound Message (configured in a Workflow Rule or Approval Process action). It sends a SOAP XML message to an external endpoint and does not wait for or process a response back into Salesforce. If using Flow, an HTTP Callout to a SOAP endpoint also works but is bidirectional. For purely one-way SOAP notification, Outbound Message is the native feature.

topics.question: A business needs to (1) create a follow-up task when a case is closed AND (2) post a Chatter message to the case record. Select two automation actions that together satisfy both requirements using a single record-triggered Flow.
topics.answer: Two actions in a single after-save record-triggered Flow: (1) Create Records element — create a Task related to the Case. (2) Post to Chatter core action (or Create a FeedItem record) — post a message to the Case's Chatter feed. Both actions can be sequential elements in one Flow, fired when Case Status = 'Closed'. No need for two separate automation tools.

topics.question: What does the Get Records element in Flow Builder do and how does it query Salesforce data?
topics.answer: The Get Records element queries Salesforce using filter conditions you define (like a SOQL WHERE clause) and returns matching records. You specify the object, filter criteria, sort order, and how many records to retrieve. The results are stored in a record variable (single record) or record collection variable (multiple records) for use in subsequent Flow elements.

topics.question: What are the two output modes of the Get Records element in Flow Builder (single record vs. record collection), and when would you choose each?
topics.answer: Single record: returns only the first matching record — use when you know only one record matches or only need one (e.g., get the Account related to the triggering Contact). Record collection: returns all matching records as a list — use when you need to process multiple records (e.g., get all open Cases related to an Account for loop processing).

topics.question: What does the Delete Records element in Flow Builder do, and what happens to child records in a master-detail relationship when the parent is deleted via Flow?
topics.answer: The Delete Records element permanently deletes specified records (moves them to Recycle Bin). If the deleted record is a master in a master-detail relationship, child records are cascade deleted — exactly as if deleted from the UI. The Flow does not need to explicitly delete child records; the platform handles cascade deletion automatically.

topics.question: What does the Create Records element in Flow Builder do, and can it create multiple records in a single element using a record collection variable?
topics.answer: The Create Records element inserts one or more new records into Salesforce. Yes — you can use a record collection variable as the input, allowing the element to create multiple records in a single bulk operation. This is important for governor limit efficiency: creating 100 records from a collection in one element is far better than looping with individual Create elements.

topics.question: What does the Update Records element in Flow Builder do, and how does it differ from updating the triggering record via a fast field update assignment in a before-save Flow?
topics.answer: Update Records element: uses a DML update operation to modify records (can update any records, including unrelated ones). Costs a DML governor limit count. Fast field update in a before-save Flow: directly modifies fields on the triggering record in memory before the record is saved — no DML operation, no governor limit consumption. Before-save fast updates are more efficient for simple field updates on the triggering record.

topics.question: What is a collection variable in Flow Builder and when is it used with a Loop element?
topics.answer: A collection variable stores multiple records (or values) of the same type — like an array. It is used with a Loop element to iterate over each item in the collection one at a time. Common pattern: Get Records returns a collection, a Loop iterates over each record, a Decision evaluates each one, and an Assignment adds qualifying records to a new collection for bulk Update/Create.

topics.question: What is the Decision element in Flow Builder, how does it create branching logic, and what is the 'Default Outcome'?
topics.answer: The Decision element evaluates one or more conditions and routes Flow execution down different paths (outcomes) based on which condition is true. Each outcome has its own set of conditions. The 'Default Outcome' is the path taken when no other outcome's conditions are met — always include a default to prevent unhandled scenarios and Flow errors.

topics.question: How is a collection variable populated using an Assignment element within a Flow loop?
topics.answer: Inside a Loop, use an Assignment element to add the current loop item to a collection variable using the 'Add' operator: Assignment sets [CollectionVariable] = [CollectionVariable] + {Loop_Current_Item}. This appends each qualifying item to the collection as the loop progresses. After the loop exits, the collection variable contains all the accumulated items for bulk processing.

topics.question: What is the Assignment element in Flow Builder and what types of operators can it apply to a variable (equals, add, subtract, remove, add at start, remove all)?
topics.answer: The Assignment element sets or modifies variable values. Operators: Equals (set the variable to a value), Add (add to a number or append to a collection), Subtract (subtract from a number), Remove (remove a specific value from a collection), Add at Start (prepend to a collection), Remove All (clear all items from a collection matching a value). Multiple assignments can be stacked in a single element.

topics.question: What is the Loop element in Flow Builder, what data type does it iterate over, and what are the two connectors that exit the loop (For Each Item and After Last Item)?
topics.answer: The Loop element iterates over a collection variable (list of records or primitive values). Two exit connectors: (1) 'For Each Item' — executes once per item in the collection (the loop body), (2) 'After Last Item' — executes once after all items have been processed (post-loop logic). Everything inside the loop body runs for each collection item.

topics.question: What running context options are available for a record-triggered Flow (System Mode Without Sharing, System Mode With Sharing, Running User)?
topics.answer: Context options: (1) System Mode Without Sharing — runs with elevated access, ignores sharing rules and OWD (sees all records). (2) System Mode With Sharing — runs elevated but respects sharing rules. (3) User or System Mode Default — inherits the context of the triggering user. The choice affects which records the Flow can query and update, with security implications.

topics.question: What is the Pause element in a Screen Flow and how does it allow the flow interview to be suspended and later resumed?
topics.answer: The Pause element suspends a Screen Flow interview and saves its state. The user can close the browser and return later to resume from the paused point. Paused interviews are accessible via the 'Paused Interviews' component. This is useful for long multi-step processes (e.g., a complex onboarding wizard that users complete over multiple sessions). It requires the Flow to be launched in Lightning Experience or Experience Cloud.

topics.question: What is the difference between using an Email Alert core action and a Send Email core action in a Flow?
topics.answer: Email Alert core action: uses a pre-configured Email Alert (with a template, recipients, and from address set up in Setup). Reusable across automation tools. Send Email core action: sends an email directly from the Flow with dynamic recipients, subject, and body — more flexible but requires configuring each detail in the Flow itself. Email Alert is better for standardized, reusable notifications; Send Email for dynamic, context-specific messages.

topics.question: What is a custom notification action in Flow Builder and how is the notification delivered to recipients?
topics.answer: The 'Send Custom Notification' core action in Flow sends a bell notification (in-app) to specified users through the Salesforce Notification Builder framework. Recipients receive it as a bell icon notification in the app and optionally as a push notification on mobile. You must first create a Custom Notification Type in Setup, then reference it in the Flow action.

topics.question: What is a scheduled path in a record-triggered Flow and how is its delay defined relative to a date/time field value on the triggering record?
topics.answer: A scheduled path is a time-delayed branch of a record-triggered Flow. The delay is defined as: X Minutes/Hours/Days/Months Before or After a specified Date or Date/Time field on the record (e.g., '3 days before Close Date'). At the defined time, Salesforce re-evaluates whether the record still meets the entry criteria and executes the scheduled path if so.

topics.question: A Flow must retrieve all open cases related to an account, evaluate each one, and update those older than 30 days. Select two Flow elements required to implement this logic.
topics.answer: Two required elements: (1) Get Records — query all open Cases related to the Account (filter: AccountId = Account, Status != Closed) and store as a record collection. (2) Loop — iterate over the collection to evaluate each Case's CreatedDate. Inside the loop, a Decision element checks age > 30 days, and an Assignment builds a collection of qualifying Cases for a bulk Update Records after the loop.

topics.question: Can a record-triggered Flow be configured to fire on record deletion, and what record event trigger option enables this?
topics.answer: Yes. Set the trigger to 'A record is deleted'. The Flow fires before the record is deleted (before-delete context). This allows you to read the record's field values, create related records, log history, or send notifications based on the deletion event. Note: you cannot update the triggering record in a delete-triggered Flow since it is being deleted.

topics.question: What is a custom label in Salesforce, where is it used, and why is it preferred over hardcoding text values in Flows, Apex, or Visualforce pages?
topics.answer: A custom label is a configurable text value stored in Salesforce metadata, accessible by name in Flows, Apex ({!$Label.Label_Name}), and Visualforce pages. Preferred over hardcoding because: (1) easily changed in one place without modifying code/Flow, (2) supports translation into multiple languages (custom labels are the foundation of Salesforce's translation framework), (3) deployable via change sets.

topics.question: What is the difference between 'System Mode Without Sharing' and 'System Mode With Sharing' as running contexts in a record-triggered Flow?
topics.answer: Without Sharing: the Flow ignores the org's sharing model — it can read and write any record regardless of OWD, sharing rules, or who owns the record. With Sharing: the Flow respects the org's sharing rules when querying and updating records, but still runs as a system user (not the triggering user's permissions). Without Sharing is riskier but sometimes necessary for automation that must touch records the triggering user can't see.

topics.question: What is the 'Run Flow' action in an approval process and what type of Flow can be launched from an approval action?
topics.answer: The 'Run Flow' action in an approval process launches an auto-launched (non-screen) Flow as part of an approval, rejection, recall, or submission action. The Flow must be of type 'Auto-launched Flow' — Screen Flows cannot be used in approval process actions. This allows complex logic (multi-record creates, external callouts) to be triggered as part of the approval lifecycle.

objectives.title: Given a set of business requirements, recommend a solution to automate business processes while avoiding errors in automation.

topics.question: What is the Salesforce order of execution when a record is saved, and why is it important for automation design?
topics.answer: Key order: (1) Before-save validation rules and before-save Flows, (2) Apex before triggers, (3) Duplicate rules, (4) Record saved to database (but not committed), (5) Apex after triggers, (6) After-save Flows, (7) Workflow rules, (8) Process Builder processes, (9) Commit. Understanding this prevents conflicts — e.g., a before-save Flow updating a field that an Apex before trigger also updates could cause unexpected overwrites.

topics.question: What is 'bulkification' in the context of record-triggered Flows and why does it matter?
topics.answer: Bulkification means the platform batches record operations together and processes them in bulk rather than one-by-one. Record-triggered Flows are bulkified — when 200 records are updated at once (e.g., via Data Loader), the Flow runs once per batch, not 200 individual times. This prevents hitting governor limits. Poorly designed Flows with DML inside loops break bulkification and can cause limit errors.

topics.question: What is a circular automation loop and how can it occur between Flows and other automation tools?
topics.answer: A circular loop occurs when automation A triggers automation B, which triggers automation A again, creating infinite recursion. Example: a Flow updates Account when Opportunity is saved, and another Flow updates Opportunity when Account is saved — each triggers the other infinitely. Prevented by: entry conditions (check if the triggering field actually changed), version-aware design, and setting 'Run Once Per Record' where appropriate.

topics.question: What happens when a Flow encounters an unhandled fault (error) during execution?
topics.answer: An unhandled fault causes the Flow to stop and roll back any changes made in that transaction. An error email is sent to the Flow admin (the user who last modified the Flow). From the user's perspective, the record save fails with a generic error message. All DML operations in the transaction are rolled back. A fault path should be configured to handle errors gracefully.

topics.question: What is a fault path in Flow Builder and how should it be configured to handle errors gracefully?
topics.answer: A fault path is an alternative connector on Flow elements that is followed when an error occurs. Best practice: connect the fault path to a Screen (for Screen Flows) displaying a user-friendly error message, or to a Create Records element that logs the error details to a custom log object, or to a Send Email action alerting an admin. Without a fault path, errors are unhandled and cause full transaction rollback.

topics.question: What is a fast field update (before-save) in a Flow and how does it differ from a DML operation in terms of governor limit consumption?
topics.answer: A fast field update in a before-save Flow directly modifies the triggering record's fields in memory — it does not execute a separate DML statement. This means it does not count against the DML statements governor limit (150 per transaction). A DML operation in an after-save Flow (via Update Records) does count. Before-save fast updates are significantly more efficient for simple field manipulations.

topics.question: When should you use a subflow to modularize complex automation logic?
topics.answer: Use a subflow when: the same logic is needed in multiple Flows (DRY principle), a Flow becomes too large to maintain easily, you want to separate concerns (e.g., notification logic vs. data update logic), or when testing individual logic blocks independently is desirable. A subflow is a reusable auto-launched Flow called from a parent Flow using the Subflow element.

topics.question: A company has multiple active record-triggered Flows on the same object. What risk must be managed to prevent runaway automation?
topics.answer: The risk is interaction and ordering conflicts between Flows — and potentially circular loops. Manage by: (1) using specific entry conditions on each Flow so they only fire when truly needed, (2) ensuring no two Flows update the same field in conflicting ways, (3) using a single 'orchestrator' Flow where possible rather than many small Flows, and (4) testing with bulk data to check for governor limit issues.

topics.question: A before-save Flow needs to update several fields on a record. An after-save Flow on the same object sends an email. What is the correct execution order?
topics.answer: The before-save Flow executes first — it runs before the record is committed. The after-save Flow executes second — after the record is committed to the database. So the order is: before-save Flow field updates → record saved → after-save Flow email. The after-save Flow will see the field values set by the before-save Flow since those updates are committed first.

topics.question: A company is migrating from legacy Workflow Rules to Flow Builder. Select two true statements about Workflow Rules that describe what Flow Builder supersedes.
topics.answer: Two true statements: (1) Workflow Rules cannot create new records — Flow Builder can. (2) Workflow Rules support only four action types (Field Update, Email Alert, Task, Outbound Message) — Flow Builder supports all of these plus many more (HTTP callouts, custom notifications, Apex actions, subflows, etc.). Flow Builder is a strict superset of Workflow Rule capabilities.

topics.question: What happens to the previously active Flow version when a new version is activated?
topics.answer: When a new version of a Flow is activated, the previously active version automatically changes status to 'Obsolete'. It no longer runs for new triggers. Any in-progress (paused) interviews on the old version continue to run on that version until they complete. Only one version of a Flow can be Active at any time.

topics.question: How do you debug a Flow using the Debug button in Flow Builder, and what information does a debug run provide to help identify errors?
topics.answer: In Flow Builder, click the Debug button to open the Debug panel. You specify input variable values and run the Flow in a simulated context. The debug log shows: each element that executed, the values of variables at each step, which path was taken at each Decision, and any errors with detailed messages. This allows identification of logic errors and unexpected variable values without deploying to users.

topics.question: A record-triggered Flow must update a Status field only when the record transitions from 'Draft' to 'In Review', not on every save. Which Flow configuration prevents it from running on unrelated saves?
topics.answer: Configure entry conditions using the $Record and $Record__Prior global variables. Set the trigger to 'A record is updated' and add an entry condition: {!$Record.Status__c} = 'In Review' AND {!$Record__Prior.Status__c} = 'Draft'. This ensures the Flow only executes when the Status field specifically transitions from Draft to In Review, not on any other save.

topics.question: What is the difference between the $Record and $Record__Prior global variables in a record-triggered Flow, and how are they used to detect whether a specific field was changed?
topics.answer: $Record: contains the current (new) values of the triggering record after the change. $Record__Prior: contains the previous values before the current save (only available on update triggers). To detect a field change, compare: {!$Record.Field__c} != {!$Record__Prior.Field__c}. If they differ, the field was changed in this save. This is the declarative equivalent of 'old vs. new' in Apex triggers.

topics.question: How do entry conditions on a record-triggered Flow prevent unnecessary executions and help avoid recursive loops?
topics.answer: Entry conditions act as a gate — the Flow only executes if the record meets the specified conditions at trigger time. For example, 'only run if Status changed from Draft to Active.' This prevents the Flow from firing on every save, reducing governor limit consumption, preventing unintended side effects, and breaking potential recursive loops where the Flow's own updates would re-trigger it.

topics.question: When a before-save record-triggered Flow and an after-save record-triggered Flow both exist on the same object, what is the execution order relative to each other and relative to Apex triggers?
topics.answer: Order: (1) Before-save Flows run, (2) Apex before triggers run, (3) Record is saved to DB (not committed), (4) Apex after triggers run, (5) After-save Flows run, (6) Transaction commits. Before-save Flows run before Apex before triggers. After-save Flows run after Apex after triggers. This ordering is critical when both automation types modify the same fields.

topics.question: What are time-based workflow actions, and how do scheduled paths in a record-triggered Flow provide a more modern equivalent?
topics.answer: Time-based workflow actions are Workflow Rule actions that fire at a future time relative to a date field (e.g., 'send reminder 7 days before due date'). Scheduled paths in a record-triggered Flow provide the same capability with much greater flexibility: you can perform any Flow action (not just 4 types), use more complex conditions, and chain scheduled paths. Scheduled paths are the modern, recommended replacement.

topics.question: What are the three version statuses a Flow can have (Draft, Active, Obsolete)?
topics.answer: Draft: the Flow is being built or edited — it is not running for any users. Active: the Flow is live and executes for triggers/users. Only one version can be Active at a time. Obsolete: a previously active version that was deactivated when a new version was activated. Obsolete versions continue processing any paused interviews but do not accept new executions.

topics.question: What is the 'Run Once Per Record' option in a record-triggered Flow and when should it be enabled?
topics.answer: 'Run Once Per Record' (also called 'Run Only When Record Is Created' or the 'Runs Once Per Record' entry condition) ensures the Flow only fires the first time a record matches the entry conditions in its lifetime — not on subsequent saves that re-match. Enable it when the Flow should only set up initial values or send a one-time welcome notification upon first meeting the criteria, not every time the record is saved.

objectives.title: Describe the user interface customization options.

topics.question: What is the difference between a Lightning App Page, a Record Page, and a Home Page in Lightning App Builder?
topics.answer: App Page: a standalone page accessible via a tab in a Lightning app — used for dashboards, embedded reports, or custom landing pages. Record Page: customizes what users see when opening a specific object's record — fields, related lists, components. Home Page: customizes the main 'Home' screen for an app or the org's default home — typically shows news, recent items, dashboard components. Each page type has different component options.

topics.question: What is Lightning App Builder and what types of pages can be customized with it?
topics.answer: Lightning App Builder is a declarative drag-and-drop tool for building Lightning pages. Page types: Record Pages (object detail pages), App Pages (standalone app pages), Home Pages (the home tab), and Email Application Panes (for Outlook/Gmail integrations). You can place standard and custom Lightning components, set component visibility, and assign pages to specific apps, profiles, and record types.

topics.question: What is Dynamic Forms in Lightning App Builder and which objects does it support?
topics.answer: Dynamic Forms moves field sections from the page layout directly into the Lightning App Builder canvas, enabling component-level visibility rules on individual fields and sections. Initially only supported custom objects; Salesforce has been progressively rolling it out to standard objects (e.g., Account, Contact, Opportunity in recent releases). Check current release notes for the latest supported objects.

topics.question: What is the advantage of Dynamic Forms over traditional page layout field sections for controlling field visibility?
topics.answer: Traditional page layouts require different layouts per profile/record type to show different fields. Dynamic Forms allows visibility rules directly on individual fields or sections — a field can be shown only when a specific picklist value is selected, a checkbox is checked, or a user has a specific permission. This eliminates the need for multiple layouts for the same object/record type combination.

topics.question: What is the key eligibility restriction for Dynamic Forms (custom objects in Lightning Experience only, not standard objects initially)?
topics.answer: Dynamic Forms was initially only available for custom objects in Lightning Experience — not supported in Classic or for standard objects at launch. Salesforce has progressively expanded support to more standard objects with each release. The exam typically tests the original constraint: Dynamic Forms is a Lightning Experience-only feature and was not available for all standard objects from the start.

topics.question: What is a record type and how does it interact with page layouts in Lightning Experience?
topics.answer: A record type determines which page layout a user sees on a record (via the profile-to-record-type-to-layout mapping). In Lightning Experience, record types also determine which picklist values are available and which business process applies. The profile specifies: for this object, users with this profile see page layout X when the record has record type Y.

topics.question: How are page layouts assigned to users in Salesforce?
topics.answer: Page layouts are assigned through the Profile (or Permission Set in newer orgs). In Setup > Object Manager > Object > Page Layout Assignment, you define the matrix: for each Profile + Record Type combination, which layout is displayed. A user's combination of profile and record type determines their layout. If no specific assignment exists, the object's default layout is used.

topics.question: What is a compact layout and where is it displayed in Salesforce (record highlights panel, mobile app, Chatter)?
topics.answer: A compact layout specifies the top fields to display in: (1) the record highlights panel at the top of a Lightning record page, (2) record cards in related lists and list views, (3) the Salesforce mobile app record card header, and (4) Chatter post previews when a record is @mentioned. It is not the full page layout — it shows only the most critical identifying fields (up to 10, but typically 4-7 are shown).

topics.question: What is a list view and what customization options does it support?
topics.answer: A list view is a filtered, column-configured view of object records. Customization options: filter criteria (field conditions), columns displayed (select which fields appear), sort order, Kanban view toggle, and sharing (private, visible to specific groups, or public). Admins can create shared list views; users can create personal ones. List views also support inline editing of records.

topics.question: What is a Lightning App and how does it differ from a Classic App in terms of navigation and component support?
topics.answer: A Lightning App offers: tab-based or console navigation, a utility bar, support for Lightning components and custom pages, mobile-responsive design, and custom themes. A Classic App is a simple collection of tabs with a custom logo — no utility bar, no console navigation, no Lightning component support. Lightning Apps are configured in Setup > App Manager.

topics.question: What are component visibility filters in Lightning App Builder and how are they configured?
topics.answer: Component visibility filters are rules that determine whether a Lightning component is shown or hidden on a record page based on conditions. Conditions can evaluate: record field values (e.g., show only when Status = Active), user profile or permission, device form factor (desktop vs. mobile), and record type. They are configured by selecting a component in App Builder and clicking the 'Set Component Visibility' option.

topics.question: A company wants certain Lightning components to be visible only to users with the 'Sales Manager' permission set. Which App Builder feature enables this?
topics.answer: Component Visibility Filters in Lightning App Builder. Add a visibility filter condition: 'User > Permission > Has Permission Set: Sales Manager' (or equivalent permission-based condition). The component is rendered only when the logged-in user has the Sales Manager permission set assigned. This does not require creating a separate page per user group.

topics.question: How are Lightning pages assigned to users — by app, record type, and/or profile?
topics.answer: Lightning pages can be assigned at three levels: (1) Default for all — applies to everyone unless overridden. (2) App default — applies when accessed from a specific Lightning app. (3) App, Record Type, and Profile — the most specific level, allowing different record pages for different combinations of app + record type + profile. The most specific assignment wins.

topics.question: A company wants to show different fields on an Opportunity record page based on record type without creating multiple page layouts. Select two Lightning App Builder features that together enable field-level visibility control by record type.
topics.answer: Two features: (1) Dynamic Forms — moves fields out of the page layout and onto the App Builder canvas as individual field components. (2) Component Visibility Filters — set a filter on each field component so it is visible only when the record's record type equals a specific value. Together, one record page with Dynamic Forms + visibility filters replaces multiple record type-specific layouts.

topics.question: What are the types of custom tabs available in Salesforce (Object Tab, Web Tab, Visualforce Tab, Lightning Component Tab) and when would you use each?
topics.answer: Object Tab: displays list/detail views of a standard or custom object. Web Tab: opens an external URL in the Salesforce window — good for embedding external web apps. Visualforce Tab: hosts a Visualforce page as a tab. Lightning Component Tab: hosts a Lightning App Page or an Aura/LWC component as a standalone tab. Choose based on whether you're surfacing object data, an external site, a VF page, or a custom Lightning page.

topics.question: How does tab visibility on a profile or permission set affect what appears in the navigation bar, and what is the difference between Default On, Default Off, and Tab Hidden?
topics.answer: Default On: the tab appears in the navigation bar for users on this profile unless they personally remove it. Default Off: the tab does NOT appear by default, but users can add it via their personalization settings. Tab Hidden: the tab is completely invisible — users cannot add it. Note: Tab Hidden does not restrict record access — users can still access records via URL or related lists.

topics.question: What is the Kanban view in Salesforce, which objects support it, and how is it organized?
topics.answer: Kanban view displays records as cards organized in columns based on a picklist field value. It is available on objects with picklist fields when using list views in Lightning Experience. Common objects: Opportunities (by Stage), Cases (by Status), Leads (by Status). Users can drag cards between columns to update the picklist field value. It is a visual, board-style workflow management view.

topics.question: What is the Path component in Lightning App Builder and what can be configured on it (stage values, key fields, guidance for success text)?
topics.answer: The Path component displays a visual progress bar of a record's stage/status values. Configuration options: which field drives the stages (typically Stage for Opportunities or Status for Cases), key fields to display for each stage (shows contextual fields when a stage is selected), and 'Guidance for Success' text for each stage (tips/checklists for advancing). It is added to a record page via App Builder.

topics.question: What is the difference between Standard Navigation and Console Navigation in a Lightning App, and when is Console Navigation appropriate?
topics.answer: Standard Navigation: clicking a record opens it as a full-page view, replacing the previous page. Tabs are breadcrumb-based. Console Navigation: records open as tabs or sub-tabs within the same app window, allowing multiple records to be open simultaneously. Console Navigation is appropriate for service reps, call center agents, or any high-volume record users who need to work across many records without losing context.

topics.question: How is a page layout assigned to a user — what is the role of the profile and the record type in determining which page layout is displayed?
topics.answer: Page layout assignment is a matrix of Profile + Record Type. In Setup > Object Manager > [Object] > Page Layout Assignment, each row represents a Profile, and each column represents a Record Type. The intersection cell specifies which layout users on that profile see when viewing records of that type. If only one record type exists, the profile directly determines the layout.

topics.question: What elements can be placed on a page layout (fields, sections, related lists, buttons, custom links, actions, Visualforce pages) and which are controlled separately from the layout?
topics.answer: Page layout elements: fields, field sections, related lists, buttons (standard and custom), links, quick actions, Visualforce pages, Canvas apps, and the mobile/Lightning actions section. Controlled separately (not on the layout): field-level security (FLS), tab visibility, record type assignment, compact layouts, and Dynamic Forms field visibility (once migrated to Dynamic Forms). FLS is the most commonly confused separate control.

topics.question: A company has two types of Contact records — individual consumers and business contacts — each requiring different visible fields and picklist values. What combination of features satisfies this?
topics.answer: Use Record Types (one for Consumer, one for Business Contact) to control different picklist values and page layouts. Assign each record type to the appropriate profiles. Configure separate page layouts for each record type showing only the relevant fields. Optionally, use Dynamic Forms with visibility filters for more granular field-level control within a single layout.

topics.question: What configuration options are available when creating a new Lightning App (navigation items, utility bar components, supported form factors, user profile assignment)?
topics.answer: When creating a Lightning App in App Manager, you configure: (1) App name, description, and logo/color (branding), (2) Navigation items (which tabs/pages appear in the nav bar), (3) Utility Bar components (persistent bottom panel items like Phone, Notes, Recent Items), (4) Supported form factors (Desktop, Phone), (5) User profile assignment (which profiles can see this app). All options are set through the guided setup wizard.

topics.question: What are Lightning App themes and how can an administrator customize the app's color and logo?
topics.answer: Lightning App themes control the visual branding of a Lightning app — specifically the header bar color (brand color) and the app logo image. These are configured in App Manager when creating or editing a Lightning App. The brand color applies to the app's navigation bar. Custom logos must be uploaded as images. Themes are per-app, not org-wide (org-wide theming uses My Domain login page settings).

objectives.title: Demonstrate the capabilities and use cases for custom buttons, links, and actions.

topics.question: What is a custom button in Salesforce and where can it be placed on a page layout?
topics.answer: A custom button is a clickable element that triggers a URL, Visualforce page, or (in Classic) JavaScript. It can be placed: in the button bar at the top of a detail page (Detail Page Button), in a related list (Related List Button), or in the list view (List Button). In Lightning Experience, custom buttons in the action bar are typically surfaced as actions rather than traditional buttons.

topics.question: What content source types are available for a custom button (URL, Visualforce Page, JavaScript — noting JavaScript is Classic only)?
topics.answer: Content source options: (1) URL — navigates to a specified URL (can include field merge syntax for dynamic URLs), (2) Visualforce Page — opens a VF page, (3) JavaScript — executes JavaScript on the page (Classic only, not supported in Lightning Experience). In Lightning Experience, URL and VF page buttons are supported; JavaScript buttons are not rendered.

topics.question: What is a custom link and how does it differ from a custom button in terms of display location?
topics.answer: A custom link appears inline within a page layout section (typically displayed as a hyperlink in the page body), while a custom button appears in the button bar area at the top of the record or in related lists. Both can navigate to URLs or VF pages, but their display placement and visual styling differ. Links blend into the field layout; buttons are standalone clickable elements.

topics.question: What is an object-specific quick action and what objects does it belong to?
topics.answer: An object-specific quick action belongs to a specific standard or custom object and appears only on records of that object. It is created in Setup > Object Manager > [Object] > Buttons, Links, and Actions. Examples: a 'Schedule Meeting' action on the Contact object, or a 'Create Related Invoice' action on the Opportunity object. They have access to the context record's fields for pre-population.

topics.question: What is a 'Log a Call' action and when would it be used?
topics.answer: A 'Log a Call' action is a pre-configured quick action that creates a Task record with Type = 'Call'.
