It is commonly placed on Contact, Lead, Opportunity, and Account objects for sales reps to quickly document call outcomes. The action layout typically includes Subject, Comments (call notes), and Status fields — minimizing required input for fast mobile logging.

topics.question: How are quick actions surfaced on a Lightning record page vs. a Classic detail page?
topics.answer: Lightning record page: quick actions appear in the 'Salesforce Mobile and Lightning Experience Actions' section of the page layout and are displayed in the action bar (the row of buttons/icons) on the record. Dynamic Actions (in App Builder) can also be used. Classic detail page: actions appear in the 'Actions in the Publisher' section and are shown in the Chatter publisher bar. The rendering and placement mechanisms differ between platforms.

topics.question: Can a quick action launch a Flow? If so, how?
topics.answer: Yes. Create a quick action of type 'Flow' and select a Screen Flow to launch. When the user clicks the action button, the Screen Flow opens as a modal overlay on the record page. The Flow can be pre-populated with record field values. This is the standard way to surface guided process wizards as clickable actions on a record without leaving the page.

topics.question: A user needs to click a button on an Account record that opens a custom Visualforce page in a new window with the Account ID in the URL. Which feature satisfies this?
topics.answer: Create a custom button (Detail Page Button) with content source 'Visualforce Page' or 'URL'. Use the URL option with merge syntax: /apex/MyVFPage?id={!Account.Id}. Set the button behavior to 'Display in new window.' Add the button to the Account page layout. This passes the Account ID to the VF page and opens it in a separate browser window.

topics.question: What are predefined field values in a quick action and how do they improve the user experience?
topics.answer: Predefined field values auto-populate specified fields on a quick action's form using values from the current record or static values. For example, a 'Create Related Contact' action on Account could pre-populate the Contact's AccountId and MailingCity from the Account. Users don't need to manually fill in known values, reducing errors and saving time — especially valuable in mobile contexts.

topics.question: What is a global action and what makes it different from an object-specific action?
topics.answer: A global action is not associated with any specific object — it is accessible from anywhere in Salesforce (global header, mobile nav, any page). It does not have access to a contextual record's fields (unlike object-specific actions). Global actions are used for org-wide tasks like 'Create New Lead' or 'New Task' from anywhere. They are configured in Setup > Global Actions.

topics.question: A company wants the 'Submit for Approval' action to appear on an Opportunity record page only when the Discount field exceeds 20%. Which feature and where must it be configured?
topics.answer: Use Dynamic Actions in Lightning App Builder. Open the Opportunity record page in App Builder, switch to Dynamic Actions mode for the actions section, find the 'Submit for Approval' action, and add a visibility filter: Discount__c > 20. The action will only render when the condition is met. This requires the page to use Dynamic Actions (not traditional page layout action assignment).

topics.question: What are Dynamic Actions in Lightning App Builder and how do they differ from placing actions on a page layout's action section?
topics.answer: Dynamic Actions moves action configuration from the page layout into Lightning App Builder, allowing visibility conditions (filters) on individual actions. Traditional page layout actions are static — either shown or not based on the profile/record type. Dynamic Actions allows conditional rendering: show 'Approve' action only when Status = 'Pending'; show 'Escalate' only for users with a specific permission. More granular and context-aware.

topics.question: How do you configure a filter condition on a Dynamic Action so it only appears when a record's field meets a certain value?
topics.answer: In Lightning App Builder, with Dynamic Actions enabled on the record page, select an action and click 'Add Filter.' Define the filter: choose 'Record Field' as the filter type, select the field (e.g., Status__c), choose an operator (equals, not equals, greater than, etc.), and enter the value. The action only renders when the condition evaluates to true at page load. Multiple conditions can be ANDed together.

objectives.title: Given a scenario, determine the declarative options available for incorporating Lightning components in an application.

topics.question: What standard Lightning components are available in Lightning App Builder for record pages?
topics.answer: Standard components available in App Builder for record pages include: Related Lists, Activity Timeline, Chatter Feed, Path, Highlights Panel, Report Chart, Recent Items, Rich Text (static text/HTML), Flow (embeds a Screen Flow), Record Detail (fields section), Tabs, Accordion, Custom components (LWC/Aura), and more. The component palette shows all available components when editing a page.

topics.question: How is a standard or custom Lightning component added to a record page using Lightning App Builder?
topics.answer: Open the record's Lightning page in App Builder (from the record page via the gear icon > Edit Page, or directly in Setup). In the left panel, find the desired component in the component palette (standard or custom). Drag it onto the page canvas and drop it in the desired region/column. Configure its properties in the right panel. Save and Activate the page to publish it to users.

topics.question: Can Lightning components be added to Experience Cloud (Community) pages declaratively?
topics.answer: Yes. Experience Builder (the Experience Cloud site editor) supports adding Lightning components to community pages declaratively — similar to App Builder for internal org pages. Standard and custom LWC/Aura components marked as available for Experience Cloud can be dragged onto community page templates. This enables rich, component-based external portals without code.

topics.question: What is the Highlights Panel component in Lightning App Builder and what does it display?
topics.answer: The Highlights Panel is the component at the top of a Lightning record page that displays the compact layout fields — the most important identifying fields for the record (e.g., Account Name, Industry, Phone, Owner). It is powered by the object's compact layout configuration. It is typically the first component visible when a user opens a record and is always displayed prominently.

topics.question: A business wants certain fields on a custom object record page to be hidden unless a picklist field equals 'Active'. What is the declarative solution?
topics.answer: Use Dynamic Forms in Lightning App Builder. Migrate the record page to Dynamic Forms, then add field components for the fields to be conditionally shown. Set a visibility filter on each field: 'Record Field: Status__c equals Active.' The fields will be hidden unless Status__c = 'Active.' No code, no multiple layouts needed.

topics.question: What is a tab in a Lightning App and how are tabs associated with objects, Visualforce pages, or Lightning pages?
topics.answer: A tab in a Lightning App is a navigation item in the app's navigation bar. Tabs are associated with: custom object tabs (showing an object's list/detail views), Visualforce page tabs (hosting a VF page), Lightning component tabs (hosting a Lightning App Page or LWC), and web tabs (hosting a URL). Tabs are created in Setup > Tabs and then added to apps via App Manager.

topics.question: What is a Dynamic Form component and how does it replace field sections on a record page?
topics.answer: The Dynamic Form component (enabled in App Builder) allows each field to be placed individually on the record page canvas — rather than having all fields in a block defined by the page layout. Each field becomes its own draggable component with its own visibility rules. This replaces the monolithic 'Record Detail' section from the page layout, enabling field-level conditional display without multiple layouts.

topics.question: What is the utility bar in a Lightning App and what types of components can be placed in it?
topics.answer: The utility bar is a persistent panel anchored to the bottom of the screen in a Lightning App. Components that can be placed in it: Open CTI (phone), Notes, History, Macros, Omni-Channel (for service), Flow (a Screen Flow accessible anytime), Custom utility components (LWC/Aura). The utility bar is always visible and provides quick access to tools without navigating away from the current page.

topics.question: What must be configured in an LWC's metadata configuration file (.js-meta.xml) to make it available as a draggable component in Lightning App Builder?
topics.answer: In the .js-meta.xml file, the component must be exposed with: <isExposed>true</isExposed>, and the <targets> must include <target>lightning__RecordPage</target> (or AppPage, HomePage, etc.) for the relevant page types. Additionally, <targetConfigs> can define design properties that appear as configurable options in App Builder's property panel. Without isExposed=true, the component won't appear in App Builder.

topics.question: What standard Lightning components can be added to a record page in App Builder to display related or contextual information (Related Lists, Activity Timeline, Chatter Feed, Path, Recently Viewed Items)?
topics.answer: Standard components for related/contextual info: Related Lists (shows child records in a list), Activity Timeline (shows tasks, events, emails, logs chronologically), Chatter Feed (shows the record's collaboration feed), Path (shows stage progression), Recently Viewed Items (shows records the user recently accessed), Report Chart (embeds a report's chart), and Record Detail (shows the layout's fields). All available in the App Builder palette.

topics.question: What is the Flow component in Lightning App Builder and how is it used to embed a Screen Flow directly on a record page?
topics.answer: The Flow component is a standard Lightning App Builder component that embeds a Screen Flow directly in the record page layout. In App Builder, drag the Flow component onto the page, then in its properties panel, select which Screen Flow to display. The Flow renders inline on the page. Input variables in the Flow can be pre-populated with record field values using the component's property bindings, allowing context-aware embedded flows.

objectives.title: Describe the programmatic customizations available for incorporating custom Lightning components in an application.

topics.question: What is a Lightning Web Component (LWC)?
topics.answer: A Lightning Web Component (LWC) is a modern JavaScript-based UI component framework built on Web Standards (Custom Elements, Shadow DOM, ES6+ modules). LWCs are the current Salesforce standard for custom UI development. They are faster, lighter, and more aligned with browser standards than their predecessor (Aura components). They can be deployed to Lightning pages, Experience Cloud, and email templates.

topics.question: What is the difference between an Aura component and a Lightning Web Component (LWC)?
topics.answer: Aura (also called 'Classic Lightning Components') uses a proprietary Salesforce framework with its own lifecycle hooks, event system, and XML/JavaScript hybrid syntax. LWC uses W3C Web Standards — HTML templates, ES6 JavaScript, and standard browser APIs. LWC is more performant, has smaller learning curve for web developers, and is the recommended choice for new development. Aura components can coexist with LWC on the same page.

topics.question: How is a custom LWC exposed in Lightning App Builder so it can be dragged onto a page?
topics.answer: The LWC's .js-meta.xml configuration file must: (1) set <isExposed>true</isExposed>, and (2) include relevant <targets> (e.g., <target>lightning__RecordPage</target>). Optional <targetConfigs> define admin-configurable properties that appear in the App Builder property panel. After deployment, the component appears in the App Builder component palette under 'Custom Components' and can be dragged onto the canvas.

topics.question: When is a custom LWC required rather than a standard Lightning component for a UI requirement?
topics.answer: A custom LWC is required when: no standard component provides the needed functionality (e.g., a custom interactive chart, a specialized data entry form, a third-party JavaScript library integration), the UI needs real-time data manipulation not possible with standard components, the business requires a branded custom widget, or the component needs to emit and respond to custom events across a complex page structure.

topics.question: What is a Visualforce page and when would it still be required in a Lightning Experience context?
topics.answer: A Visualforce page is an HTML-like markup page that uses Apex controllers for server-side logic. In Lightning Experience, VF pages are rendered in an iframe. They are still required when: migrating legacy Classic applications that haven't been rewritten, custom buttons link to VF pages, specific PDF rendering (using renderAs='pdf' on the <apex:page> tag) is needed, or integrations use VF-specific endpoints. New development should use LWC/Aura instead.

objectives.title: Given a set of business requirements, recommend a solution for key milestones and considerations when managing the application lifecycle and various types of sandboxes.

topics.question: What are the four types of Salesforce sandboxes?
topics.answer: Four sandbox types: (1) Developer — small storage, copies metadata only, 1-day refresh. (2) Developer Pro — more storage than Developer, copies metadata only, 1-day refresh. (3) Partial Copy — copies metadata + a sample of data (via sandbox template), 5-day refresh. (4) Full — exact copy of production including all data and metadata, 29-day refresh. Higher tiers cost more and take longer to provision.

topics.question: Does a Developer sandbox copy production data records?
topics.answer: No. A Developer sandbox copies only metadata (configurations, code, custom objects, page layouts, etc.) — not production data records. This makes it fast to provision and appropriate for development and unit testing. If you need data for testing, you must manually create test records or use a data generation tool. Only Partial Copy and Full sandboxes include production data.

topics.question: What is the data storage limit for a Developer sandbox?
topics.answer: A Developer sandbox has 200 MB of data storage and 200 MB of file storage. This is sufficient for development and unit testing but not for performance testing or UAT with realistic data volumes. The small storage cap is intentional — it keeps developers from relying on large datasets in their isolated environments.

topics.question: What is the data storage limit for a Developer Pro sandbox?
topics.answer: A Developer Pro sandbox has 1 GB of data storage and 1 GB of file storage. This is larger than a standard Developer sandbox, making it better suited for integration testing, more complex development scenarios, or teams that need slightly more data for testing without committing to a Partial Copy sandbox.

topics.question: What is the data storage limit for a Partial Copy sandbox?
topics.answer: A Partial Copy sandbox has 5 GB of data storage. It includes a sample of production data (filtered by a sandbox template). The 5 GB limit is designed for UAT and QA testing with representative data without requiring a full production dataset. Templates define which objects and records are copied.

topics.question: What is the data storage limit for a Full sandbox?
topics.answer: A Full sandbox matches production's data storage allocation — it has the same storage capacity as the production org. It contains a complete copy of all production data and metadata. This makes it suitable for performance testing, load testing, and final UAT with real data volumes. Full sandboxes are the most expensive type.

topics.question: What is the refresh interval for a Developer and Developer Pro sandbox?
topics.answer: Both Developer and Developer Pro sandboxes can be refreshed once every 1 day (24 hours). This frequent refresh capability allows developers to quickly reset their environment if needed or create a fresh copy from production. After a refresh, the sandbox URL and ID change, so connected tools may need reconfiguration.

topics.question: What is the refresh interval for a Partial Copy sandbox?
topics.answer: A Partial Copy sandbox can be refreshed once every 5 days. The 5-day interval reflects the time needed to copy the data sample from production. After refresh, existing sandbox configuration is replaced, so any sandbox-specific settings or post-refresh customizations must be re-applied.

topics.question: What is the refresh interval for a Full sandbox?
topics.answer: A Full sandbox can be refreshed once every 29 days. The long interval is due to the time required to copy all production data. Full sandbox refreshes are major operations typically planned around sprint cycles or release events. Between refreshes, production changes must be manually deployed into the sandbox.

topics.question: What is a sandbox template and with which sandbox type is it used?
topics.answer: A sandbox template is a configuration that defines which objects and records are copied when creating or refreshing a Partial Copy sandbox. You specify which standard and custom objects to include. Salesforce will copy a sample of records (up to the 5 GB limit) from those objects. Templates are used only with Partial Copy sandboxes — Developer sandboxes copy no data, Full sandboxes copy all data.

topics.question: A company needs to perform UAT with a representative subset of production data. Which sandbox type is appropriate?
topics.answer: Partial Copy sandbox. It provides up to 5 GB of production data (selected via a sandbox template) and all production metadata. This gives UAT testers realistic data to validate business processes without needing the full production dataset. Developer sandboxes lack data; Full sandboxes are more expensive and have 29-day refresh intervals.

topics.question: A company needs to run performance and load tests that mimic production-scale data. Which sandbox type is required?
topics.answer: Full sandbox. Only a Full sandbox contains a complete copy of all production data at production scale. Performance and load testing requires production-volume data to accurately simulate governor limit behavior, query performance, and automation throughput. Partial Copy's 5 GB limit is insufficient for true production-scale load testing.

topics.question: What is the recommended application lifecycle management (ALM) deployment path from development through production?
topics.answer: Standard ALM path: (1) Development in Developer sandboxes (individual developers), (2) Integration sandbox (merge and integration test), (3) QA/Staging sandbox (quality assurance testing), (4) UAT sandbox (Partial Copy or Full for user acceptance testing), (5) Production deployment. Change sets or DevOps tools (DevOps Center, Copado, Gearset) move metadata between environments.

topics.question: What is DevOps Center in Salesforce and how does it compare to change sets as a deployment mechanism?
topics.answer: DevOps Center is Salesforce's native Git-based DevOps tool that provides version control integration, work item tracking, and pipeline-based deployments. It is more robust than change sets: it tracks all changes in Git, supports branching strategies, provides deployment history, and enables team collaboration. Change sets are manual, point-in-time, and lack version control. DevOps Center is Salesforce's recommended modern replacement for change-set-based deployments.

topics.question: What is a scratch org in the Salesforce DX development model and how does it differ from a sandbox in terms of purpose and lifespan?
topics.answer: A scratch org is a short-lived (up to 30 days), source-driven, fully configurable Salesforce environment created from a project configuration file. It is designed for development and testing in the Salesforce DX model where source code is the source of truth. Unlike sandboxes (which are copies of production), scratch orgs are created from scratch with only the features you need. They are disposable and version-controlled.

topics.question: When multiple developers are working in separate Developer sandboxes on overlapping customizations, what process risk must be managed before merging to a shared integration sandbox?
topics.answer: The risk is metadata conflicts — two developers may have modified the same metadata component (e.g., the same page layout, Flow, or Apex class) in incompatible ways. Before merging, teams must: compare changes, resolve conflicts (manually reconciling differences), and sequence deployments carefully. This is why version control (Git) is strongly recommended — it enables diff/merge tooling to manage overlapping changes systematically.

objectives.title: Given a use case, demonstrate knowledge, viability, and troubleshooting when using change sets.

topics.question: What is a change set and what types of metadata components can be included in one?
topics.answer: A change set is a deployment container that packages metadata components (not data) for migration between connected Salesforce orgs (typically sandbox to production). Components that can be included: Apex classes/triggers, Visualforce pages/components, custom objects/fields, page layouts, profiles (partial), permission sets, Flows, reports, dashboards, email templates, and many other metadata types. Data records cannot be deployed via change sets.

topics.question: What is an outbound change set vs. an inbound change set?
topics.answer: Outbound change set: created in the source org (e.g., sandbox), where you add components and upload the set to the connected target org. Inbound change set: received in the target org (e.g., production) from a connected source org — it appears in the 'Inbound Change Sets' section where it can be validated and deployed. The same change set is outbound from the sender's perspective and inbound from the receiver's perspective.

topics.question: What is a deployment connection and what must be configured between two orgs before change sets can be sent?
topics.answer: A deployment connection establishes a trusted pathway between two Salesforce orgs for change set transfers. To send change sets from Sandbox A to Production, a connection must be authorized in both orgs (typically configured under Setup > Deploy > Deployment Settings). Without an authorized connection, the upload button in the outbound change set is not available.

topics.question: What is the difference between 'Validate' and 'Deploy' when processing an inbound change set?
topics.answer: Validate: runs all component checks and Apex tests against the target org without actually saving any changes. It confirms that the change set would succeed if deployed — useful for pre-deployment verification. Deploy: applies the changes permanently to the target org. A validated deployment can be Quick Deployed within 10 days if no changes occur, skipping the test phase for faster deployment.

topics.question: What Apex test coverage requirement must be met before deploying to a production org via change set?
topics.answer: Production deployments require: overall org Apex code coverage of at least 75%, AND every Apex trigger must have at least 1% test coverage. Change sets including Apex classes/triggers will run all local Apex tests. If coverage drops below 75% after including the new code, the deployment fails. Always check current org coverage before deploying.

topics.question: What happens if a component in a change set has a dependency on another component that is not included in the change set?
topics.answer: The deployment fails with an error identifying the missing dependent component. Change sets do not automatically include dependencies — the admin must manually add all required components. Best practice: use the 'Add Dependencies' button when adding components to a change set to identify and include all required related components.

topics.question: Can change sets be used to delete metadata components from a target org?
topics.answer: No. Change sets cannot delete components — they can only add or update. To delete metadata from a target org, you must manually delete it in that org, or use the Metadata API with a destructiveChanges.xml file via Workbench, SFDX CLI, or a third-party DevOps tool. This is one of the key limitations of change sets as a deployment mechanism.

topics.question: What is a Quick Deploy and when is it available after a successful change set validation?
topics.answer: Quick Deploy allows you to deploy a previously validated change set without re-running Apex tests, provided: (1) the change set was validated within the last 10 days, (2) all tests passed during validation, and (3) no changes have been made to the org since validation. This speeds up production deployments by skipping the (sometimes slow) test execution phase.

objectives.title: Describe the use cases and considerations when using unmanaged and managed packages.

topics.question: What is an unmanaged package and what are its primary use cases?
topics.answer: An unmanaged package is a collection of metadata components that can be installed into any Salesforce org. After installation, all components are fully editable — there is no code protection. Primary use cases: sharing open-source Salesforce solutions, distributing starter templates or developer tools, internal org-to-org metadata transfer, and community-shared resources on the AppExchange (typically free, open components). No upgrade path exists — each install is standalone.

topics.question: What is a managed package and what protections does it provide to the package developer?
topics.answer: A managed package is a locked distribution of metadata from a registered Salesforce Partner ISV org. Apex code is obfuscated (not readable by installers), core components are protected from modification, and the ISV can push upgrades to installed orgs. A namespace prefix prevents component name conflicts with the installing org. Managed packages are required for publicly listed AppExchange products that undergo Security Review.

topics.question: What is a namespace prefix in a managed package and why does it matter?
topics.answer: A namespace prefix is a unique string registered to the ISV's org that is prepended to all API names of package components (e.g., myapp__CustomObject__c, myapp__MyFlow). This prevents naming conflicts between package components and the installing org's custom components. Namespace prefixes must be globally unique across all Salesforce orgs and cannot be changed after registration.

topics.question: Can a managed package be uninstalled from a Salesforce org and what are the considerations?
topics.answer: Yes, a managed package can be uninstalled, but with significant considerations: all components (objects, fields, Apex code, layouts) installed by the package are removed, along with all data stored in the package's custom objects. Uninstalling is irreversible for the data. If the org has custom code or automation referencing package components, those references will break after uninstall. Always test uninstall in a sandbox first.

topics.question: What is Salesforce Package 2 (2GP) and how does it differ from first-generation packages (1GP)?
topics.answer: Second-generation packages (2GP) use the Salesforce DX development model — they are source-driven, version-controlled, and support unlocked packages (editable by the installer) and managed packages (protected). 2GP packages are created using SFDX CLI. First-generation packages (1GP) are created through the classic package setup UI and are less integrated with version control. 2GP is Salesforce's modern packaging model.

objectives.title: Given a scenario, determine the appropriate deployment plan.

topics.question: When deploying a set of changes that includes new custom fields, a new Flow, and updated page layouts, what is the correct deployment sequence to minimize errors?
topics.answer: Deploy in dependency order: (1) Custom fields first (the Flow and layouts depend on them), (2) Flow (depends on the new fields), (3) Page layouts (depend on the new fields and potentially reference the Flow as an action). Deploying in wrong order causes errors because dependent components reference components that don't yet exist in the target org.

topics.question: What deployment tool should a team use when deploying to production with a requirement for version control, rollback capability, and automated testing?
topics.answer: A Git-integrated DevOps tool such as Salesforce DevOps Center, Copado, Gearset, or Flosum. These tools connect to a Git repository for version control, maintain deployment history (enabling rollback), integrate with CI/CD pipelines for automated testing before deployment, and provide audit trails. Change sets lack all these capabilities. Salesforce CLI + source-format deployments are also viable for advanced teams.

topics.question: A deployment to production failed due to a code coverage error. What steps should the team take to troubleshoot and resolve it?
topics.answer: Steps: (1) Review the deployment error log to identify which classes or triggers have insufficient coverage. (2) In the sandbox, run all Apex tests and review coverage report — identify untested code paths. (3) Write additional test methods to cover the failing code. (4) Re-run tests to confirm coverage exceeds 75% org-wide and all triggers have >1% coverage. (5) Redeploy via change set or CLI after confirming coverage.

topics.question: What is the difference between a delta deployment and a full deployment, and when would you use each?
topics.answer: Delta deployment: deploys only the components that have changed since the last deployment — faster, lower risk, smaller footprint. Full deployment: deploys all metadata components in the project, regardless of changes — ensures the target org exactly matches the source. Use delta for routine incremental releases. Use full for initial org builds, after a full refresh, or when you suspect the target org has drifted from the source.

topics.question: What is a destructiveChanges.xml file and when must it be used in a Salesforce deployment?
topics.answer: A destructiveChanges.xml file is a metadata API artifact that specifies components to be deleted in the target org during a deployment. It must be used when you want to remove custom fields, objects, classes, Flows, or other metadata components via CLI or API deployment — since change sets cannot delete components. Include it alongside the package.xml in the deployment package to perform deletions.

objectives.title: Assess development methodologies and recommend governance strategies based on customer maturity

topics.question: Assessing ALM maturity of a customer organization
topics.answer: ALM maturity signals: Low (ad hoc) = manual deployments, no source control, undocumented processes, tribal knowledge. Medium = repeatable but inconsistent processes, some version control, informal testing. High = automated CI/CD, enforced governance, full traceability. Gaps at each level imply specific risks: low maturity risks data loss and untracked changes; medium risks inconsistency; high maturity requires continuous optimization. Always assess people (skills, roles), process (standards, approvals), and technology (tooling) dimensions together.

topics.question: Ad hoc and repeatable ALM maturity levels
topics.answer: Ad hoc: no documented processes, each deployment is unique, relies on individual heroics. Risks: high error rate, no rollback. To advance: introduce source control (Git), define a basic deployment runbook, assign a release manager. Repeatable: processes exist but are not enforced consistently. Some version control in use. To advance: formalize branching strategy, add CI validation, document all deployment steps, create sandbox hierarchy.

topics.question: Defined and managed ALM maturity levels
topics.answer: Defined: standardized processes documented and enforced across all teams; CI/CD pipeline in place; sandbox strategy defined; code reviews required. To advance: add metrics and KPIs (deployment frequency, lead time, MTTR). Managed: processes are measured and controlled; dashboards track release health; governance boards review changes. To advance: automate quality gates, adopt predictive analytics for risk, implement feature flags for safer releases.

topics.question: Optimizing ALM maturity level
topics.answer: At the optimizing level, the org uses data-driven continuous improvement: post-release retrospectives feed back into process changes, automated test suites are tuned based on defect trends, and deployment pipelines are self-healing. Key practices: chaos engineering, value stream mapping, AI-assisted code review, proactive capacity planning, and regular ALM health audits. The goal is reducing lead time and defect escape rate while increasing deployment frequency.

topics.question: Comparing waterfall vs. agile vs. hybrid methodologies in Salesforce ALM
topics.answer: Waterfall: fixed requirements, sequential phases, best for highly regulated projects with stable scope (e.g., compliance-driven implementations). Risk: late defect discovery. Agile (Scrum/Kanban): iterative sprints, continuous feedback, best for evolving requirements and experienced teams. Risk: scope creep without governance. Hybrid: agile delivery within waterfall phase gates, ideal for large programs with multiple workstreams or mixed team maturity. Recommend based on project risk level, regulatory requirements, team capability, and release cadence constraints.

topics.question: Risk-based trade-offs between agile speed and governance control
topics.answer: Agile speeds delivery but can conflict with change control requirements in regulated industries (finance, healthcare). Mitigations: add lightweight approval gates at sprint boundaries instead of blocking every commit; use automated testing as the quality gate; maintain a formal CAB for production deployments while allowing agile development in lower environments. The key is preserving auditability (who changed what, when, and why) without slowing iteration speed.

topics.question: Governance strategy selection based on team size, project complexity, and regulatory requirements
topics.answer: Small teams / low complexity: lightweight governance (PR reviews, basic runbook). Medium complexity: add environment strategy, release calendar, and CAB for production. Large/regulated: full ITIL or SAFe governance with formal change records, risk assessments, traceability matrices, and executive sign-off. Regulatory requirements (SOX, HIPAA) demand immutable audit trails, segregation of duties, and documented approval chains. Always match governance overhead to actual risk.

topics.question: Role of a Center of Excellence (CoE) in Salesforce ALM governance
topics.answer: A CoE provides centralized standards, best practices, and reusable assets for Salesforce delivery across the enterprise. It owns: coding standards, metadata architecture guidelines, approved tooling list, sandbox strategy, training curriculum, and ALM governance policies. Recommend establishing a CoE when: multiple teams are building on Salesforce independently, technical debt is accumulating, or org mergers require standardization. The CoE enables consistency without stifling team autonomy.

topics.question: Release approval gates in a Salesforce deployment pipeline
topics.answer: Approval gates are checkpoints that must pass before a deployment can proceed to the next environment. Common gates: code review approval (PR merged), CI validation pass (no test failures, static analysis clean), QA sign-off (test cases executed), UAT sign-off (business users approved), CAB approval (production deployment). Gates enforce quality and governance. They should be automated where possible (CI/CD quality gates) and manual only where human judgment is required (UAT, go/no-go).

topics.question: Change Advisory Board (CAB)
topics.answer: A CAB is a governance body that reviews, approves, or rejects production change requests. Composition typically includes: Release Manager (chair), IT Operations, Security, Business Stakeholders, Architects, and representatives from affected teams. Use CAB for: high-risk or high-impact production changes, emergency changes, and changes affecting multiple systems. CAB ensures changes are assessed for risk, dependencies are identified, rollback plans exist, and accountability is established. In agile contexts, lightweight 'mini-CABs' can review changes at sprint boundaries.

objectives.title: Assess ALM maturity and identify people, technology, and processes required

topics.question: Identifying ALM maturity gaps across people, process, and technology
topics.answer: For a customer with ad-hoc deployments and no source control: People gaps = no dedicated release manager, developers deploying directly to production, no QA role. Process gaps = no deployment runbook, no change approval workflow, no sandbox strategy. Technology gaps = no version control, no CI/CD tooling, change sets only or manual Metadata API calls. Remediation roadmap: Phase 1 - introduce Git and a sandbox hierarchy. Phase 2 - add CI validation and PR reviews. Phase 3 - automate deployments and add governance gates.

topics.question: Developer, QA, admin, and architect roles and handoffs in a mature Salesforce ALM team
topics.answer: Developer: writes Apex/LWC, creates feature branches, writes unit tests, submits PRs. QA Engineer: writes and executes test cases, validates deployments in QA sandbox, signs off before UAT. Admin/Declarative Developer: configures flows/processes, works in sandbox, tracks changes for source control. Architect: defines environment strategy, approves technical designs, resolves cross-team dependencies. Handoffs: Dev > QA (code merged to integration branch triggers QA deployment) > UAT (QA sign-off triggers UAT) > Release Manager (UAT approval triggers production deployment).

topics.question: Release manager role and responsibilities
topics.answer: The Release Manager coordinates all activities required to move code from development to production. Responsibilities: maintain the release calendar, chair CAB meetings, manage sandbox environments, own the deployment runbook, track release readiness (test pass rates, open defects), communicate release status to stakeholders, and ensure rollback plans exist. They are NOT responsible for writing code but must understand technical risks. In smaller orgs, this role may be filled by a Senior Developer or Architect.

topics.question: Source control and CI/CD tool evaluation for a Salesforce ALM pipeline
topics.answer: Source control options: GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure DevOps Repos. Evaluate on: Salesforce CLI integration, branching model support, PR review workflows, and team familiarity. CI/CD platforms: GitHub Actions, Jenkins, Azure DevOps Pipelines, Bitbucket Pipelines, CircleCI. Evaluate on: Salesforce plugin/orb availability, parallel job support, secret management, cost, and existing enterprise toolchain. Key capability: ability to run 'sf project deploy validate' and 'sf apex run test' as pipeline steps.

topics.question: Static analysis and deployment tooling evaluation
topics.answer: Static analysis tools: PMD (open-source, Apex rules), Salesforce Code Analyzer (combines PMD, ESLint, RetireJS, Graph Engine for dataflow analysis). Use PMD for fast CI gate on critical violations; Code Analyzer for deeper security and dataflow analysis. Deployment tools: Salesforce CLI (sf deploy) for scripted/automated deployments, Copado/Gearset/Flosum for managed DevOps with GUI and rollback features, ANT Migration Tool (legacy, largely replaced by CLI). Evaluate on: support for destructive changes, delta deployments, test execution options, and rollback capability.

topics.question: Building a roadmap to improve ALM maturity from manual change sets
topics.answer: Sequenced roadmap: (1) Introduce Git source control - retrieve existing org metadata, establish baseline. (2) Define sandbox hierarchy (Dev > Integration > UAT > Staging > Prod). (3) Establish branching strategy (feature branches, main branch mirrors production). (4) Replace change sets with Salesforce CLI deployments. (5) Add CI pipeline for automated validation on PR. (6) Integrate static analysis and test execution gates. (7) Add third-party DevOps tooling (Copado/Gearset) for advanced governance. Training must accompany each phase - tools without process adoption fail.

objectives.title: Understand customer environment risks and articulate appropriate mitigation strategies

topics.question: Risks introduced by direct production changes
topics.answer: Direct production changes (by admins or developers) bypass source control, CI validation, and testing, creating configuration drift where production no longer matches what is tracked in version control. Mitigation steps to restore ALM integrity: (1) Retrieve the change from production using Salesforce CLI. (2) Commit it to the appropriate branch in source control. (3) Back-propagate it to all lower sandboxes to keep environments in sync. (4) Document the change with a justification and approver. (5) Implement org lockdown policies to prevent recurrence.

topics.question: Configuration drift and data leakage as environment risks
topics.answer: Configuration drift: production diverges from source control and lower environments due to direct changes, sandbox refresh timing gaps, or ad hoc hotfixes. Mitigation: automated drift detection tools (Gearset, Copado), regular environment audits, enforce change-only-through-pipeline policies. Data leakage: sensitive production data (PII, PHI) exposed in non-production sandboxes. Mitigation: data masking/anonymization before sandbox creation, Full Copy sandboxes restricted to authorized personnel only, data classification policies enforced at sandbox creation.

topics.question: Technical debt accumulation risk in long-lived orgs
topics.answer: Signals of technical debt: high code complexity scores (PMD violations), large numbers of deprecated API calls, unused metadata components, tightly coupled customizations, absence of test data factories, manual processes that should be automated. Governance controls to prevent further drift: mandatory static analysis in CI pipeline, periodic technical debt sprints, architecture review board approval for new patterns, regular code coverage audits, metadata cleanup campaigns using tools like Salesforce Optimizer or Health Check.

topics.question: Mitigating risk of conflicting parallel development streams sharing a single sandbox
topics.answer: When multiple teams share a single integration sandbox, changes collide - metadata overwrites, broken deployments, and unclear ownership. Mitigation: (1) Allocate dedicated developer sandboxes per team. (2) Use feature branches in Git; merge to integration branch only when ready. (3) Establish a daily/weekly integration sandbox refresh schedule. (4) Use CI pipeline to validate all feature branch deployments in isolation before merging. (5) Consider scratch orgs for complete isolation per feature.

topics.question: Sandbox refresh lag as an environment risk
topics.answer: Sandbox refresh lag occurs when a sandbox has not been refreshed recently and has diverged from production metadata and data, causing tests to fail against stale configurations. Mitigation: define a sandbox refresh schedule aligned to release cadences (e.g., refresh UAT after each production release). Automate post-refresh steps (permission set assignments, custom setting values, test data seeding). Use Partial Copy sandboxes for representative data. Track sandbox age and alert when environments exceed the refresh threshold.

objectives.title: Analyze and recommend the appropriate governance framework

topics.question: Selecting a governance framework (ITIL, SAFe, Agile, custom hybrid)
topics.answer: ITIL: best for IT operations-heavy orgs needing formal change management, incident management, and CMDB. Use when SLA compliance and audit trails are top priority. SAFe: best for large enterprises running Salesforce as part of a broader enterprise portfolio; provides Program Increments (PI) as release cadence anchors. Agile (Scrum/Kanban): best for small-to-medium product teams with frequent releases and low regulatory burden. Custom Hybrid: most common in Salesforce - agile delivery within PI or release train structure, with CAB-controlled production gates. Match framework to organizational culture; forcing ITIL on a startup culture creates resistance.

topics.question: Defining approval gates and escalation paths in a governance framework
topics.answer: For an enterprise with multiple business units: define tiered approval gates. Dev gate: peer code review + CI pass. Integration gate: integration test pass + Tech Lead approval. UAT gate: business stakeholder sign-off per BU. Staging gate: performance test pass + Security review. Production gate: CAB approval + Release Manager go/no-go. Escalation paths: if a critical defect is found post-UAT, escalate to Release Manager who decides defer or emergency fix path. Document all escalation paths in the release governance runbook so there are no ambiguous decisions under pressure.

topics.question: Release coordination across vendor partners in multi-vendor implementations
topics.answer: Multi-vendor Salesforce programs require a vendor-neutral Release Manager (often the customer's own staff) to own the release train. Key practices: shared release calendar accessible to all vendors, joint CAB meetings, clear API versioning contracts between vendor-developed components, integration testing environment jointly owned and refreshed on a defined schedule, vendor change freeze windows enforced equally. Define handoff points clearly in SLAs and contracts - ambiguous handoffs cause delay and blame-shifting.

topics.question: Change ownership and IP rights in multi-vendor implementations
topics.answer: In multi-vendor Salesforce programs, IP ownership of custom metadata, Apex code, and data models must be contractually defined. Key questions: who owns the source code repository - customer or vendor? Who retains rights if a vendor contract is terminated? Managed packages protect ISV IP but limit customer customization. Unlocked packages or unmanaged code deployments leave IP with whoever controls the source repo. Best practice: customer should own the source control repository and CI/CD pipeline, with vendor teams contributing via PRs, never directly to production.

objectives.title: Recommend strategies to mitigate risks from a new Salesforce seasonal release

topics.question: Strategies for assessing impact of a Salesforce seasonal release
topics.answer: Three-step approach: (1) Analyze release notes - identify 'Enforce by default' and 'Critical Update' items that auto-activate. (2) Sandbox preview testing - deploy to a preview sandbox 4-6 weeks before production upgrade; run full regression test suite including UI automation. (3) Regression test planning - prioritize tests for features touched by the release (Lightning components, API version changes, Apex governor limits). Key risk areas: API version deprecation, LWC rendering changes, new validation behavior, and changed governor limits.

topics.question: Salesforce release preview sandbox window and opt-out mechanisms
topics.answer: Salesforce upgrades sandbox instances to the upcoming release approximately 4-6 weeks before the production upgrade window. Developer, Developer Pro, and Partial Copy sandboxes on preview instances receive the new release first. Full Copy sandboxes typically do NOT receive preview. Orgs can opt out of the preview window for a specific sandbox by contacting Salesforce support before the cutoff date. The opt-out window is limited - typically 2-3 weeks before the sandbox upgrade. Know which sandbox types are on preview instances in your org.

topics.question: Using sandbox preview instances to evaluate seasonal release impacts
topics.answer: Timing: preview sandboxes receive the new release ~4-6 weeks before production. Access: any user with sandbox login credentials can access the preview sandbox. Testing scope: run the full automated regression suite first; then focus manual testing on components the release notes flag as changed. Considerations: the preview sandbox may have slightly different behavior from final production release (release candidates can be updated). Plan a second test cycle in the week before production upgrade if high-risk changes are identified.

topics.question: Impact of a Salesforce seasonal release on an active CI/CD pipeline
topics.answer: Potential breakage points: (1) API version changes - if your CI pipeline deploys using a deprecated API version, deployments may fail. Update sf CLI and API versions in pipeline scripts before the release. (2) Apex test failures - new platform behavior can break existing tests (e.g., stricter validation, changed default field values). Run full test suite in preview sandbox and fix failures before production upgrade. (3) LWC/Aura breaking changes - component rendering or event behavior changes can break UI tests (Selenium, Provar). Update selectors and test scripts as needed.

topics.question: Critical update opt-in and auto-activation timelines
topics.answer: Critical Updates (now 'Release Updates' in Salesforce) are platform behavior changes that require customer opt-in initially but auto-activate after a defined date (typically 1-2 releases later). Architectural implications: deferring auto-activation buys time but creates a deadline you cannot miss. If deferred updates affect your Apex or flows, technical debt accumulates. Best practice: opt in to critical updates in a sandbox as soon as they are available, test proactively, and resolve issues before auto-activation. Surprises at auto-activation = production incidents.

topics.question: Communicating seasonal release changes to business stakeholders
topics.answer: Create a release impact summary document (non-technical) for business stakeholders: what is changing, when, what users will see differently, and what actions stakeholders need to take (e.g., re-approve UAT test cases, attend a demo of new feature behavior). Schedule UAT cycles BEFORE the production upgrade window, not after. Coordinate with Salesforce's published release schedule (typically available 8+ weeks in advance). Set expectations that some post-release support may be needed even with thorough testing.

objectives.title: Explain the advantages of using agile tools to support an agile development process

topics.question: Capabilities and benefits of agile project management tools (Jira, Azure Boards)
topics.answer: Agile tools provide: backlog management (user stories, epics, priority ordering), sprint planning (capacity planning, sprint boards), velocity tracking, burndown charts, and release planning views. In Salesforce context: user stories map to deployable units of work; sprints align to sandbox deployment cycles; release plans tie to production deployment windows. Benefits: visibility into work in progress, impediment tracking, cross-team coordination, and stakeholder reporting without status meetings. Choose tools the team already uses over adopting something new just for Salesforce.

topics.question: Integrating agile tracking tools with Salesforce source control and CI pipelines
topics.answer: Traceability from story to deployment artifact: (1) Link Git commits to Jira/Azure Boards tickets using smart commit syntax (e.g., 'PROJ-123 Fixed account trigger'). (2) Automate PR creation from branch naming conventions that include ticket IDs. (3) CI pipeline posts build results back to the ticket (GitHub Actions + Jira integration, Azure DevOps native linking). (4) Deployment tools (Copado, DevOps Center) link user stories to specific metadata components. Full traceability enables audit reports: for any production change, trace back to the story, the developer, the PR reviewer, the test results, and the approver.

objectives.title: Evaluate business, technical, and architectural considerations for org strategy

topics.question: Single-org vs. multi-org architecture trade-offs
topics.answer: Single-org: simpler data model, no integration overhead, shared governor limits, easier cross-BU reporting. Best when BUs share data and processes. Multi-org: full data isolation, independent release cycles, separate governor limit pools, but requires integration layer (middleware, APIs) for cross-org data, duplicated customizations, and more complex governance. Use multi-org when: regulatory/compliance requires data separation, BUs have completely different processes, a subsidiary has its own Salesforce instance post-acquisition, or governor limits are a constraint. Multi-org dramatically increases operational complexity.

topics.question: Org strategy considerations for an acquisition scenario
topics.answer: Key decision factors: (1) Data overlap - does the acquired company have duplicate Account/Contact records? Merging requires data migration and deduplication. (2) Process compatibility - if both orgs use different sales processes, merging forces standardization (political risk). (3) Technical complexity - the acquired org may have managed packages or custom metadata that conflicts. (4) Timeline - merging orgs is a 6-18 month project; maintaining separate orgs is faster short-term but costly long-term. (5) Licensing - consolidating may save licenses. Recommendation: evaluate 'merge' vs 'coexist' using a formal feasibility study before committing.

topics.question: Governor limits and platform capacity constraints as architectural drivers
topics.answer: Key Salesforce governor limits that influence org design: SOQL queries (100 synchronous per transaction), DML statements (150), heap size (6MB sync), CPU time (10s sync), async Apex queue limits, API call limits per 24 hours. When a single org approaches these limits due to scale or integration volume, consider: multi-org split (separate high-volume processes to a dedicated org), Platform Events / Async processing to flatten peaks, Bulk API for large data operations. Governor limits should be analyzed during architecture review before design decisions are finalized, not after.

objectives.title: Define an environment (sandbox) strategy

topics.question: Developer and Developer Pro sandbox types
topics.answer: Developer sandbox: 200MB data storage, 200MB file storage, can be refreshed every 1 day. No production data copied. Best for individual developer feature work and unit testing. Developer Pro: 1GB data storage, 1GB file storage, refresh every 1 day. Supports moderate data volume testing. Best for feature development that requires more metadata or data than a Developer sandbox can handle. Neither type copies production data on creation - data must be manually seeded.

topics.question: Partial Copy and Full Copy sandbox types
topics.answer: Partial Copy: copies all metadata + a sample of production data (up to 10,000 records per object, configurable via sandbox template). Refresh every 5 days. Best for QA/UAT where representative data is needed without full production volume. Full Copy: exact replica of production (all metadata + all data). Refresh every 29 days. Highest cost. Best for performance testing, staging (pre-prod gate), and compliance testing. Full Copy requires data masking before granting access to non-privileged users. Refresh cycle length limits how frequently Full Copy can be used in fast-moving release cycles.

topics.question: Sandbox refresh strategy
topics.answer: When to refresh: (1) After each production release to resync the environment. (2) Before a major test cycle to ensure stable baseline. (3) After a Salesforce seasonal release upgrades production. Impact on active development: refreshing a sandbox destroys all work in progress in that sandbox - always align refreshes with the end of a sprint or release cycle. Sequencing: refresh lower environments (Developer) most frequently; refresh UAT/Staging less often but more deliberately. Communicate planned refreshes via the team calendar so developers can commit and retrieve work before the refresh.

topics.question: Designing a sandbox environment hierarchy for multiple parallel streams
topics.answer: Recommended hierarchy for parallel development: (1) Individual Developer Sandboxes (one per developer/team) for feature development. (2) Integration Sandbox: receives merged feature branches daily for integration testing. (3) QA Sandbox (Partial Copy): receives validated builds for QA test execution. (4) UAT Sandbox (Partial Copy): business-facing environment for user acceptance testing. (5) Staging Sandbox (Full Copy): production-equivalent for final validation, performance testing. (6) Production. Training environment: separate Developer Pro or Partial Copy sandbox, refreshed from a stable release, never connected to the CI pipeline.

topics.question: Hotfix environment strategy
topics.answer: A hotfix sandbox is a dedicated Developer or Developer Pro sandbox kept at (or close to) production parity, used exclusively for emergency production fixes. It is NOT used for ongoing development. Process: (1) Create hotfix branch from the production tag in Git. (2) Develop and test the fix in the hotfix sandbox. (3) Deploy fix to production directly from hotfix branch (bypassing long integration queue). (4) Merge hotfix back into the main development branch immediately. (5) Deploy hotfix branch changes to integration and lower sandboxes to prevent regression. Key rule: hotfix changes MUST be merged back to main branch before the next regular release.

topics.question: Scratch org usage in package-based development environment strategy
topics.answer: Scratch orgs are temporary, fully configurable Salesforce environments created from a definition file. They expire after 1-30 days (default 7). Use scratch orgs to: provide isolated, reproducible environments for each feature (no shared state), test package installation and configuration, run CI builds in clean environments. They replace developer sandboxes in a package-based model. Complement traditional sandboxes: use scratch orgs for unit/component development; use a Partial Copy sandbox for integration/UAT where production-like data is needed. Scratch orgs require a Dev Hub org to be enabled.

objectives.title: Compare, contrast, and recommend components and tools of a successful deployment strategy

topics.question: Native deployment tools: Change Sets, Salesforce CLI, and ANT Migration Tool
topics.answer: Change Sets: GUI-based, no version control, point-to-point (only between connected orgs), no destructive changes, good for simple org-to-org migrations. Best for low-maturity teams or infrequent deployments. Salesforce CLI (sf deploy): scriptable, supports all metadata types, integrates with CI pipelines, supports destructive changes, delta deployments. The modern standard. ANT Migration Tool: XML-based, command-line, legacy tool pre-dating SF CLI. No longer recommended; use CLI instead. SF CLI is the right choice for any team investing in automation.

topics.question: Change Set limitations
topics.answer: Key Change Set limitations: (1) No destructive changes - cannot delete metadata in the same deployment; must delete separately in target org. (2) No version tracking - no history of what was deployed or when. (3) Point-to-point topology only - can only deploy between orgs with a defined deployment connection (cannot deploy to arbitrary targets). (4) Manual dependency ordering - must manually add all dependent components; no automatic resolution. (5) No scripted automation - entirely GUI-driven, cannot integrate with CI/CD. These limitations make Change Sets unsuitable for teams with multiple environments or frequent releases.

topics.question: When Change Set limitations warrant migration to CLI or CI/CD tooling
topics.answer: Migrate away from Change Sets when: (1) Deployments require destructive changes (field/class deletions). (2) Team has more than 2-3 developers working in parallel. (3) Release frequency is more than once per month. (4) An audit trail of deployments is required. (5) The team wants to introduce automated testing as a gate. (6) Multiple sandboxes need to be kept in sync. (7) A branching strategy has been adopted. Transition path: start by using SF CLI with manual commands, then automate those commands in a CI pipeline.

topics.question: Deployment validation vs. quick deploy
topics.answer: Deployment validation: runs all specified tests and checks for deployment errors WITHOUT committing changes to the org. Creates a 'validated deployment' record. Quick Deploy: after a successful validation, you can deploy the same set of changes WITHOUT re-running tests within a 10-day window, significantly reducing deployment time. Conditions for quick deploy: validation must have passed with no errors, all required tests passed with 75%+ coverage, no changes to the validated metadata since validation. Risk: if the target org has changed between validation and quick deploy, the deployment may fail or behave unexpectedly. Use in production deployment windows to minimize downtime.

topics.question: CI/CD pipeline architecture for Salesforce
topics.answer: Stages: (1) Build: resolve metadata delta (what changed since last deployment), package components for deployment. (2) Validate: run 'sf project deploy validate' against target org - checks metadata validity and runs tests without committing. (3) Test: run Apex test suite (RunSpecifiedTests or RunLocalTests), generate coverage report, run static analysis (PMD/Code Analyzer), optionally run UI automation (Provar/CRT). (4) Deploy: if all gates pass, run 'sf project deploy start' to commit changes to the target org. (5) Post-deploy: run post-deployment scripts (assign permission sets, activate flows, seed data). Tools: GitHub Actions/Jenkins orchestrate; SF CLI executes; Slack/Teams notify.

topics.question: Salesforce DevOps Center
topics.answer: DevOps Center is Salesforce's native release management layer built on top of the platform itself. It integrates with GitHub for source control and provides a GUI for managing work items (user stories), pipelines, and deployments without needing third-party tools. Key capabilities: pipeline visualization, work item tracking, change bundling, and GitHub-based source truth. Best for: teams moving off Change Sets who want a guided, native experience without third-party tooling cost. Preferred over third-party tools when: budget constraints exist, team is not technically ready for raw CI/CD pipeline management, and GitHub is already the SCM of choice.

topics.question: Third-party deployment tools (Copado, Gearset, Flosum)
topics.answer: Copado: enterprise-grade Salesforce DevOps platform with full pipeline management, user story tracking, conflict resolution, rollback, compliance features, and AI-assisted capabilities (Agentia). Best for large enterprises needing full ALM governance. Gearset: developer-friendly, strong UI for comparing orgs and deploying delta changes, CI/CD integration, backup/restore. Best for teams wanting quick adoption with minimal setup. Flosum: native Salesforce AppExchange app, all data stays in Salesforce. Best for orgs with strict data sovereignty requirements. All three reduce CLI complexity but add licensing cost and vendor dependency.

topics.question: CI/CD platform selection for Salesforce
topics.answer: GitHub Actions: native to GitHub repos, excellent Salesforce community support (sfdx-cli action, salesforce-cca action), YAML-based, free tier available. Best for teams already on GitHub. Jenkins: highly customizable, self-hosted, large plugin ecosystem, SF CLI Jenkinsfile patterns well-documented. Best for enterprises with existing Jenkins infrastructure and need for complex pipelines. Azure DevOps Pipelines: integrated with Azure Boards and Azure Repos, YAML or classic editor, good for Microsoft-stack enterprises. Bitbucket Pipelines: tightly integrated with Bitbucket repos, YAML-based, simpler than Jenkins. Evaluate based on: existing toolchain, team skills, hosting requirements, and pipeline complexity.

topics.question: Metadata API deployment order dependencies
topics.answer: Salesforce Metadata API requires components to be deployed in dependency order or in the same deployment package. Key dependency rules: (1) Custom Objects must deploy before their fields. (2) Custom Fields must deploy before Page Layouts and Compact Layouts that reference them. (3) Apex Classes must deploy before Apex Triggers that reference them. (4) Permission Sets must deploy before assigning them in post-deploy scripts. (5) Flows must deploy before Process Builders that call them. Failure to respect dependency order causes deployment errors. CI tools like Copado handle dependency ordering automatically; raw CLI deployments require you to manage this manually or deploy all components in a single package.

objectives.title: Explain and recommend source control branching, versioning, and merging strategies

topics.question: Git branching strategies for Salesforce development
topics.answer: Trunk-based development: all developers commit frequently (daily) to a single main branch; feature flags used to hide incomplete work; lowest merge conflict risk; requires high test automation maturity. Best for high-maturity teams with strong CI. Gitflow: long-lived develop, release, and hotfix branches; releases are bundled and merged to main; high governance but high merge conflict risk in large metadata files. Best for scheduled release cadences. Feature branching: one branch per user story/feature, merged to main via PR; balances isolation and integration speed. Most common in Salesforce. Choose based on team size, release frequency, and test automation maturity.

topics.question: Branching strategy for a customer with a hotfix alongside an active feature branch
topics.answer: Recommended approach: (1) Create a hotfix branch from the production release tag (not from main/develop, which may contain unreleased features). (2) Develop and test the fix in the hotfix branch. (3) Merge the hotfix directly to production (or the production branch). (4) Immediately merge the hotfix branch back into the main/develop branch and all active feature branches to prevent regression. (5) Tag the hotfix release in Git. Risk: if feature branches are not updated with the hotfix, the next regular release will revert the fix. Use merge or rebase strategy consistently.

topics.question: Handling declarative changes alongside programmatic changes in source control
topics.answer: Declarative changes (flows, layouts, approval processes, custom fields) are stored as XML metadata files in source control alongside Apex code. Use 'sf project retrieve start' to pull declarative changes from a sandbox into the local source format. Track flows as FlowDefinition and Flow metadata types. Layouts as Layout type. Key challenge: admins making declarative changes in a sandbox must remember to retrieve and commit those changes, or they will be lost on sandbox refresh. Solution: establish a 'retrieve and commit' workflow step as part of every admin's daily process. Consider using source-tracked orgs (scratch orgs or opted-in sandboxes) to automate change detection.

topics.question: Managing merge conflicts in Salesforce XML metadata
topics.answer: Salesforce metadata files (especially Profiles, Permission Sets, and Object XML) are large, auto-generated XML files that conflict frequently when multiple developers modify the same file. Prevention strategies: (1) Use Permission Sets instead of Profiles to reduce Profile file size and conflict surface. (2) Split object metadata into sub-files (source format does this automatically). (3) Keep feature branches short-lived to reduce divergence. Resolution strategies: use a git merge tool with XML awareness; resolve conflicts by keeping both sets of changes and removing only the XML diff markers. Tooling: Gearset and Copado have built-in conflict resolution UIs that compare metadata semantically rather than as raw XML.

topics.question: Semantic versioning and tagging strategies in Salesforce source control
topics.answer: Apply Git tags at every production deployment using semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH). MAJOR: breaking changes or significant feature releases. MINOR: new features, backward-compatible. PATCH: bug fixes / hotfixes. Tag format example: 'v2.3.1'. Benefits: (1) Clear rollback point - if a production issue occurs, revert to the previous tag. (2) Audit trail - associate a Git tag with a deployment record and CAB approval. (3) Package versioning alignment - unlocked package versions can map to Git tags. Script tagging into the CI/CD pipeline post-successful production deployment so tagging is never forgotten.

objectives.title: Describe appropriate approaches to test data strategy and unit tests

topics.question: Minimum Apex code coverage requirements for production deployment
topics.answer: Salesforce requires at minimum 75% org-wide Apex code coverage to deploy to production. Additionally, every Apex trigger must have at least 1% coverage. What counts: executable lines covered by at least one test method. What does NOT count: comments, blank lines, class/method declarations, System.debug statements, test class code itself. Coverage is calculated org-wide (all Apex in the org), not per-class. Deploying a new class with 0% coverage is allowed as long as org-wide total remains at or above 75%. Avoid 'coverage-only' tests that hit lines without asserting behavior.

topics.question: Positive path and negative path Apex unit test design
topics.answer: Positive path tests verify that the code works correctly under expected conditions: valid input, correct record creation, expected field values updated, expected trigger behavior. Negative path tests verify that the code fails gracefully under invalid conditions: null inputs, missing required fields, unauthorized access, bulk limits exceeded, duplicate records. Both are required for robust test coverage. Negative path tests often catch the real bugs. Example: a positive test creates a valid Opportunity and confirms the stage updates correctly; a negative test attempts to create an Opportunity with a null Account and confirms a meaningful exception or error message is returned.

topics.question: Permission-based unit tests using System.runAs()
topics.answer: System.runAs(user) executes a block of test code in the context of a specified user, enforcing sharing rules, FLS, and CRUD permissions. Use it to: (1) Test that users without a certain permission set cannot access or modify records. (2) Verify record visibility under org-wide defaults and sharing rules. (3) Confirm that FLS is enforced for sensitive fields. Pattern: create a test user with a specific profile/permission set, call System.runAs(testUser) { ... } around the code under test. Important: System.runAs does NOT enforce governor limits per-user in tests; it only enforces security context. Every test that involves record-level security should use System.runAs.

topics.question: Test data isolation in Apex: @isTest(SeeAllData=false)
topics.answer: @isTest(SeeAllData=false) is the default behavior: tests cannot see any org data; all data must be created within the test. This is the correct and safe default. SeeAllData=true allows tests to see real org data; this makes tests environment-dependent and fragile (they pass in one sandbox, fail in another because data differs). Use SeeAllData=true only when absolutely required (e.g., testing against standard price books, which require SeeAllData=true). Risks of SeeAllData=true: tests are brittle, data-dependent, hard to maintain, and can cause false positives/negatives depending on org state.

topics.question: Test data factory patterns in Apex
topics.answer: Test data factory: a shared Apex class (e.g., TestDataFactory) with static methods that create and optionally insert standard test records. Benefits: DRY principle - test data creation logic in one place; consistent test records across all tests; easy to update when schema changes. @testSetup: a method annotated @testSetup runs once before all test methods in the class and creates shared data. More efficient than creating data in each test method. Prefer @testSetup for data shared across many tests in the same class; prefer factory methods for complex, varied, or cross-class data needs. Combine both: factory generates records, @testSetup inserts them once.

topics.question: Apex mock frameworks for callout testing
topics.answer: Apex tests cannot make real HTTP or web service callouts. Two interfaces to mock them: (1) HttpCalloutMock: implement the respond() method to return a fake HttpResponse for REST/HTTP callouts. Set it with Test.setMock(HttpCalloutMock.class, mockInstance). (2) WebServiceMock (StubProvider): implement the doInvoke() method to simulate SOAP web service responses. Set it with Test.setMock(WebServiceMock.class, mockInstance). Pattern: create a mock class that implements the interface, return a predefined response, then assert that your Apex code processes the response correctly. This isolates the unit test from external dependencies and makes it deterministic.

topics.question: Bulk and large data volume Apex unit test design
topics.answer: Salesforce triggers and batch Apex must handle bulk operations (up to 200 records per trigger invocation in synchronous DML, up to 2000 records per batch chunk). Unit tests must verify bulk behavior: create 200 records in a single DML operation and assert the trigger handles all 200 correctly. Test for: SOQL queries not exceeding limits in bulk context, DML statements not exceeding limits, CPU time remaining within limits, no row-by-row processing. A trigger that works for 1 record but fails at 200 is a critical production bug. Always include at least one bulk test per trigger.

topics.question: Large data volume testing in Apex using Test.startTest/stopTest
topics.answer: Test.startTest() resets governor limit counters for the code between startTest() and Test.stopTest(). This allows tests to set up data before startTest() without consuming the limits the code under test will use. stopTest() also flushes async operations (future methods, queueable, batch Apex scheduled within startTest). To simulate large data volumes: create large record lists in @testSetup (or before startTest), then call startTest(), trigger your Apex, call stopTest(), and assert results. Note: actual data volume is still capped at DML limits in tests - you cannot test true millions-of-records scenarios in unit tests; use sandbox performance testing for that.

objectives.title: Describe the appropriate development model and development environment

topics.question: Org-based development vs. package-based development
topics.answer: Org-based development: the production org is the system of record; changes are made in sandboxes and deployed to production; source control may be used but the org is the truth. Simpler, familiar to admins. Package-based development: source control is the system of record; changes are assembled into packages (unlocked or managed) that are installed into orgs; the org is just a package installation target. More scalable, enables modular architecture, better for large teams. Key differences: source tracking (packages track what is installed), deployment mechanism (package installation vs. metadata deploy), and team collaboration model (package subscribers vs. sandbox deployments).

topics.question: Salesforce CLI source-tracking in org-based development
topics.answer: 'sf project deploy start' (formerly sfdx force:source:push) pushes local source changes to a source-tracked org. 'sf project retrieve start' (formerly sfdx force:source:pull) pulls org changes to local source. Source tracking is available for scratch orgs by default and for opted-in sandboxes (source tracking sandboxes, introduced in recent releases). This differs from the traditional Metadata API model where you specify which components to retrieve/deploy explicitly - source tracking automatically detects what changed. Source tracking sandboxes give org-based teams scratch-org-like workflow without full package-based development adoption.

topics.question: Scratch org capabilities and limitations
topics.answer: Capabilities: fully configurable via scratch org definition JSON file (features, org preferences, edition), can be created in seconds, can be seeded with data via scripts, enable source tracking, isolated per developer/CI run, no licensing cost (included with Dev Hub). Limitations: expire after 1-30 days (default 7), maximum 40 active per Dev Hub (200 with expanded allocation), no production data, features must be enabled in definition file (cannot just test with production config), managed package installations can be slow. Best for: feature development, CI testing, package development. Not ideal for: UAT (needs representative data), performance testing (needs data volume).

topics.question: Choosing between scratch orgs and developer sandboxes
topics.answer: Choose scratch orgs when: team is doing package-based development, full isolation per feature is needed, CI pipeline needs clean environments per build, team is comfortable with SF CLI and Dev Hub. Choose developer sandboxes when: team is doing org-based development, long-running development tasks span multiple weeks, declarative admins need a persistent environment, team lacks CLI expertise. Cost: scratch orgs are included with Dev Hub license (typically included with Enterprise+); developer sandboxes have a per-sandbox cost but are typically included in most Salesforce editions. Team size matters: scratch orgs scale better for large dev teams needing many isolated environments.

topics.question: Scratch org expiry and lifecycle management
topics.answer: Default scratch org expiry: 7 days. Maximum: 30 days. When a scratch org expires, all work in it is lost - metadata and data are deleted. Implications for long-running feature branches: if a feature takes longer than the scratch org lifetime, you must either extend the scratch org (up to 30 days max) or recreate and re-push. Strategies to avoid losing work: commit and push to source control daily (the source control branch is the permanent record, not the scratch org). Use 'sf org create scratch --duration-days 30' for long features. Document data seeding scripts so a new scratch org can be re-seeded quickly if needed.

topics.question: sfdx-project.json structure and packageDirectories configuration
topics.answer: The sfdx-project.json file is the project manifest for Salesforce DX projects. Key properties: 'packageDirectories' defines which source folders belong to which package (path, package name, version number, dependencies). 'sourceApiVersion' sets the Metadata API version for source format. 'namespace' sets the namespace prefix (required for managed packages). 'plugins' registers SF CLI plugin settings.
