Dashboard components: gauge for current error rate vs SLA threshold, bar chart for volume by system, and a list of recent failures requiring attention. Share dashboards with business stakeholders via Salesforce access (no dev tools required). Schedule report emails for daily/weekly health summaries. Use Report Types to join log records to related Salesforce objects for context.

topics.question: Designing integration audit trail reports that capture message volumes, success/failure rates, and SLA compliance over time for stakeholder reporting
topics.answer: Audit trail report design: log each integration execution in a custom object with timestamps (start time, end time), volume processed, success count, failure count, and SLA target. Create Salesforce Report Types joining the log object to related records. Build matrix reports showing volume and error rates by day/week/month. SLA compliance: calculate processing time against the SLA threshold (e.g., percentage of records processed within 15 minutes). Schedule reports to run automatically and email to stakeholders. Archive older log records to Big Objects if long-term retention is required.

topics.question: Defining reporting requirements that distinguish transient failures (auto-recovered) from persistent failures (requiring business escalation) in integration monitoring dashboards
topics.answer: Transient failures: initially failed but successfully retried automatically. These should be logged with status 'Auto-Recovered' and tracked in a separate report metric (retry rate). Persistent failures: failed after all retry attempts and require human intervention. Log with status 'Failed - Pending Review' and trigger an automated alert. Dashboards should show: two separate gauges (transient vs persistent failure rates), a list of persistent failures pending review, and a trend line showing if the retry rate is increasing (early warning of a systemic issue). Distinguish these clearly so business stakeholders don't confuse auto-recovered events with true failures.

topics.question: Establishing integration governance reporting: tracking API consumer usage by connected app, enforcing rate limits per consumer, and providing capacity planning data to integration architects
topics.answer: Integration governance reporting: use the /limits REST endpoint and EventLogFile to extract API call counts per Connected App. Build a Salesforce Dashboard or external BI report showing: API consumption per Connected App as a percentage of daily limits, trends over 30/60/90 days for capacity planning, and Connected Apps approaching their fair-share threshold. Enforce rate limits: configure API gateway (MuleSoft API Manager) policies to throttle per Connected App. Provide monthly capacity planning reports to integration architects showing growth rates and projected limit exhaustion dates to inform licensing and architecture decisions.

reasoningengine.title: The Mental Model: What Agentforce Actually Is

objectives.title: Understand the three-layer hybrid execution architecture of the Agentforce runtime.

topics.question: What 'Daisy' refers to and how it formally manifests in Salesforce metadata
topics.answer: Daisy is the informal name for the Agentforce runtime planner — the engine that receives a user message, interprets the AgentScript file, and produces a response. When you run 'sf agent publish', it formally compiles into the GenAiPlannerBundle metadata artifact. Daisy is not a single large language model. It is a hybrid execution environment composed of three distinct layers: (1) a deterministic resolver that functions like a compiler pass, evaluating all authored logic before any LLM is involved; (2) an LLM reasoning loop where an underlying foundation model makes probabilistic decisions within the constraints the resolver has already enforced; and (3) the Einstein Trust Layer, a runtime security boundary that wraps every LLM call with guardrails, zero-retention enforcement, and toxicity detection. Every design decision, every bug, and every optimization traces back to the interaction between these three layers. This three-layer architecture is the foundational mental model for all Agentforce development.

topics.question: The fundamental split between what the deterministic layer controls versus what the LLM layer controls
topics.answer: The deterministic layer handles: if/else condition evaluation, variable injection into prompt text, run @actions.X execution, available when filtering of tool schemas, transition to routing, and set variable capture. The LLM layer handles: which action to call, how to fill slot parameters, what to say to the user, whether to respond or call a tool, how to phrase and sequence the response, and which of multiple valid paths to take. The critical insight is that the LLM never sees raw AgentScript syntax. It never sees if blocks, run statements, @variables.X references, or available when guards. It only ever sees the output of the deterministic pass — a clean, resolved prompt string plus a filtered set of tool schemas. In summary: deterministic logic controls WHAT the agent knows, the LLM controls WHETHER and HOW to act on that knowledge, and the Trust Layer controls what leaves and enters the Salesforce boundary.

topics.question: The difference between the authoring domain and the runtime domain, and why 'deploy' is not 'publish'
topics.answer: There are two completely separate metadata domains in Agentforce. The authoring domain contains the AiAuthoringBundle — the .agent file plus bundle-meta.xml — which is created by the developer at authoring time via the Salesforce CLI. The runtime domain contains the GenAiPlannerBundle, the Bot, and the BotVersion metadata — all of which are created by the Salesforce platform when you run 'sf agent publish'. The most important operational consequence of this split: deploy does NOT create runtime entities. Running 'sf project deploy start' only stages the authoring bundle in the org. Publish compiles the agent and creates the full runtime graph. An agent that has been deployed but not published cannot be activated or tested. This distinction is critical in every deployment conversation.

topics.question: The Atlas engine, the Agent Graph, and the two mathematical structures that underpin runtime execution
topics.answer: A common misconception is that AgentScript is interpreted live, line-by-line, at runtime. In reality, the Atlas engine employs a compilation phase when you publish an agent. The .agent file compiles into an Agent Graph that the runtime executes. This graph encodes two underlying mathematical structures. First, a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG): tool invocations, sequential dependencies, and deterministic actions are mapped as a DAG, which prevents infinite loops within automated workflows and guarantees that prerequisites (such as retrieving an account ID) are met before downstream actions (such as updating a balance) occur. Second, a Finite State Machine (FSM): transitions between subagents and internal states are managed via an FSM, which records 'backward arrows' indicating when the LLM must retry an action due to a failure, preventing catastrophic workflow degradation. Understanding the DAG/FSM duality explains why the runtime behaves with predictability in the deterministic path and flexibility in the LLM path.

objectives.title: Understand Phase 1 deterministic resolution and the precise sequence of operations it performs.

topics.question: The complete sequence of operations performed by Phase 1 during each reasoning iteration
topics.answer: Every reasoning iteration passes through Phase 1 before the LLM is ever involved. Phase 1 reads reasoning.instructions: -> from top to bottom and performs the following operations in order: (1) Evaluates if/else if/else conditions against the current values of all variables — only the matching branch's content proceeds; non-matching branches are discarded entirely. (2) Executes run @actions.X calls synchronously — the action runs (Apex, Flow, etc.) and its outputs are immediately available. (3) Executes set @variables.X statements, updating variable state immediately. (4) Injects {!@variables.X} tokens by replacing them with current variable values in the pipe text. (5) Evaluates available when guards on each action in the reasoning.actions block — actions that fail their guard are completely removed from the tool schema; the LLM will have no awareness they exist. (6) Fires 'transition to' immediately if one is reached, discarding the current prompt and starting fresh in the target subagent — the LLM is never called. The output of Phase 1 is a resolved prompt string (only the pipe lines matching current state) and a filtered tool schema (only actions where available when evaluated to True).

topics.question: The precise diagnostic question to ask when an agent behaves unexpectedly, using the Phase 1 / Phase 2 split
topics.answer: The two-phase architecture provides a precise binary diagnostic framework for unexpected agent behavior. If the wrong branch was shown to the LLM, it is a Phase 1 problem: the cause is a wrong variable value, a wrong condition expression, or the use of pipe (|) mode instead of procedural (->) mode in the instructions block. If the right branch was shown but the LLM acted incorrectly, it is a Phase 2 problem: the cause is a poor action description, ambiguous instructions text, a missing stop condition, or an action description conflict. This binary framing cuts diagnostic time dramatically because it immediately narrows the investigation to either the authored logic or the LLM behavior, which require different debugging tools (trace variable state for Phase 1, trace LLMStep.messages_sent and tool schemas for Phase 2).

objectives.title: Understand Phase 2 LLM reasoning and the three decisions the LLM can make.

topics.question: What the LLM receives as input during Phase 2 and the three decisions it can make
topics.answer: The resolved prompt string and filtered tool schemas from Phase 1 pass through the Einstein Trust Layer and are then handed to the underlying foundation model. The LLM receives exactly four things: (1) one system prompt — either the global system.instructions or the subagent-level system override, never both merged; (2) the full conversation history for the current session; (3) the resolved reasoning.instructions — only the pipe text matching the current variable state, with no conditionals, no run blocks, and no set statements; (4) tool schemas as JSON function schemas for only the actions that passed their available when guard. With this context, the LLM makes one of three decisions: call an action (selects one tool, fills its slot parameters using ellipsis extraction from conversation, and submits the call); produce a terminal response (writes a text reply to the user and ends the current reasoning loop); or delegate to a subagent if a delegation action is available (calls a subagent as a tool, which runs its own reasoning loop and returns control).

topics.question: What the LLM explicitly does NOT see, and the practical authoring rule that follows from this
topics.answer: The LLM never sees: raw if or else keywords or the conditions they contain; run statements; set statements; available when conditions (failing actions simply do not appear in the tool schema); before_reasoning or after_reasoning block content; subagent names or the concept of subagents as a structural entity; the @variables.X syntax (it only sees the resolved value after {!@variables.X} injection); or any action invocations that fired deterministically during Phase 1. The practical authoring rule that follows directly: never write a reasoning instruction that tells the model to 'check @variables.X' or 'look at the active subagent.' The model cannot do this. Instructions must state the concrete operational task in plain English based on what Phase 1 has already resolved and injected into the prompt text.

objectives.title: Understand the re-resolution loop and the backward arrow FSM retry mechanic.

topics.question: The re-resolution loop: what it is, when it fires, and why post-action checks must be placed at the TOP of instruction blocks
topics.answer: The single most misunderstood mechanic in Agentforce: after every tool call, the entire reasoning.instructions block is rebuilt from scratch using the updated variable state. This is not 'continue from where you left off.' It is a full re-evaluation of the entire instruction block, top to bottom. This has one critical authoring consequence: post-action conditional checks MUST be placed at the TOP of instructions: -> blocks. When the loop re-evaluates after a tool call, it reads from the top. If a 'did the action succeed?' check is at the bottom, the LLM sees all the prior instructions (for example, 'please ask the user for their order number') again before ever reaching the success check, causing double-execution, confusion, and non-deterministic behavior. The correct pattern places the result-check first: 'if @variables.order_status != "": transition to @subagent.show_status' at the top, followed by the initial user-facing instruction below it.

topics.question: The backward arrow: what it means in FSM terms and how it appears in AgentLens diagnostics
topics.answer: The Atlas FSM records 'backward arrows' — a formal concept that describes what happens when the LLM attempts a tool call and receives an error payload. Rather than crashing, the FSM records the failure and the LLM reasons into an alternative approach. This retry mechanic prevents catastrophic workflow degradation when an action fails. In AgentLens, the visual trace inspector, backward arrows appear as literal visual edges in the Chain of Thought graph showing exactly where the LLM attempted a tool call, received an error, and pivoted to an alternative path. This makes AgentLens especially valuable for diagnosing retry storms, where a missing parameter or a misconfigured action causes the LLM to loop through repeated failed attempts before reaching the 3-4 iteration hard cap and forcing a turn exit.

objectives.title: Trace the complete execution sequence for a single user message from arrival to response.

topics.question: The full turn execution sequence from user message arrival to turn end
topics.answer: A complete Agentforce turn executes in this sequence. First, the user message arrives and triggers the before_reasoning hook (if present), which runs once per turn in deterministic-only mode — it can set variables, run actions, evaluate conditions, and fire transitions; if a transition fires here, the LLM is never called for this turn. Second, if no transition fired, the reasoning loop begins. The loop repeats until a terminal response is produced or the 3-4 iteration hard cap is reached. Each iteration of the loop runs Phase 1 (deterministic resolution) followed by the Einstein Trust Layer, then Phase 2 (LLM reasoning). If the LLM calls an action, the action executes, outputs are captured, the loop counter increments, and Phase 1 re-resolution begins immediately from the top with updated variable state. If the LLM produces a terminal response, the response is sent to the user and the loop exits. Third, after the reasoning loop exits with a terminal response, the after_reasoning hook fires once per turn, running deterministically. Finally, the turn ends and the agent awaits the next user message.

topics.question: The 3-4 reasoning iteration hard cap: what it is and what happens when it is reached
topics.answer: Agentforce enforces a hard platform guardrail of approximately 3-4 reasoning iterations per turn before forcing a turn exit. A reasoning iteration is one complete Phase 1 + Phase 2 cycle. Each time the LLM calls an action and re-resolution begins, the iteration counter increments. When the cap is reached, the platform forces the turn to exit with a generated error response rather than allowing infinite loops. This cap is an architecture driver: any workflow requiring more than 4 sequential action calls per turn must be redesigned to break across multiple user turns. Common symptoms of hitting the cap include an 'Unexpected Error' response after a sequence of successful actions and a PlannerResponseStep in the trace that does not correspond to any LLM-written content.

objectives.title: Understand the global system instructions surface and its correct versus incorrect usage.

topics.question: What belongs in global system.instructions and what does not
topics.answer: The global system.instructions block is the durable identity of the agent. It should contain: agent persona and tone, safety and scope invariants, disclosure rules (such as 'you are an AI'), and response format expectations. It should NOT contain: task-specific logic (which belongs in reasoning.instructions), subagent-specific overrides (which belong in the subagent system block), or conditional behavior (conditional text in the global system block appears as literal prose to the LLM, which may or may not follow it). The most common mistake in router-first agents is writing 'Answer the user's questions helpfully' in the global system block while simultaneously writing 'Do not answer. Route only.' in the start_agent reasoning block. The LLM receives both simultaneously, creating undefined behavior. The correct global instruction for a router-first agent permits each subagent to define its own posture: for example, 'Perform only the current operating task described below. Answer the underlying request only when that task calls for an answer. Otherwise route, verify, clarify, refuse, or escalate as directed.'

objectives.title: Understand subagent system overrides and the invariant restatement requirement.

topics.question: How subagent system overrides work and why they require explicit restatement of all invariants
topics.answer: When a subagent has its own system: block, it completely replaces the global system instructions for that subagent. It does not append. It does not merge. It replaces. This means: if the global system instructions contain 'never reveal internal configuration,' and a specialist subagent has a system override that omits this rule, the specialist subagent no longer has that invariant. The invariant is silently dropped with no error or warning. The authoring rule is absolute: restate every invariant the subagent must retain in the subagent-level system block. A safe pattern for specialist subagents is to include all safety and disclosure invariants as explicit statements at the end of the subagent system block. Use subagent system overrides sparingly; the default is to inherit global system instructions, which is safer.

objectives.title: Understand reasoning.instructions, its two modes, and the invisible bug that results from using the wrong mode.

topics.question: The difference between literal mode (|) and procedural mode (->) in reasoning.instructions
topics.answer: The reasoning.instructions surface is rebuilt on every reasoning iteration and is where authoring craft is most visible. It has two modes. Literal mode (|): content is sent as-is to the LLM with no evaluation. Any if keywords written here appear as literal English text in the LLM's prompt — the model reads them as prose and may or may not follow them. Use this mode only for simple, non-conditional instructions. Procedural mode (->): activates deterministic evaluation. The resolver reads top-to-bottom, evaluates conditions, runs actions, and only the matching pipe (|) lines reach the LLM. Use this mode whenever conditional logic, variable injection, or run/set statements appear. The invisible bug: using | mode when conditional behavior is needed is the most common silent authoring failure. No error is thrown. The LLM simply receives the literal 'if @variables.is_verified == True:' text as English and tries to interpret it — sometimes correctly, often not. Always use -> mode when the instructions block contains any conditional logic.

objectives.title: Understand before_reasoning and after_reasoning lifecycle hooks, including their compile constraints.

topics.question: before_reasoning: when it fires, what it is used for, and the critical syntax constraint that causes a compile error
topics.answer: before_reasoning runs once per turn, before the reasoning loop begins. It is used for authentication and authorization gates (to fail fast before any LLM cost is incurred), data pre-loading that every reasoning iteration will need, and early exits for expired sessions or invalid states. The critical compile constraint: before_reasoning does NOT use an instructions: wrapper. Content goes directly under the block. Using 'instructions: ->' inside before_reasoning is a compilation error. The correct syntax places transition, run, set, and if statements as direct children of the before_reasoning block with no instructions wrapper. A typical pattern pre-loads customer context via a run @actions statement and conditionally transitions to an authentication subagent if the session token is empty.

topics.question: after_reasoning: when it fires, what it is used for, and two critical behavioral distinctions
topics.answer: after_reasoning runs once per turn, after the reasoning loop produces a terminal response. The LLM has already spoken before after_reasoning executes. It is used for state cleanup and logging, conditional transitions based on what the turn accomplished, and recording that a turn was completed. Two critical behavioral distinctions: First, after_reasoning fires after the reasoning loop ends with a response — it does NOT fire after each tool call within the loop. Second, if a subagent transitions mid-reasoning via @utils.transition to (LLM-driven), the original subagent's after_reasoning does NOT run. Only a terminal text response triggers after_reasoning. Like before_reasoning, after_reasoning does not use an instructions: wrapper — direct content only, or the file will not compile.

objectives.title: Distinguish mutable variables from linked variables and their correct declaration syntax.

topics.question: Mutable variables: syntax, required default value, and valid types
topics.answer: Mutable variables are session-persistent values the agent can both read and write. They must have a default value declared at definition. Valid types for mutable variables are string, number, boolean, object, and list. Example declarations include: customer_name as mutable string = '', order_count as mutable number = 0, is_verified as mutable boolean = False, preferences as mutable object = {}, and item_list as mutable list[string] = []. Critical type constraints: integer, long, datetime, and time are action-parameter-only types and are NOT valid for mutable variable declarations. Use number for mutable variables that represent integers. Boolean default values must be capitalized: True or False. The parser rejects lowercase true and false, producing a compile error. This boolean capitalization mistake is one of the most common compile errors in AgentScript development.

topics.question: Linked variables: syntax, required source, and what makes them different from mutable variables
topics.answer: Linked variables are read-only values populated from external session context. They must have a source declaration and must NOT have a default value (a default value on a linked variable is a compile error). Common linked variables include: EndUserId linked string sourced from @MessagingSession.MessagingEndUserId, RoutableId linked string sourced from @MessagingSession.RoutableId, ContactId linked string sourced from @MessagingSession.ContactId, and session_user_id linked string sourced from @session.sessionID. Linked variables expose the identity and session context that Salesforce establishes at session start. They are the primary mechanism for knowing who the user is without asking them. Employee agents use @session.sessionID as their primary linked source; service agents use the MessagingSession object.

objectives.title: Master the three scope zones and the silent failure zone that produces no error.

topics.question: The three scope zones: @variables, @outputs, and @inputs — and when each is valid
topics.answer: AgentScript has three distinct variable scope zones. @variables.X is session-persistent state — valid anywhere in AgentScript logic and in {!@variables.X} injection in pipe text. @outputs.X holds action return values — valid ONLY in set and if statements IMMEDIATELY after the action's run block; the scope expires after those statements complete. @inputs.X holds action input values — valid ONLY in with clauses DURING action invocation, NOT valid in set or post-execution checks. Understanding these scope boundaries is essential because violations produce silent failures with no error messages.

topics.question: The silent failure zone: why @inputs and @outputs scope violations are the most dangerous bugs in AgentScript
topics.answer: The @inputs and @outputs scope violations are the most dangerous bugs in AgentScript because they produce no error. The action executes successfully. The variable simply does not get set. No trace error appears. The FunctionStep in the session trace shows no output capture. Example of an @inputs violation: using 'set @variables.station = @inputs.station_name' after the action has already run — the @inputs scope has expired and the set silently drops. Example of an @outputs violation: referencing '{!@outputs.customer_location}' in a pipe line after the immediate set statements from the action have already completed — @outputs is gone at that point. The correct pattern captures ALL needed output values immediately in set statements directly under the run block, then uses @variables references everywhere else. Diagnosis in traces: a FunctionStep that completes with no output capture in the postVars diff indicates an @inputs or @outputs scope violation.

topics.question: Variable persistence across subagent transitions and why this is the primary data-passing mechanism
topics.answer: Variables persist across subagent transitions. A variable set in Subagent A is fully available in Subagent B. This is the primary mechanism for passing data through a multi-subagent workflow. For example, an identity verification subagent can set @variables.is_verified = True and @variables.customer_id = @outputs.customer_id after running a verification action, then transition to an order management subagent. The order management subagent's before_reasoning block can then check if @variables.is_verified == False and redirect back to the verification subagent if the check fails. This pattern creates a stateful, secure multi-step workflow without any external storage or session middleware.

topics.question: @utils.setVariables: the turn-end side effect and the correct pattern for capture-then-act workflows
topics.answer: @utils.setVariables is the LLM-driven slot-filling utility that lets the LLM extract values from conversation and populate variables. It has a non-obvious and frequently misunderstood behavior: it ends the turn after capturing values. Instructions do not re-evaluate in the same turn after setVariables runs. This means any action listed after setVariables in the same reasoning.actions block will NOT fire in the same turn — the turn has already ended. The correct pattern for 'capture then immediately act' is LLM slot-fill directly on the target action using the ellipsis operator: 'with order_id = ...' lets the LLM extract the order_id and call the action in one turn without the turn-ending side effect of setVariables. Use setVariables only when collecting multiple variables across multiple turns is the explicit design intent.

objectives.title: Understand the three input binding patterns and their runtime implications.

topics.question: The three ways to populate action parameters and when each is appropriate
topics.answer: Action parameters can be populated three ways with different runtime behavior. LLM slot-fill (syntax: 'with param = ...'): the LLM extracts the value from conversation context using natural language understanding at reasoning time (Phase 2). If the value is not present in the conversation, the LLM will ask the user. Variable binding (syntax: 'with param = @variables.X'): the runtime reads the variable value at resolution time (Phase 1), before the LLM is ever involved. If the variable is empty, the action receives an empty string silently. Literal value (syntax: 'with param = "fixed"'): a compiled constant resolved at Phase 1 time. The ellipsis operator specifically signals the LLM to extract — choosing between ... and @variables.X is a security-critical decision: use @variables.X when the value has been pre-verified and should not be extractable from arbitrary user input, use ... only when the LLM legitimately needs to extract from conversation.

reasoningengine.title: Actions: The Bridge to the Real World

objectives.title: Distinguish deterministic invocation from LLM-driven invocation and the implications of each.

topics.question: Deterministic invocation (run @actions.X): when it fires, who controls it, and what it costs
topics.answer: Deterministic invocation uses the 'run @actions.X' syntax and fires during Phase 1 before the LLM is called. The action always executes when the code path is reached, regardless of what the LLM would think. The LLM never sees the run statement — it only sees the resolved pipe text with injected variable values after the action completes. Deterministic invocation is used for pre-loading data that every reasoning iteration will need, security checks and authorization gates, mandatory logging, and chaining multiple actions in a guaranteed order. Each execution costs 20 credits. Because it fires every time the code path is reached, a run statement in a reasoning.instructions block without a preceding condition guard can fire on every reasoning iteration, multiplying credit costs.

topics.question: LLM-driven invocation (reasoning.actions block): when the LLM calls it, how descriptions drive selection, and what makes a good description
topics.answer: LLM-driven invocation places actions in the reasoning.actions block. The LLM decides whether and when to call the action based on the action's description field and the current conversation context. The description is the primary signal — it must be specific enough for unambiguous tool selection. A vague description like 'Get data' is an anti-pattern; the LLM cannot distinguish reliably between tools with similar vague descriptions and will hallucinate or select incorrectly. A correct description is specific and complete: 'Look up the current status, estimated delivery date, and tracking number for a customer order by order ID.' Each LLM-driven invocation also costs 20 credits when the LLM chooses to call it. If the LLM does not call the action in a turn, no credits are charged for that action.

objectives.title: Master available when as a hard compiler filter for authorization and security.

topics.question: How available when works at compile time and why it is fundamentally different from prose authorization instructions
topics.answer: available when is not a soft hint to the LLM. It is a hard compiler-level filter that operates during Phase 1. When the condition evaluates to False, the action is completely absent from the tool schema handed to the LLM. The model has zero awareness the action exists. This is fundamentally different from a prose instruction like 'only call this action if the user is verified,' which is probabilistic — the LLM may or may not follow it depending on context, phrasing, and model behavior. available when is deterministic — unauthorized tool invocation becomes impossible, not just unlikely. The rule for any action with financial impact, PII access, or irreversible effects: it MUST be gated with available when. Multiple available when clauses on a single action are evaluated as a logical AND — all conditions must be True for the action to appear in the tool schema.

objectives.title: Know the action target types and their implementation requirements.

topics.question: Apex target (apex://): wrapper class requirements, exact field name matching, and reserved field names
topics.answer: Apex targets use the apex://ClassName protocol and call an Apex @InvocableMethod. Apex actions require wrapper classes with @InvocableVariable annotations for all inputs and outputs — bare List<String> parameters without wrappers are incompatible. The input and output field names in the .agent file must EXACTLY match the @InvocableVariable field names including case — camelCase matters. For example, if the Apex field is declared as 'public Decimal orderAmount', the .agent file must use 'orderAmount', not 'order_amount'. Three field names are reserved and cannot be used as @InvocableVariable names: model, description, and label. Using these reserved names causes a compile-time error during agent compilation (not during Apex compilation, so it appears as a confusing late error). Only one @InvocableMethod is permitted per Apex class.

topics.question: Flow target (flow://): the processType requirement and why Screen Flows are invalid
topics.answer: Flow targets use the flow://FlowApiName protocol and call a Salesforce Flow. The Flow must have processType set to AutoLaunchedFlow. Screen Flows are invalid targets because they require user interaction in the Salesforce UI, which is incompatible with the agent runtime. An AutoLaunchedFlow can contain all the same data logic — queries, record creates/updates, external callouts via External Services — but executes programmatically without screen interaction. I/O field names in the .agent file must match the Flow's input and output variable names exactly.

topics.question: Prompt Template target (generatePromptResponse://): input name format, output binding, and use cases
topics.answer: Prompt Template actions use the generatePromptResponse://TemplateName protocol and delegate content generation to a Salesforce Prompt Template while the agent manages conversation flow. Input names must use the quoted 'Input:fieldName' format — this is a non-obvious syntax requirement. The API name of the template must match exactly. The output is always bound to the variable named promptResponse. Prompt Templates support grounded data integration through data providers, enabling personalized responses based on org data without requiring Apex. Use cases include content generation, summarization, and recommendation responses where the generation logic belongs in the template rather than in the agent instructions. Prompt Template executions cost 2-16 credits rather than the 20-credit cost of Apex and Flow actions.

objectives.title: Distinguish the three transition mechanisms and understand handoff versus supervision.

topics.question: The three transition mechanisms, where each is valid, and what happens if you use the wrong one in the wrong context
topics.answer: There are three transition mechanisms with distinct syntax and valid contexts. Bare 'transition to @subagent.X': valid in before_reasoning, after_reasoning, and inside run post-conditions. No LLM is involved — it is deterministic, one-way with no return. @utils.transition to @subagent.X: valid in reasoning.actions only. The LLM decides when to call it. One-way with no return — the caller does not resume. @subagent.X referenced in reasoning.actions (delegation): valid in reasoning.actions only. The LLM decides when to call it. Two-way — control returns to the caller after the child subagent completes. Using the wrong syntax in the wrong context causes compilation errors that often produce unhelpful error messages. A common mistake is placing '@utils.transition to' in an after_reasoning block or bare 'transition to' in a reasoning.actions block — both are compile errors.

topics.question: Handoff versus supervision: the behavioral difference and the known Canvas UI bug
topics.answer: Handoff uses @utils.transition to: control transfers completely to the called subagent, which generates the final response. The caller never resumes. Supervision uses @subagent.X as an action reference in reasoning.actions: the parent orchestrates, the child subagent runs its full reasoning loop, produces a result, and control returns to the parent, which synthesizes the final response. Supervision is the delegation-with-return pattern. The design implication: supervision produces composable agents where the parent remains in control and can synthesize results from multiple child agents. Known bug: adding any new action in the Canvas UI view may inadvertently change Supervision references into Handoff transitions. Always verify the .agent file directly after any Canvas edits.

topics.question: The zero-hallucination routing pattern using filter_from_agent and is_used_by_planner output flags
topics.answer: Two output flags on action definitions control what the LLM can see and say. filter_from_agent: True prevents the LLM from displaying the output value to the user — used for internal routing flags, risk scores, and system IDs. is_used_by_planner: True allows the LLM to reason about the output value for routing decisions — used for intent classification outputs and decision flags. Combining both creates the zero-hallucination routing pattern: the LLM must actually call the action to get the value (it cannot guess or hallucinate it) and can use the value for routing decisions but cannot expose it to the user. This is the correct pattern for any intent classification action used in routing — it eliminates hallucinated routing by forcing the LLM to invoke the classifier before making a routing decision.

reasoningengine.title: The Posture Spectrum: Determinism vs. LLM Latitude

objectives.title: Understand the three posture types and when each is appropriate.

topics.question: The three posture types: Agentic, Mixed, and Scripted — and the default
topics.answer: Posture defines the spectrum between agentic (LLM has latitude to decide) and deterministic (authored control structures govern). Agentic posture is the default: the LLM chooses which actions to call and when, extracts slot parameters from conversation, and determines response content and sequencing. Best for open-ended tasks, information retrieval, and conversational flows with no security or ordering requirements. Mixed posture applies selective determinism: some actions are gated with available when, some parameters are pinned to variable values instead of LLM extraction, and some conditional instructions restrict LLM behavior to matched branches. Best for tasks with security gates, irreversible actions, or external system ordering requirements. Scripted posture is fully deterministic: all transitions use bare 'transition to', all action invocations use 'run', all variables are pre-set from deterministic sources, and the LLM has zero discretion about what happens next. Best for regulated workflows, strict legal compliance, and zero-tolerance for variation.

topics.question: The five justifications for adding determinism, and the principle that adding determinism without justification increases brittleness
topics.answer: Only add deterministic controls when justified by one of these five causes. First, regulatory requirement: a compliance rule mandates specific sequencing or disclosure. Second, trust gate: identity verification must complete before access is granted. Third, irreversible action: once fired, the action cannot be undone (refund, cancellation, deletion). Fourth, external system ordering: an external API requires operations in a specific sequence. Fifth, observed production failure: a specific behavior has failed in production and deterministic control is the proven fix. If the justification does not match one of these five, keep the posture agentic. Adding determinism for 'just in case' reasons increases brittleness without improving safety — it constrains the LLM's ability to handle natural variation in user input, produces more rigid failure modes, and increases maintenance burden without a concrete benefit.

topics.question: The three control primitives for implementing determinism: available when, parameter pinning, and conditional instructions
topics.answer: Three primitives implement deterministic control. available when: hard-removes an action from the tool schema when the condition is False. Used for authorization gates and irreversible action guards. Parameter pinning: binding a parameter to @variables.X instead of the ellipsis operator forces a specific value and removes the LLM slot-fill decision. Used for pre-filling verified data (such as a confirmed customer ID on a payment action) so the LLM cannot extract a different value from malicious user input. Conditional instructions: if/else blocks in 'reasoning.instructions: ->' mode ensure the LLM only sees the branch matching the current state. Used for security-state-dependent instruction sets (showing different instructions to verified versus unverified users). Each primitive operates at a different layer and can be combined for defense-in-depth.

topics.question: The minimal instructions principle and why shorter instructions produce better LLM performance
topics.answer: Keep instructions minimal. Optimal LLM performance comes from concise, focused instructions. Push as much logic as possible OUT of AgentScript instructions and INTO actions. Logic in actions is reusable across subagents and agents. Shorter instructions produce better LLM performance because the model has fewer competing signals to resolve and a cleaner operational context. Adding instructions without a concrete reason actively degrades LLM quality — it introduces noise that the model must filter. The minimal instructions principle is also directly connected to the 10,000-token heuristic: every unnecessary instruction token brings the context budget closer to the threshold where latency and accuracy degrade.

objectives.title: Know the four core architecture patterns and when each is appropriate.

topics.question: Single Scope pattern: the default starting point and when NOT to add a router
topics.answer: The Single Scope pattern uses one start_agent with one or a few subagents and no routing layer. This is always the starting point. Use Single Scope unless you have genuine multiple business domains that require different handling — not theoretical future domains, but concrete present requirements. A single-scope agent can handle dozens of actions and multiple subagents for functional separation while avoiding the routing overhead, additional debugging complexity, and the after-reasoning router transition trap that comes with a router layer. The minimalist principle: default to single-domain agentic design and add complexity only when justified by a named, concrete requirement.

topics.question: Router-First pattern: when it applies, what the router's job is, and what it must NOT do
topics.answer: The Router-First pattern uses start_agent as a routing hub that transitions to domain-specific subagents using @utils.transition to. Use this pattern when you have multiple genuinely different business domains that each require different action sets, instructions, and behavior — not when a single subagent with more actions would suffice. The router's only job is routing. It does not answer questions. It does not retrieve data. It does not collect user information. A router that answers questions is a design failure because it conflates routing logic with domain logic. The router's reasoning.instructions block should contain a single clear directive: 'Route the customer's request to the right specialist. Do not answer. Route only.' Each @utils.transition to action description must be MECE — Mutually Exclusive and Collectively Exhaustive — to prevent topic thrashing where the LLM cannot decide between two similarly described destinations.

topics.question: Verification Gate pattern: structure, how it intercepts flow, and how all protected actions are guarded
topics.answer: The Verification Gate pattern uses a gate subagent that intercepts the flow, verifies identity deterministically, and then transitions to the protected domain subagent. The gate uses 'instructions: ->' exclusively (procedural mode) because the routing decision is security-critical. The gate's before_reasoning block checks if @variables.is_verified == True and immediately transitions to the protected subagent if already verified — ensuring re-entry to the gate does not re-run verification. The gate's reasoning.actions block contains the verification action with output captured to @variables.is_verified and @variables.customer_id. All protected subagents should guard sensitive actions with 'available when @variables.is_verified == True' as an additional defense layer, preventing access even if the routing logic is bypassed.

topics.question: Post-Action Re-Resolution pattern: structure and why the result check must be at the top
topics.answer: The Post-Action Re-Resolution pattern handles 'do X, then based on the result, do Y or Z' workflows. The pattern requires placing the result-check at the TOP of reasoning.instructions so it fires immediately on re-resolution after the action completes. The structure: (1) at the very top, check if the result variable is set and branch to the appropriate outcome; (2) below the result check, place the initial user-facing instruction that only the LLM sees on first entry when no result exists yet. Example: 'if @variables.order_created == True: transition to @subagent.order_confirmation' at the top, followed by 'What items would you like to order?' below. Without the top placement, re-resolution causes the LLM to see the initial instruction again after the action completes, leading to double-execution and confusion.

objectives.title: Identify and resolve the after-reasoning router transition trap.

topics.question: The after-reasoning router transition trap: scenario, root cause, and fix
topics.answer: This is one of the most common production bugs in multi-subagent implementations. The scenario: a gate subagent captures data (for example, an email address for identity verification), then transitions to a router via after_reasoning. Both subagents process in the SAME user turn. The router receives control while the user's original message (for example, 'My email is john@example.com') is still the active utterance. The router tries to classify this identity-collection message as a business intent and routes it incorrectly — often to a random domain. The root cause: the user's original utterance has been consumed by the gate subagent but is still presented to the router as the current turn input. The fix: add an instruction in the router's reasoning block explicitly handling the post-setup case: 'If the customer just completed identity verification or any other setup step, greet them and ask what they need help with — do NOT route their previous message.'

objectives.title: Apply the minimalist decision hierarchy for agent architecture.

topics.question: The four-step minimalist decision hierarchy for agent architecture
topics.answer: Agentforce architecture follows a four-step decision hierarchy. Step 1: Start with a single agentic subagent. This is the default for all new agents. Step 2: Add subagents only when you have genuinely separate domains with different behavior requirements — different action sets, different personas, or different posture requirements. Step 3: Add deterministic controls only when one of the five justifications applies (regulatory requirement, trust gate, irreversible action, external ordering, or observed production failure). Step 4: Add a router only when multiple genuine domains require routing and the single-scope pattern cannot accommodate them. Every additional subagent, every additional variable, and every additional deterministic control adds maintenance burden and debugging complexity. Complexity must solve a named, concrete problem — not anticipate theoretical future needs.

reasoningengine.title: Production Constraints and the Credit Model

objectives.title: Understand the Einstein credit cost model and how it drives architectural decisions.

topics.question: Credit costs per action type and the architectural implication for poorly designed agents
topics.answer: Every Apex action call and every Flow action call costs 20 Einstein credits per execution. Prompt Template actions cost 2-16 credits. Framework operations — transitions, control flow, lifecycle hooks, variable evaluations — are free. At scale, poorly architected agents with unnecessary deterministic actions or unguarded run statements become expensive. The credit model is an architecture driver because actions that fire on every reasoning iteration (due to missing guards or incorrect placement) multiply costs unpredictably. Patterns that reduce credit consumption: using before_reasoning to pre-load data needed throughout the turn (one action call per turn instead of per iteration), guarding run statements with conditions that prevent re-firing after the first call, and using available when to suppress actions that are not currently relevant. Critically: token count drives LATENCY and LLM ACCURACY. Credit billing is per ACTION EXECUTION, not per token. These are separate optimization concerns with separate levers.

topics.question: The 10,000-token heuristic: what it governs and how to stay within it
topics.answer: The 10,000-token heuristic is an architectural target for the total context package delivered to the LLM per transaction — including system instructions, conversation history, resolved reasoning instructions, tool schemas, and any grounding data. Approaching or exceeding 10,000 tokens degrades both latency and LLM accuracy. Latency increases because larger context packages take longer to process. Accuracy decreases because the LLM has more competing content to navigate and relevant instructions become diluted. Strategies for staying within the heuristic: keep system instructions concise (under approximately 500 tokens); use available when to suppress unused actions and remove their schemas from the context; use ADL with relevancy-ranked retrieval to limit injected knowledge text; for voice agents, treat 10,000 tokens as a hard ceiling rather than a soft guideline.

topics.question: The 1MB response cap and the two consecutive ungrounded responses rule
topics.answer: Two additional production guardrails affect agent design. The 1MB response cap limits the total size of any single agent response — actions that return large data payloads or grounding results can cause silent truncation if this limit is approached. The two consecutive ungrounded responses rule: if the ReasoningStep in the session trace shows category: UNGROUNDED for two consecutive reasoning iterations, the platform forces an error response to the user ('Unexpected Error' or similar). Grounding failures occur when the LLM's response cannot be attributed to the provided context. Design implications: avoid actions that return unbounded data, always provide sufficient grounding context for the LLM's expected response, and use the filter_from_agent flag to suppress internal data that should not appear in responses.

reasoningengine.title: Safety, Governance, and the Deployment Lifecycle

objectives.title: Know the five-phase deployment lifecycle and the critical ordering rule.

topics.question: The five phases of Agentforce agent deployment and the critical ordering constraint
topics.answer: Agentforce agent deployment follows five phases. Phase 1, Safety Review: LLM-based semantic analysis of the .agent file for risks across seven categories before deployment proceeds. Phase 2, Draft Validation: syntax checking via 'sf agent validate --json'. Phase 3, Metadata Deployment: action implementations (Apex classes and Flows) must be deployed FIRST, then the AiAuthoringBundle. This ordering is a critical constraint — deploying the AiAuthoringBundle before its Apex and Flow targets exist in the org causes runtime failures. The CLI command is 'sf project deploy start --json -m AiAuthoringBundle:AgentName'. Phase 4, Publish: compiles the agent and runtime entities — 'sf agent publish authoring-bundle --json --api-name AgentName'. This is when the GenAiPlannerBundle is created. Phase 5, Release Gate: human approval is required before activation, including live preview testing with realistic utterances, verified routing traces, and verified action invocation traces.

topics.question: The release gate: what 'explicit approval' means and what must be verified before activation
topics.answer: The release gate requires five elements before activation is permitted. First, at least one live preview session with realistic utterances — not trivial happy-path inputs that do not represent real user behavior. Second, correct routing behavior verified in session traces — the TransitionStep confirms which subagent handled each turn. Third, correct action invocation verified in traces — the FunctionStep confirms actions actually fired and outputs were captured. Fourth, at least one escalation path tested if the agent supports escalation. Fifth, a named human who reviews the preview results and explicitly approves activation. Agents that pass validation (syntax check) but fail in preview (behavioral check) must not be activated. The validation command checks syntax. The release gate checks behavior. These are separate gates with separate purposes, and only behavior matters in production.

objectives.title: Know the seven safety review categories and their severity levels.

topics.question: The seven safety review categories, their severity levels, and the consequence of a BLOCK finding
topics.answer: The Agentforce safety review uses LLM semantic analysis — not regex pattern matching — to detect risks. The seven categories and their severity levels: Identity Transparency (BLOCK): does the agent identify itself as AI when directly asked? User Safety (BLOCK): could the agent cause physical or psychological harm? Data Privacy (BLOCK): is the agent exposing PII, logging restricted data, or retaining data beyond the session? Content Safety (BLOCK): harmful, offensive, illegal, or inappropriate content? Fairness (WARN): discriminatory outcomes or biased behavior? Deception Prevention (BLOCK): does the agent misrepresent its capabilities or fabricate information? Scope Boundaries (WARN): is the agent acting outside its defined business domain? BLOCK findings prevent deployment with no override — the finding must be remediated before any deployment can proceed. Agents designed to 'pretend to be human' or 'never admit to being AI' are BLOCK-level findings with no business justification bypass.

objectives.title: Understand the Einstein Trust Layer as the runtime security boundary.

topics.question: The Einstein Trust Layer: what it is, when it operates, and how it differs from the deployment-time safety review
topics.answer: The Einstein Trust Layer (ETL) is the RUNTIME security boundary that operates milliseconds before every LLM call, on every turn, for every user session. This is distinct from the deployment-time safety review, which catches authoring-level risks once before deployment. The ETL operates continuously in production. The ETL sits between the Phase 1 deterministic resolver output and the LLM. It processes every assembled context package before it exits the Salesforce trust boundary. The trust layer stack in sequence: Phase 1 output (resolved prompt + tool schemas) flows through ETL sharing rule and field-level security checks, then ETL input toxicity and injection screening, then ETL zero-retention boundary establishment for the call, then into the LLM gateway and foundation model, then back through ETL output toxicity and grounding checks, then to the reasoning loop as the LLM response.

topics.question: The ETL Zero-Retention Policy: what it guarantees and how to explain it to enterprise clients
topics.answer: The ETL Zero-Retention Policy guarantees that customer CRM data used for grounding is never stored, logged, or used to train external public models by the underlying LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and others). The data flows into the LLM gateway only for that specific inference call and is discarded immediately after the inference completes. This is a contractual and architectural guarantee from Salesforce, not just a configuration option. When an enterprise client asks 'does our customer data train OpenAI's models if we use Agentforce?', the answer is no — the mechanism is the ETL zero-retention policy. The Gen AI Audit log in Data Cloud provides a full audit trail of every agent decision, tool call, and LLM inference for compliance verification. ETL also enforces Salesforce sharing rules and field-level security at the LLM boundary — grounding data pulled for the LLM call respects the same permission model as a direct SOQL query.

reasoningengine.title: Voice Modality as a Separate Reasoning Dimension

objectives.title: Understand how voice changes the authoring contract and the core response constraint.

topics.question: The modality voice: block configuration and the core constraint that drives all voice authoring decisions
topics.answer: Voice agents use the 'modality voice:' block, which configures voice_id, outbound_speed, outbound_stability, and outbound_similarity for the text-to-speech layer. They are deployed via 'connection customer_web_client:'. The core constraint that drives all voice authoring decisions: every response must be speakable in under 2 seconds. TTS reads everything — a bulleted list becomes an incomprehensible stream and a JSON payload becomes noise. This constraint changes every aspect of how instructions, actions, and responses are authored. Voice-specific authoring rules: response length is capped at 1-2 sentences maximum; no markdown of any kind (no bullets, bold, or headers); numbers should be spelled out in words; acronyms should be spelled out; URLs and citation references must never be read aloud; confirmation patterns must be used before acting on extracted values ('I heard order number 12345 — is that correct?'); and filler phrases for action latency are essential ('Let me look that up for you' before any lookup action).

topics.question: The eight voice latency anti-patterns and the sub-2-second response window they threaten
topics.answer: Eight anti-patterns degrade the sub-2-second response window required for natural voice conversation. Synchronous writes in actions block response delivery until the write completes — fix with async writes or fire-and-forget patterns. Bulky data retrievals put too much data in context, slowing reasoning — fix by retrieving only specific fields needed. Chained callouts (multiple sequential external API calls per turn) compound latency — fix by batching externally or pre-loading in before_reasoning. Over-routing (too many subagent transitions per turn) adds transition overhead — fix by flattening the architecture for voice. Long turn responses compound TTS latency — enforce a hard 1-2 sentence cap in instructions. TTS garbling occurs with special characters, abbreviations, and numerals — use plain English, spell out numbers. STT endpointing errors occur when user pauses are misread as turn-end — design for short user utterances. SIP hops in telephony routing add 200-400ms — use filler phrases and design with the awareness that latency exists. Voice agents suffer the consequences of bloated context most acutely: a text agent can tolerate 500ms of additional reasoning latency while a voice agent cannot.

reasoningengine.title: Knowledge Grounding via the Agentforce Data Library

objectives.title: Understand what the Agentforce Data Library is and its three source types.

topics.question: What the Agentforce Data Library (ADL) is and the infrastructure prerequisite that gates its use
topics.answer: The Agentforce Data Library (ADL) is the retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) layer for Agentforce. It enables agents to answer questions grounded in organizational content by indexing that content and retrieving relevant chunks at inference time. ADL requires Data Cloud provisioning — organizations without Data Cloud cannot use ADL. This is a critical prerequisite check for any knowledge-grounded agent deployment. The ADL is configured in the .agent file using a 'knowledge:' block that lists sources, and the AnswerQuestionsWithKnowledge action is added to the reasoning.actions block to trigger retrieval.

topics.question: The three ADL source types, their key requirements, and when each is appropriate
topics.answer: ADL supports three source types. SFDRIVE indexes files from Salesforce Files and Content (PDFs, documents, and similar). Key requirement: files must be accessible to the agent user. Best for internal documentation, policy documents, and product guides stored in Salesforce Files. KNOWLEDGE indexes published Salesforce Knowledge Articles. Key requirements: the CRM Connector must be active, articles must be published (draft articles are not indexed), and the language of the articles must match the language setting of the agent user. Best for support knowledge bases and FAQ content managed through the Knowledge lifecycle. RETRIEVER connects to custom vector search endpoints using external infrastructure. Best for organizations with existing vector search infrastructure outside Salesforce. For the Dynamic Retriever pattern with custom RAG, use the '{!$EinsteinSearch:sfdc_ai__DynamicRetriever.results}' syntax in a Prompt Template — not directly in the .agent file.

reasoningengine.title: Diagnosing Agents: Traces, Symptoms, and Fixes

objectives.title: Know the session trace step types and how to read a trace to diagnose agent failures.

topics.question: The eight step types in a session trace and what each one tells you
topics.answer: Session traces are stored in Data Cloud via the Session Trace Data Model (STDM), where the core object AIAgentInteractionStep logs every micro-decision. Eight step types appear in traces. UserInputStep: the trigger for the current turn. NodeEntryStateStep: which subagent is running and the current variable state at subagent entry. EnabledToolsStep: what actions are available to the LLM after available when filtering — if an expected action is absent here, the available when condition evaluated to False. LLMStep: the full prompt sent to the LLM (messages_sent), available tools (tools_sent), and the LLM's decision (response_messages) — the most diagnostic step for Phase 2 issues. FunctionStep: the action that executed, showing name, inputs, outputs, and variable state before and after (preVars and postVars) — the most diagnostic step for @outputs capture failures. ReasoningStep: whether the response passed grounding checks (category GROUNDED or UNGROUNDED). TransitionStep: which subagent routing occurred. PlannerResponseStep: what the user actually received. Read traces in order: UserInputStep → NodeEntryStateStep → EnabledToolsStep → LLMStep → FunctionStep → ReasoningStep → PlannerResponseStep.

topics.question: The symptom-to-cause diagnostic map: matching observed symptoms to trace locations and root causes
topics.answer: Eight common symptoms and their diagnostic path. Agent asks for information the user already provided: look in LLMStep.messages_sent to check if the variable was injected — likely cause is that the variable was not set or {!@variables.X} syntax was wrong. Action fires multiple times: check FunctionStep count and loop iterations — likely cause is no available when guard and no post-action stop condition at the top of instructions. Agent routes to wrong subagent: look in LLMStep.output to see what the LLM decided — likely cause is ambiguous action descriptions or contradicting system and reasoning instructions. Variable not capturing after action: compare FunctionStep postVars to preVars — likely cause is @inputs scope violation (silent failure) or @outputs used outside immediate scope. Agent says unhelpful response after gate transition: check LLMStep.messages_sent to see what the subagent received — likely cause is the after-reasoning router transition trap. Unexpected condition branch fires: check ReasoningStep variable values at resolution time — likely cause is variable value not what was expected. LLM ignores an available action: check LLMStep tools_sent to see if the action appears in the schema — if absent, available when evaluated to False or the action description was too vague. 'Unexpected Error' response: check ReasoningStep.category — two consecutive UNGROUNDED findings force an error response.

topics.question: AgentLens: what it provides that raw trace JSON does not, and the three-tool diagnostic workflow
topics.answer: AgentLens is the visual trace inspector that renders the Chain of Thought as a connected graph rather than raw JSON. Its most distinctive feature is backward arrows — visual edges that show exactly where the LLM attempted a tool call, received an error payload, and reasoned into an alternative approach. AgentLens also provides: a visual subagent routing graph with nodes as subagents and edges as transitions; step-by-step state evolution without manual JSON parsing; a side-by-side view of instructions sent versus LLM response; and grounding pass/fail status as color-coded nodes. The three-tool diagnostic workflow: (1) use AgentLens during development and live preview testing for rapid visual diagnosis; (2) switch to STDM AIAgentInteractionStep queries in Data Cloud for production-scale pattern analysis across many sessions; (3) use CLI jq queries for specific, scripted extraction of trace fields during incident investigation. CLI example for what the LLM received: 'jq -r ".planTrace.steps[] | select(.type == \"LLM_STEP\") | .input" trace.json'.

objectives.title: Apply the 14-item pre-deployment validation checklist.

topics.question: The 14-item pre-deployment validation checklist
topics.answer: Before any agent deployment, verify all 14 items. (1) -> mode is used wherever conditional logic appears in reasoning.instructions. (2) Post-action checks are placed at the TOP of all instructions: -> blocks. (3) All mutable variables have default values. (4) All linked variables have a source and no default value. (5) All boolean values use True or False (capitalized, not lowercase). (6) before_reasoning and after_reasoning blocks use no instructions: wrapper — direct content only. (7) @utils.transition to is only in reasoning.actions, never in directive blocks. (8) Bare transition to is only in directive blocks, never in reasoning.actions. (9) All @InvocableVariable field names exactly match action I/O names including case sensitivity. (10) No reserved @InvocableVariable names are used (model, description, and label are reserved). (11) Irreversible actions are gated with available when. (12) Service agents have a default_agent_user; employee agents do NOT unless using AnswerQuestionsWithKnowledge. (13) Employee agents have no connection messaging:, no @utils.escalate, and no MessagingSession linked variables. (14) The developer_name in the config exactly matches the AiAuthoringBundle directory name.

objectives.title: Understand per-subagent model configuration and the three-tier model strategy.

topics.question: The model_config block: syntax, precedence rules, and the three-tier model strategy
topics.answer: The model_config block enables routing different subagents to different foundation models. It can be defined at three levels with clear precedence: subagent overrides agent, agent overrides org default. The three-tier model strategy for a router-first architecture: use Salesforce's HyperClassifier model (model://sfdc_ai__DefaultEinsteinHyperClassifier) for the routing subagent — it is purpose-built for intent classification, extremely fast, and cheap, which reduces routing turn latency. Use a smaller model such as Claude Haiku (model://sfdc_ai__DefaultBedrockAnthropicClaude45Haiku) for simple structured tasks with known answer shapes. Use a larger model such as Gemini Pro or Claude Sonnet (model://sfdc_ai__VertexAIGemini25Pro) for complex CRM reasoning, multi-step analysis, or nuanced customer interactions. Verification: the Gen AI Audit log in Data Cloud records which model was used for each inference call, allowing architects to confirm the intended model routing is actually happening in production.

objectives.title: Understand Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol and Model Context Protocol (MCP) at the architectural level.

topics.question: The A2A protocol: its four layers and how it enables Agentforce to communicate with third-party agents
topics.answer: Agent-to-Agent (A2A) is an emerging open-standard protocol that enables Agentforce agents to communicate with third-party AI agents outside the Salesforce ecosystem. The A2A protocol defines four layers. Capability Discovery: agents advertise their skills and requirements using 'Agent Cards,' allowing other agents to discover what they can do. Task and Execution: agents exchange Tasks containing the request and context; the receiving agent processes and returns an Artifact. Communication: agents negotiate content format and UI capabilities using synchronous, asynchronous (SSE/streaming), or push notification patterns. Security: agents declare their authentication requirements in Agent Cards and clients must authenticate accordingly before task exchange. Architect advisory: A2A is an active area of development. Design current production systems using established patterns (Apex callouts, External Services, Named Credentials). Plan for A2A in architecture discussions but do not take a production dependency without confirming current GA status with Salesforce documentation.

topics.question: The Model Context Protocol (MCP): what it does, where it sits in the architecture, and its security considerations
topics.answer: Model Context Protocol (MCP) is the complementary protocol to A2A. Where A2A defines how agents talk to each other, MCP defines how an agent connects to external tools and services that expose themselves as MCP servers. In the Agentforce context, the MCP Client sits between the agent's action layer and external third-party tools. MCP removes the need to write custom Apex callout classes for every external integration — the external system exposes itself as an MCP server, and Agentforce connects as an MCP client and can discover and invoke its tools dynamically. The MCP management CLI is available as developer preview: 'sf agent mcp create' registers a server, 'sf agent mcp fetch' discovers the server's advertised tools and prompts, and 'sf agent mcp asset replace' whitelistscific assets for agent use. Security: MCP server registration involves OAuth secrets and external server URLs — follow least-privilege principles. The sf agent mcp commands are in developer preview and behavior may change.

topics.question: Supervision versus Superagent orchestration: the distinction and the correct design posture today
topics.answer: Three multi-agent coordination patterns exist at different maturity levels. Router-First (GA, recommended today): routes to one subagent per turn using @utils.transition to — one-way handoff. Supervision / delegation with return (GA, available today): the parent calls a child subagent as an action reference using @subagent.X, the child runs its full reasoning loop, produces a result, and control returns to the parent, which synthesizes the final response. Superagent orchestration (emerging, in active development): an orchestrating agent coordinates multiple specialized agents potentially running tasks concurrently and synthesizing their outputs. The correct design posture today: build for supervision-capable architecture by using @subagent.X delegation with return rather than pure @utils.transition to handoffs wherever the parent needs to synthesize results. This makes current agents composable when multi-agent orchestration patterns mature, without requiring architectural rework.

objectives.title: Identify and remediate the twelve named anti-patterns in Agentforce development.

topics.question: AP-1: Pipe (|) mode with conditional logic — the invisible bug
topics.answer: Anti-Pattern: using | (literal) mode in reasoning.instructions when the block contains if/else conditional logic. The result: the LLM receives the literal text 'if @variables.is_verified == True:' as English prose and attempts to interpret it. Sometimes it follows the intent correctly; often it does not. No error is thrown. This is the most common silent authoring failure. Remediation: always use -> (procedural) mode when the instructions block contains any conditional logic, variable checks, run statements, or set statements. The pipe character (|) then marks only the individual lines of text that should reach the LLM after conditions are evaluated.

topics.question: AP-2: Post-action check at the bottom — the re-resolution trap
topics.answer: Anti-Pattern: placing a post-action result check (such as 'if @variables.order_status != ""') at the BOTTOM of a reasoning.instructions block rather than at the top. When re-resolution fires after a tool call, the resolver reads from the top and the LLM sees the initial instruction ('What is your order number?') again before reaching the result check. This causes double-execution of initial prompts and non-deterministic behavior where the agent asks the user for information it has already retrieved. Remediation: always place post-action conditional checks at the TOP of instructions: -> blocks so they fire first on every re-resolution. The initial user-facing instruction goes below the result check and is only visible to the LLM when no result yet exists.

topics.question: AP-3: Prose-based authorization — the security failure
topics.answer: Anti-Pattern: using a prose instruction in reasoning.instructions to restrict action access ('Only call the refund action if the customer is verified') instead of using available when. The LLM may or may not follow prose authorization instructions depending on context and phrasing — this is probabilistic security. A sufficiently crafted user input can sometimes convince the LLM to ignore prose restrictions. Remediation: always use 'available when @variables.is_verified == True' on any action with financial impact, PII access, or irreversible effects. available when is a hard Phase 1 filter — unauthorized tool invocation becomes structurally impossible, not just discouraged. Prose instructions and available when can be used together for defense-in-depth, but never rely on prose alone for security.

topics.question: AP-4: @inputs used after action execution — the silent failure
topics.answer: Anti-Pattern: using 'set @variables.X = @inputs.paramName' after the action's run block has completed. The @inputs scope expires immediately after the with clauses during action invocation. Any reference to @inputs.X in a set statement after the run block silently fails — the variable is not set, no error is thrown, and the FunctionStep trace shows no output capture in postVars. Remediation: use @outputs for post-action value capture (the action's return values), and @variables for values that need to persist. If the input value itself needs to be preserved, capture it to a @variables before the action call using a separate set statement.

topics.question: AP-5: instructions: wrapper in lifecycle hooks — the compile error
topics.answer: Anti-Pattern: wrapping before_reasoning or after_reasoning content in an 'instructions: ->' block. These lifecycle hooks do not support the instructions: wrapper syntax. Using it causes a compilation error. Remediation: place transition, run, set, and if statements as direct children of the before_reasoning or after_reasoning block with no instructions wrapper. The hooks support the same deterministic operations as procedural mode instructions, but without the wrapper keyword.

topics.question: AP-6: Wrong transition syntax in wrong context — the compile error
topics.answer: Anti-Pattern: placing @utils.transition to in a directive block (before_reasoning or after_reasoning) or placing bare transition to in a reasoning.actions block. Both combinations are compile errors. The correct pairings: bare 'transition to @subagent.X' is valid only in before_reasoning, after_reasoning, and inside run post-conditions. '@utils.transition to @subagent.X' is valid only in reasoning.actions. Mixing these produces compile errors with unhelpful messages that can be difficult to diagnose without knowing this rule.

topics.question: AP-7: After-reasoning router transition trap — the logic bug
topics.answer: Anti-Pattern: a gate subagent that transitions to a router via after_reasoning, causing the router to receive and attempt to classify the user's previous utterance (which was appropriate for the gate, not for routing). For example, if the gate collected an email address, the router receives 'My email is john@example.com' as the message to route, and routes it incorrectly. Remediation: add an explicit instruction in the router's reasoning block handling the post-gate state: 'If the customer just completed a setup step, greet them and ask what they need — do NOT route their previous message.' This gives the router the context to recognize it has received a post-gate transition and ask fresh.

topics.question: AP-8: Contradicting system and reasoning instructions — undefined behavior
topics.answer: Anti-Pattern: the global system.instructions says 'Answer the user's questions helpfully' while a router subagent's reasoning.instructions says 'Do not answer. Route only.' The LLM receives both simultaneously as part of the same system context and resolves the conflict in undefined ways — one instruction will win, but which one is unpredictable across turns and model updates. Remediation: write global system instructions that permit the posture of every subagent: 'Perform only the current operating task. Answer only when the task calls for an answer. Otherwise route, verify, or escalate as directed.' This is neutral toward all subagent postures and allows each subagent's reasoning.instructions to define the actual behavior without contradiction.

topics.question: AP-9: @utils.setVariables followed by immediate action — the turn-end trap
topics.answer: Anti-Pattern: listing @utils.setVariables and an action in the same reasoning.actions block, expecting the action to fire in the same turn after variables are collected. setVariables ends the turn after capturing values — the subsequent action never fires in the same turn. Remediation: use the ellipsis slot-fill operator directly on the target action ('with order_id = ...') instead of first collecting the value via setVariables and then looking it up. The LLM extracts the value and calls the action in one turn, achieving the same result without the turn-end side effect.

topics.question: AP-10: Vague action descriptions leading to wrong tool selection
topics.answer: Anti-Pattern: using generic descriptions such as 'Get data' or 'Look up information' for actions in the reasoning.actions block. The LLM uses the description as its primary signal for tool selection — vague descriptions make it impossible to reliably distinguish between similar actions and lead to wrong tool invocation or hallucinated parameters. Remediation: write descriptions that are specific enough for unambiguous LLM selection. Include: what the action retrieves or does, the specific data it returns, the parameter it requires, and any relevant context about when to use it.
